teile.einleitung: French is spoken not only in France but on several continents. The community of these countries and people is called the Francophonie. Switzerland belongs to it too.
wichtigste: The Francophonie links countries where French plays an important role.
The organisation for it is called the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie, OIF for short.
Most people who speak French every day live in Africa.
International Francophonie Day is on 20 March.
French is an official language in, for example, Belgium, Canada, Monaco and Haiti.
In 2010 the Francophonie summit took place in Montreux.

abschnitte.text: **Francophonie** means all the people and countries that speak French. There is also an organisation for it: the **Organisation internationale de la Francophonie**, **OIF** for short. It links states in which French plays an important role. Switzerland is a member. According to the organisation, the majority of people who speak French every day live in **Africa**, and their share is growing.

In **Belgium** French is spoken in the south, in Wallonia, Dutch in the north and also German in the east. In Canada the province of **Quebec** is French-speaking; there French is the only official language. The small principality of **Monaco** lies on the Mediterranean and has French as its official language. In the Caribbean, **Haiti** is a former French colony. There French and Haitian Creole are official languages.

On **20 March 1970** a forerunner organisation was founded in **Niamey**, the capital of Niger. The OIF later grew out of it. That is why **International Francophonie Day** is celebrated every year on 20 March. One of the founding fathers is considered to be the Senegalese poet and president **Léopold Sédar Senghor**. Together with politicians from Tunisia, Niger and Cambodia, he worked to create this community.

In Switzerland French is spoken in the **Romandie**, French-speaking western Switzerland. The cantons of Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel and Jura are French-speaking. Bern, Fribourg and Valais are **bilingual**. In October 2010 the Francophonie summit took place in **Montreux**. Heads of state and government of the member countries met there.

gewusst: In 1983 Senghor became the first African member of the Académie française.
The capital of the province of Quebec is also called Quebec.

teile.einleitung: “Le Petit Prince”, in English “The Little Prince”, is one of the best-known books in the world. Antoine de Saint-Exupéry wrote it and illustrated it himself. It tells of a boy from a faraway asteroid and is a fairy tale for children and adults.
wichtigste: The book first appeared in New York in April 1943, and in France only in 1946.
Antoine de Saint-Exupéry was a writer and a pilot.
The little prince comes from asteroid B 612.
The narrator meets him after an emergency landing in the Sahara.
The fox says: “On ne voit bien qu'avec le cœur.”
“Apprivoiser” means to tame or to make familiar.
Saint-Exupéry disappeared in 1944 on a reconnaissance flight over the Mediterranean.

abschnitte.text: **Antoine de Saint-Exupéry** was a writer and a **pilot**. Among other things, he flew mail planes over the Sahara and the Andes. These experiences shape many of his books, including “Le Petit Prince”. During the Second World War he lived in exile in the **USA**. There the book appeared in **New York** in April 1943, in English and French. In France it was only published in 1946.

abschnitte.titel: A hat that isn't a hat
abschnitte.text: The book begins with a drawing the narrator made as a child. It shows a **giant snake**, a boa, that has swallowed an **elephant**. But the grown-ups only see a hat in it. Disappointed, the narrator gives up drawing. Already here the book shows that adults often miss what really matters.

As an adult, the narrator has to make an emergency landing with his plane in the **Sahara**. He has water for about eight days. Suddenly a little boy stands in front of him and asks: “**Dessine-moi un mouton.**” Draw me a sheep! The narrator suspects that the prince comes from asteroid **B 612**. There are volcanoes there, baobab trees and a **rose** that the prince loves.

On his journey the prince visits various planets with strange grown-ups. On Earth he meets the **fox**. The fox asks the prince to tame him, in French “**apprivoiser**”. For the fox this means “créer des liens”, to create ties. When they say goodbye, he reveals his secret: “**On ne voit bien qu'avec le cœur. L'essentiel est invisible pour les yeux.**” One sees clearly only with the heart; what is essential is invisible to the eye.

On 31 July 1944 Saint-Exupéry set off on a **reconnaissance flight** over the Mediterranean and did not return. For a long time nobody knew what had happened to him. Only in 2003 were parts of his plane recovered from the sea off **Marseille**. His book lives on: it has been translated into a great many languages, including Swiss German.

gewusst: Saint-Exupéry painted the pictures in the book himself with watercolours.
The sentence about what is essential being invisible to the eye is one of the best-known sentences in world literature.

teile.einleitung: **Australia** is a country and at the same time a whole continent in the Southern Hemisphere. It is known for kangaroos, koalas, vast deserts and the largest coral reef in the world. The main language is English.
wichtigste: Australia lies in the Southern Hemisphere between the Indian and Pacific Oceans.
The capital is Canberra; the largest city is Sydney.
The Great Barrier Reef is the largest coral reef in the world.
The kangaroo and the emu support Australia's coat of arms.
The Aboriginal peoples have lived in Australia for more than 50,000 years.
At Christmas it is summer in Australia.

abschnitte.text: Australia is about **186 times the size of Switzerland**, but a large part of the interior is dry desert and scrubland, known as the **Outback**. Most people live on the coasts. The largest city is **Sydney**, with its famous Opera House and Harbour Bridge. The capital, however, is **Canberra**, which was built specially for this purpose. People pay with the **Australian dollar**.

Australia is home to many animals that are found nowhere else. They include **kangaroos**, **koalas** and **wombats**. They are **marsupials**: their young grow up in a pouch on the mother's tummy. The **emu** is a large running bird that cannot fly. The kangaroo and the emu can be seen on Australia's coat of arms.

Off the north-east coast lies the **Great Barrier Reef**, the largest coral reef on Earth. It is more than 2,000 kilometres long and can even be seen from space. Countless fish, turtles and other sea creatures live there. The reef is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Warmer sea water harms the corals, which can then bleach.

The first inhabitants of Australia are the **Aboriginal peoples**. They have lived on the continent for more than 50,000 years and have a very ancient culture with rock paintings, songs and stories. The **boomerang** and the wind instrument called the **didgeridoo** are well known. From 1788 British settlers arrived, which brought great suffering to the Aboriginal peoples. By the way, the Māori are the indigenous people of New Zealand, not of Australia.

Because Australia lies in the **Southern Hemisphere**, its seasons are the opposite of ours. In December it is **summer** there. Many families celebrate Christmas with a picnic or a barbecue on the beach. In July, on the other hand, it is winter, and there can even be snow in the mountains in the south-east.

gewusst: The great red rock of **Uluru** in the middle of Australia is a sacred place for the Aboriginal peoples.
More kangaroos than people live in Australia.

teile.einleitung: Basic English vocabulary covers the words you need most often in everyday life: numbers, colours, days, months, animals, family and things in the house. With a few thousand words you can already understand most simple texts and conversations. Many English words are related to German ones, which makes them easy for German speakers to remember.
wichtigste: The Swiss “Velo” is a “bicycle” or “bike” in English.
“Kitchen” means “Küche” in German, and “grandmother” means “Grossmutter”.
The German “Mittwoch” is “Wednesday” in English.
In English, too, August is followed by September.
The opposite of “expensive” is “cheap”.
Many English words are related to German ones, for example “house” and “Haus”.
In English, days of the week and months are always written with a capital letter.

abschnitte.text: **Basic vocabulary** is the collection of the most important and most frequent words of a language. Experts estimate that the roughly 2000 most frequent English words cover a large part of everyday texts. They include small words such as “the”, “and” or “is”, but also everyday words such as “school” or “friend”. If you know these words well, you can guess a lot from the context.

In the house there is the “kitchen”, the “bedroom” and the “bathroom”. The family includes “mother”, “father”, “sister”, “brother” and the **“grandmother”**. Things such as “table”, “chair” and “window” also belong to basic vocabulary. Many of these words are needed every day.

Animals and nature come up early in almost every textbook. The German “Schmetterling” is a **“butterfly”**, “Wolke” is “cloud” and “Sonne” is “sun”. Pets are “dog”, “cat” and “rabbit”. The Swiss “Rüebli” is a “carrot” in English, and the German “Kartoffel” is a “potato”.

The days of the week are Monday, Tuesday, **Wednesday**, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday. Wednesday is the German “Mittwoch”, and it is pronounced roughly “wenz-day”. The months are very similar to the German ones: August is followed by September. In English, days of the week and months are always written with a capital letter.

Many words are best learnt as **pairs of opposites**. “Expensive” goes with “cheap”, “big” with “small” and “hot” with “cold”. Pairs like these stay in your memory more easily. You can also link them with little drawings or movements.

English and German are both **Germanic languages** and are therefore related. That is why “hand” and “Hand” or “water” and “Wasser” are similar. But watch out for **false friends**: “become” means “werden” in German and not “bekommen” (to get), and the German word “Gift” means poison, while the English “gift” is a present. The Swiss word “Velo”, by the way, comes from French; in English you say “bicycle” or “bike”.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single word of a foreign language that you learn.
The most important and most frequent words of a language.
A word that looks like a word in another language but means something different.
The language family that German, English, Dutch and the Scandinavian languages belong to.

gewusst: English took over a great many words from French after the Normans conquered England in 1066.
The name “Wednesday” recalls the Germanic god Woden.
The word “the” is one of the most frequent words in the English language.

teile.einleitung: The indefinite article corresponds to the English “a” or “an” and the German “ein” or “eine”. In French there are “un”, “une” and, in the plural, “des”.
wichtigste: Before masculine words, “a” is “un” in French.
Before feminine words you use “une”.
The plural of un and une is “des”.
In the plural the noun usually gets an s: des ballons.
The gender is often different from German: “une pomme”, but “der Apfel”.
Nothing is shortened before “un” and “une”: “un ami”.

abschnitte.text: The **indefinite article** stands in front of a noun when you mention something for the first time or do not say exactly which one you mean. For masculine words it is **un**: un chien (a dog), un vélo (a bike). For feminine words it is **une**: une fille (a girl), une voiture (a car). By the way, “un” and “une” are also the number one.

In French the gender of a word is often different from German. “Der Apfel” (the apple) is masculine in German, but in French it is **une pomme**. “Die Tasche” (the bag) is feminine, but in French it is **un sac**. “Das Auto” (the car) is **une voiture**. French has only two genders, masculine and feminine. There is no neuter gender as in German.

In the plural, un and une both become **des**. “Un ballon” (a ball) becomes “des ballons”, “une fille” becomes “des filles”. The noun usually gets an **s**, but you cannot hear it. That is why, when speaking, you recognise the plural mainly from the article. In English and German the article is simply left out in the plural: “balls”, “Bälle”.

With the definite article, “le” becomes l' before a vowel: l'ami. With the indefinite article this does **not** happen. You say “**un ami**” (a friend, male) and “**une amie**” (a friend, female). When speaking, however, you link the n to the following word: “un-nami”. This link is called a **liaison**.

gewusst: With “Il y a” you say “there is” (in Swiss German “Es hat”), for example “Il y a une fille dans le jardin” (there is a girl in the garden).
In French the word “vélo” is a short form of “vélocipède”.

teile.einleitung: Victor Hugo (1802 to 1885) is one of the most famous writers in France. He wrote novels, poems and plays and fought for justice and against the death penalty.
wichtigste: Victor Hugo is seen as the most important poet of French Romanticism.
His novel “Les Misérables” appeared in 1862; its main character is the former convict Jean Valjean.
In “Notre-Dame de Paris” from 1831 lives the hunchbacked bell-ringer Quasimodo.
After Napoleon III's coup of 1851 Hugo lived in exile for many years, mostly on Guernsey.
All his life he fought against the death penalty.
After his death in 1885 he was given a state funeral and buried in the Panthéon.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century young artists wanted to break free from the strict rules of **classical** theatre. Victor Hugo became their spokesman. In the **preface to “Cromwell”** of 1827 he called for the sublime and the grotesque to be combined. It is seen as the manifesto of French **Romanticism**. At the first performance of his play “Hernani” at the Comédie-Française in 1830, classicists and Romantics argued loudly. This evening is called the **Bataille d'Hernani** (the battle of Hernani).

In 1831 the novel **“Notre-Dame de Paris”** (known in English as The Hunchback of Notre-Dame) appeared. At its centre is **Quasimodo**, the deformed bell-ringer of the cathedral, who loves the dancer Esmeralda. The novel made the cathedral famous. It helped the building, which was neglected at the time, to be valued again and later restored. The story has been filmed many times, including as an animated film.

Hugo's best-known work is **“Les Misérables”** of 1862, “The Wretched” in English. The main character is **Jean Valjean**. He is released after 19 years in prison, where he was sent for stealing a loaf of bread and kept for his attempts to escape. The police inspector **Javert** pursues him for decades. The novel tells of poverty, injustice and the strength to become a better person.

Hugo was also a politician. After the **coup** by Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, later Napoleon III, he went into **exile** in 1851. First he lived in Brussels and on Jersey, then from 1855 on the Channel Island of **Guernsey**. There he lived in Hauteville House. Only after the end of the Second Empire in 1870 did he return to France.

As early as 1829 Hugo wrote **“Le Dernier Jour d'un condamné”** (The Last Day of a Condemned Man). This short novel describes the last hours of a condemned man from his own point of view. All his life Hugo campaigned against the **death penalty**. He also wrote famous poems. In “Demain, dès l'aube” (Tomorrow, at dawn) from the collection “Les Contemplations”, he describes the way to the grave of his daughter **Léopoldine**, who had drowned in the Seine in 1843. In 1885 hundreds of thousands followed his funeral procession to the **Panthéon**.

gewusst: For Hugo's funeral the Panthéon was turned back into a secular hall of fame for France's great figures.
“Les Misérables” became one of the most successful musicals in the world.

teile.einleitung: Most French verbs end in -er in the infinitive, for example parler, jouer or manger. Almost all of them follow the same pattern, and if you know it you can conjugate a great many verbs.
wichtigste: For the present tense you remove -er and add the endings -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent.
Example: je parle, tu parles, il parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils parlent.
The forms for je, tu, il and ils sound the same, because -es and -ent are not pronounced.
With verbs ending in -ger you write an e before -ons: nous mangeons.
With verbs ending in -cer the c gets a cédille: nous commençons.
“Aller” ends in -er, but it is completely irregular.

abschnitte.text: A verb consists of a **stem** and an **ending**. In “parler” (to speak) the stem is “parl-”. For the present tense you add these endings: je parl**e**, tu parl**es**, il parl**e**, nous parl**ons**, vous parl**ez**, ils parl**ent**. It works like this with almost all verbs ending in -er: jouer (to play), regarder (to watch), habiter (to live), chanter (to sing) and many more.

abschnitte.titel: What you hear and what you don't
abschnitte.text: Many endings are written but not heard. The s in “tu manges” and the -ent in “ils jouent” are **silent**. That is why je parle, tu parles, il parle and ils parlent sound **exactly the same**. Only the endings for nous (-ons) and vous (-ez) can be heard. The ending -ez is pronounced like a closed e, a bit like the vowel in “day”.

Verbs like **manger** (to eat) have a small special feature. Before a, o and u, g would sound hard as in “go”. That is why with nous you insert an **e**: “nous mangeons” (we eat). This keeps the g soft, like the s in “measure”. In the same way you write “nous nageons” (we swim) and “nous voyageons” (we travel).

With verbs like **commencer** (to begin), the c before a, o and u would sound like k. So that it still sounds like s, it gets a little hook, the **cédille**: ç. That is why you write “nous commençons” (we begin). The same applies to “nous avançons” (we move forward) and “nous lançons” (we throw). In all the other forms you do not need the cédille: je commence, vous commencez.

Not every verb ending in -er is regular. **Aller** (to go) is conjugated quite differently: je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont. It is the only verb ending in -er that departs so far from the rule. All the others follow the pattern, sometimes with small changes in spelling.

gewusst: About nine out of ten French verbs end in -er.
New verbs in French almost always get the ending -er, for example “surfer” or “cliquer” (to click).

teile.einleitung: A question tag is a little question at the end of a sentence, like “nicht wahr?” or “oder?” in German. In English it depends on the auxiliary verb and the subject of the sentence.
wichtigste: A question tag is a short question added on, like “nicht wahr?” in German.
A positive sentence is followed by a negative tag: You're from Zurich, aren't you?
A negative sentence is followed by a positive tag: She doesn't like coffee, does she?
You take the auxiliary from the sentence, otherwise do, does or did.
With I'm the tag is aren't I.
Let's is followed by shall we, an order often by will you.
Never and nobody count as negatives, so a positive tag follows.

abschnitte.text: A **question tag** is a short question that you add to a statement. You use it to get **confirmation** or to make a conversation friendlier. In German people simply say “oder?” or “nicht wahr?”. In English, however, the tag changes depending on the sentence. It consists of an **auxiliary verb** and a **pronoun**.

The most important rule: if the sentence is **positive**, the tag is **negative**. “You're from Zurich, **aren't you**?” If the sentence is **negative**, the tag is **positive**. “She doesn't like coffee, **does she**?” Words such as **never**, **nobody** or nothing make a sentence negative. That is why it is “She never eats meat, **does she**?”

In the tag you repeat the **auxiliary verb** from the sentence. “He has finished his homework, **hasn't he**?” “You can swim, can't you?” If the sentence has no auxiliary, you use **do, does** or **did**: “You like pizza, don't you?” The subject is replaced by a pronoun. With **nobody** or **everybody** you use **they**: “Nobody called, did they?”

Some tags have to be remembered. With **I'm** the standard tag is **aren't I**: “I'm late, aren't I?” **Let's** is followed by **shall we**: “Let's go, shall we?” After an **order**, **will you** often fits: “Open the window, will you?” This sounds friendlier than a plain order.

How you pronounce a tag changes its meaning. If your voice goes **down** at the end, you are sure and just expect agreement. If your voice goes **up**, it is a real question, because you are unsure. So the same sentence can be almost a statement one time and a question another time.

gewusst: In parts of England, instead of many different tags you often just hear “innit”, a casual form of isn't it.
Question tags are typical of British English. Americans often simply say “right?”.

teile.einleitung: In the Romandie people speak French, but not quite in the same way as in Paris. Some numbers, meals and everyday words are typically Swiss.
wichtigste: In Switzerland people say “septante” for 70 and “nonante” for 90.
In France 70 is “soixante-dix” and 90 “quatre-vingt-dix”.
“Huitante” for 80 is said mainly in Vaud, Valais and Fribourg.
In Geneva, Neuchâtel and the Jura people usually say “quatre-vingts” for 80.
In the Romandie “le dîner” is lunch and “le souper” is supper.
Typically Swiss words are “natel” for a mobile phone and “cornet” for a carrier bag.

abschnitte.text: In France counting from 70 onwards is a bit complicated. 70 is **soixante-dix**, sixty and ten. 90 is **quatre-vingt-dix**, four times twenty plus ten. In Switzerland and Belgium people say the simpler **septante** for 70 and **nonante** for 90. So 99, for example, becomes “nonante-neuf”.

For the number 80 many people in **Vaud**, **Valais** and **Fribourg** say “huitante”. In **Geneva**, **Neuchâtel** and the **Jura**, on the other hand, you usually hear the French “quatre-vingts”. So the numbers are not even the same across the whole Romandie. But both forms are understood everywhere.

In the Romandie breakfast is called **le déjeuner**, lunch **le dîner** and supper **le souper**. In France it is different: there “le petit-déjeuner” is breakfast, “le déjeuner” lunch and “le dîner” the evening meal. So if you are invited to “dîner” in Paris, you should not come until the evening.

In Switzerland a mobile phone is often called a **natel**; in France it is “le portable”. At the till you ask for **un cornet** if you want a carrier bag. In France you say “un sac”. If a room is untidy, people in the Romandie exclaim: “Quel **cheni** !” The word is also spelt “chenit” and means mess.

gewusst: Words that are used in this way only in Switzerland are called Helvetisms.
In Belgium people also say “septante” and “nonante”, but usually “quatre-vingts” for 80.

teile.einleitung: The subjonctif (subjunctive) is a special verb form in French. You need it after expressions of wanting, having to and feeling, and after certain conjunctions.
wichtigste: The subjonctif usually appears in a subordinate clause that begins with “que”.
It follows expressions such as “il faut que”, “je veux que” or “je suis content que”.
The subjonctif is also used after conjunctions such as “bien que” and “avant que”.
The stem of regular verbs comes from the “ils” form in the present: ils finissent, que je finisse.
The endings are -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent.
A positive “je pense que” requires the indicative: “Je pense qu'il a raison.”

abschnitte.text: The **subjonctif** does not express a fact, but a wish, a necessity, a feeling or a doubt. It is almost always in a subordinate clause after **que**. Typical triggers are “il faut que” (it is necessary that), “je veux que” (I want … to) and “je suis content que” (I am glad that). An example: “Il faut que vous finissiez ce travail.” (You must finish this work.)

With regular verbs you take the **3rd person plural** of the present indicative. You remove the ending “-ent” and add **-e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent**. So “ils finissent” becomes “que je finisse”, “que nous finissions”, “que vous finissiez”. “Ils parlent” becomes “que je parle”. With many verbs, the forms for je, tu, il and ils sound the same as in the present.

Some important verbs have their own stem. **Faire** forms all its forms with “fass-”: que je fasse, que nous fassions. **Savoir** has “sach-”: qu'il sache. **Aller** has two stems, “aill-” for je, tu, il and ils, but “all-” for nous and vous: que j'aille, que nous allions. **Être** is que je sois, que tu sois, qu'il soit. **Avoir** is que j'aie, qu'il ait.

Certain conjunctions always require the subjonctif. They include **bien que** (although), **avant que** (before), **pour que** (so that) and **à condition que** (on condition that). That is why you say “Je pars avant qu'il pleuve.” (I am leaving before it rains.) Other conjunctions such as “parce que” (because), “pendant que” (while) and “puisque” (since), on the other hand, take the **indicative**.

After a positive **penser que** or **croire que** (to think that, to believe that) the indicative is used, because you are convinced of something: “Je pense qu'il a raison.” (I think he is right.) If the sentence is **negative** or a question, you are less sure. Then the subjonctif is usually used: “Je ne pense pas qu'il ait raison.” (I don't think he is right.) This rule shows nicely that the subjonctif has to do with uncertainty.

gewusst: German has a similar form, the Konjunktiv, but it is used much less often.
The subjonctif forms of “finir”, such as “que nous finissions”, look exactly the same as the forms in the imparfait.

teile.einleitung: Adjectives describe what something is like: small, black, happy. In French they adapt to the noun they belong to. They change depending on whether the noun is masculine or feminine, singular or plural.
wichtigste: For the feminine form you usually add an e: petit becomes petite.
For the plural you usually add an s: noir becomes noirs.
Adjectives ending in -eux become -euse in the feminine: heureux, heureuse.
Adjectives ending in -if become -ive in the feminine: sportif, sportive.
Some are irregular: beau becomes belle, blanc becomes blanche.
If an adjective already ends in a silent e, it stays the same: rouge.

abschnitte.text: The adjective agrees with the **noun**. If the noun is feminine, the adjective usually gets an **e**: “une **petite** maison” (a small house). If the noun is plural, an **s** is added: “des chats **noirs**” (black cats). If it is feminine and plural, both are added: “des robes **noires**” (black dresses). You often cannot hear the extra e or s at all, but you must write it.

Some endings change in the feminine form. Adjectives ending in **-eux** become **-euse**: “un garçon heureux”, “une fille **heureuse**” (a happy boy, a happy girl). Adjectives ending in **-if** become **-ive**: “un garçon sportif”, “des filles **sportives**” (a sporty boy, sporty girls). With some adjectives the last letter is doubled. So “gentil” (kind) becomes **gentille**, and “bon” (good) becomes bonne.

Some adjectives have to be learnt by heart. **Beau** (beautiful) becomes **belle**: “une belle journée” (a beautiful day). **Blanc** (white) becomes **blanche**: “une robe blanche” (a white dress). It is similar with “vieux” (old), which is “vieille” in the feminine, and with “nouveau” (new), which becomes “nouvelle”.

If an adjective already ends in a **silent e**, it does not get an extra e. That is why you say “un pull **rouge**” (a red jumper) and “une veste **rouge**” (a red jacket). It is the same with “jaune” (yellow), “rapide” (fast) or “facile” (easy). In the plural, however, an s is still added: “des pulls rouges”. A tip: in French most adjectives come **after** the noun; short, common ones such as petit or beau come before it.

gewusst: Before a masculine noun beginning with a vowel, “beau” becomes “bel”: “un bel arbre” (a beautiful tree).
With “petit” you can hear the difference: the t is silent in “petit”, but in “petite” it is pronounced.

teile.einleitung: A hobby is something you like doing in your free time. Talking about hobbies in English is a good topic for first conversations, because almost everyone has something they enjoy.
wichtigste: With “What is your hobby?” you ask about someone's hobby.
With “I like” and a verb ending in -ing you say what you like doing: I like swimming.
Reading means lesen, dancing tanzen and painting malen.
To play football is play football, to ride a bike is ride a bike.
With musical instruments you use the: play the piano.
With ball sports there is no the: play football, play tennis.

abschnitte.text: If you want to know what someone likes doing, you ask: **“What is your hobby?”** or **“What do you do in your free time?”** The answer might be: “My hobby is reading.” You can also ask: “Do you like dancing?” The short answer is then “Yes, I do” or “No, I don't”.

To say what you like doing, you use **I like** and a verb with the ending **-ing**. “I like swimming” means that you enjoy swimming. “I like painting” means that you enjoy painting. **I love** works in the same way for something you like doing very much, and **I don't like** for something you do not enjoy. Here the -ing form acts like a noun.

With many sports you use **play**: **play football**, play tennis, play basketball. There is no the here. In Great Britain the game is called **football**; in the USA people say **soccer**. For a bike you say **ride a bike**, using the same verb as for riding a horse. Other sports are named just with -ing: swimming, skiing or running.

With musical instruments there is **the** before the instrument: **play the piano**, play the guitar. If you like singing, you say “I like singing”. **Painting** means making pictures with paint, **drawing** making pictures with pencils or pens. **Dancing** is also a popular hobby for many children.

Not all hobbies are sporty. **Reading**, **cooking** and **baking** are popular too. If you like collecting things, you say “I collect stamps”. **Playing computer games** and **listening to music** are also common answers. **Hiking** is very popular in Switzerland, with its many footpaths.

gewusst: The English word hobby comes from an old word for a small horse, which gave its name to the toy hobby horse.
In German people also say “Hobby”; the word was borrowed from English.

teile.einleitung: Halloween is celebrated every year on 31 October, the evening before All Saints' Day. Children dress up, go from house to house and collect sweets. You can learn lots of words to do with this festival in English lessons.
wichtigste: Halloween is on 31 October, the evening before All Saints' Day.
The name comes from “All Hallows' Eve”, the evening before All Saints' Day.
Its roots are in Ireland and Scotland; from there the festival came to North America.
The carved pumpkin lantern is called a jack-o'-lantern.
At the front door children call out “Trick or treat!”.
Important words: pumpkin means Kürbis, witch means Hexe and ghost means Gespenst.

abschnitte.text: The name Halloween is a shortened form of **All Hallows' Eve**. This means “the evening before All Saints' Day”, because 1 November is **All Saints' Day**. The customs have old roots in Ireland and Scotland. There, at this time of year, the Celts celebrated the festival of **Samhain**, the beginning of the dark season. Emigrants later took the customs to North America, where Halloween became very big.

The best-known symbol of Halloween is the **jack-o'-lantern**. You hollow out a **pumpkin** and carve a face into it. Then you put a candle or a light inside. In Ireland people used to carve turnips; in America they then used the bigger pumpkins. The name comes from an old Irish legend about a man called Jack.

In the evening children go from door to door in costume. They call out **“Trick or treat!”**. A **treat** is something nice to eat, a **trick** is a prank. Usually the children get **sweets** or, as people say in America, **candy**. Luckily a trick is only rarely played.

Many characters belong to Halloween. A **witch** is a Hexe, a **ghost** a Gespenst. A **skeleton** is a Skelett, a **bat** a Fledermaus and a **spider** a Spinne. The outfit is called a **costume**. If something frightens you, you say “That's scary!”.

In Switzerland Halloween has only been widespread since the 1990s. Today you see pumpkins and costumes in many shops in October. But a similar custom has existed here for a long time: in November children walk through the streets with **Räbeliechtli**. These are hollowed-out turnips with patterns carved into them and a candle inside, very much like the old Irish turnip lanterns.

gewusst: The first Halloween lanterns in Ireland were made of turnips, not pumpkins.
The word “Eve” in All Hallows' Eve means the evening before, as in Christmas Eve.

t191j4yz.t: Parts of the body in English

teile.einleitung: Parts of the body are among the first words people learn in English. You need them at the doctor's, in sport and when you describe someone.
wichtigste: Head means Kopf, eye means Auge.
Nose means Nase, ear means Ohr, mouth means Mund.
Leg means Bein, foot means Fuss.
The plural of foot is feet.
Hair means Haare and is usually singular: My hair is long.
With parts of the body English uses my, your or his: I brush my teeth.

abschnitte.text: The **head** is the Kopf. On the **face** are the **eyes** and the **nose**. With your **mouth** you speak and eat. Inside it are your **teeth** and your **tongue**. On the sides of your head are your **ears**.

The head sits on the **neck**. Below it are the **shoulders**. The **arms**, **hands** and **fingers** come next. The belly is called the **tummy** or **stomach**, and the Rücken is called the **back**. The **legs** are the Beine, the **knees** the Knie.

Most parts of the body form the plural with s: eye becomes eyes, hand becomes hands. But there are exceptions. **Foot** becomes **feet**, **tooth** becomes **teeth**. The word **hair** is usually not counted. You say “My hair **is** long”, even though there are lots of hairs. A single hair is “a hair”.

In German people say “Ich putze mir die Zähne” (I clean to me the teeth). In English you use **my** for this: “I brush **my** teeth.” Likewise: “Wash **your** hands!” and “He hurt **his** leg.” So with parts of the body there is almost always a **possessive determiner**, not the. This is a common mistake when translating.

If something hurts, you say **“My … hurts”**: “My head hurts” or “My foot hurts”. For certain pains there are special words with **ache**: headache, toothache and stomach ache. So “I've got a headache” means your head hurts. That way you can explain what is wrong even when you are on holiday.

gewusst: The song “Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes” helps children all over the world learn the parts of the body in English.
Zehen are called toes in English, and the big one is called the big toe.

teile.einleitung: With reported speech you pass on what someone else has said without quoting them word for word. In English you often shift the tense and adjust words for time and place.
wichtigste: In reported speech you give what was said without quotation marks.
After said or told the tense often moves one step back: am becomes was.
Will becomes would, can becomes could.
Tomorrow becomes the next day, here often becomes there.
Yes-no questions are introduced with if or whether.
In indirect questions the normal word order is used: where I lived.
Orders are reported with told and to: told us to close the door.

abschnitte.text: In **direct speech** you write exactly what someone said: “I am tired,” she said. In **reported speech** you tell it afterwards: She said that she was tired. You can also leave out the word **that**. With **say** you simply report what someone said. With **tell** you need a person as well: “She told me that she was busy.”

If the introducing verb is in the past, the tense often moves one step back. This is called **backshift**. Am or is becomes **was**, will becomes **would**, can becomes **could**. So “I will call you” becomes “He said that he would call me”. “I can swim” becomes “She said that she could swim”.

Words for time and place often change too. If something is reported later, **tomorrow** becomes **the next day** and **yesterday** becomes the day before. **Today** becomes that day. If you report it in a different place, **here** becomes **there**. That way the sentence stays clear for the listeners.

For **questions** you use asked. Question words such as where or what stay, but the word order becomes that of a normal statement: “Where do you live?” becomes “He asked me **where I lived**”. The auxiliary do disappears. For **yes-no questions** you need **if** or **whether**: “She asked if I was coming.”

Orders and requests are reported with **tell** or **ask** and **to** with the basic form. “Close the door!” becomes “The teacher told us **to close** the door”. A request becomes “She asked me to help her”. In the negative, **not** comes before to: “He told me not to be late.” Here the tense does not change.

gewusst: If what was said is still true, you can often keep the tense: “He said that Bern is the federal city.”
If the introducing verb is in the present, for example “She says”, the tense is not shifted at all.

teile.einleitung: With possessive words you show whom something belongs to. In English there are two groups: possessive determiners such as my stand before a noun, possessive pronouns such as mine stand on their own.
wichtigste: Possessive determiners come before a noun: my book, your bike.
The determiners are my, your, his, her, its, our and their.
Possessive pronouns stand without a noun: It is mine.
The pronouns are mine, yours, his, hers, ours and theirs.
Its means “belonging to it” for animals and things: The dog is wagging its tail.
Its without an apostrophe is not the same as it's, which means it is.

abschnitte.text: If you want to say whom something belongs to, you have two options. **Possessive determiners** come directly before a noun: “This is **my** book.” **Possessive pronouns** replace the noun and stand alone: “It is **mine**.” Both sentences say almost the same thing. But the pronoun means you do not have to repeat the noun.

Each person has its own **determiner**. I goes with **my**, you with **your**, he with **his**, she with **her** and it with **its**. We goes with **our**, they with **their**. Your is used for one person and for several, like the German du, Sie and ihr. In English these words never change, whatever noun follows.

The **possessive pronouns** are **mine, yours, his, hers, ours** and **theirs**. “That bike belongs to Lisa. It's **hers**.” “The house belongs to us. It's **ours**.” “This isn't my jacket. It's **his**.” With his, the determiner and pronoun are the same. Most of the other pronouns end in s; only mine does not.

For animals and things you use **its**: “The dog is wagging **its** tail.” The word has **no apostrophe**. With an apostrophe, **it's** is something quite different, namely the short form of it is or it has. This mix-up happens even to people whose first language is English. A trick: if you can put in it is, you need the apostrophe.

Possessive pronouns never have an apostrophe: it is **yours**, **hers** and **ours**, not your's or her's. Also, no noun follows a pronoun. You say “It's mine”, but not “It's mine book”. In German people say “Das ist meins” or “Das gehört mir” (that belongs to me), which helps you remember.

gewusst: If you want to say with a name whom something belongs to, you add 's: Lisa's bike.
Its used as a possessive pronoun without a noun hardly ever occurs in English.

teile.einleitung: A greeting is the first thing you say when you meet someone. Every language has its own words for it, for example “Hello” in English and “Bonjour” in French. If you greet people properly, you make a friendly first impression.
wichtigste: The German “Hallo” is “Hello” in English, or informally “Hi”.
The German “Guten Morgen” is “Good morning”, and “Gute Nacht” is “Good night”.
When saying goodbye in English, you say “Goodbye” or “Bye”.
With “How are you?” you ask how someone is, in German “Wie geht es dir?”.
You can introduce yourself with “My name is Anna”.
The German “Danke” is “Thank you”, and “Bitte”, when asking for something, is “Please”.
In Switzerland people greet each other very differently in the four national languages.

abschnitte.text: In English people greet each other with **“Hello”**, and among friends also with “Hi” or “Hey”. In the morning you say “Good morning”, in the afternoon “Good afternoon” and in the evening “Good evening”. “Good night”, on the other hand, is only said when going to bed. In French people say “Bonjour” during the day and “Bonsoir” in the evening.

After the greeting people often ask **“How are you?”**. Typical answers are “I’m fine, thank you.” or “Not bad.” In Britain and the USA the question is often just a friendly set phrase, and people answer briefly. In French you ask “Ça va ?” and answer “Ça va bien, merci.”

To introduce yourself, you say **“My name is Anna”** or, more briefly, “I’m Anna”. Then you can ask “What’s your name?” In French it is “Je m’appelle Anna.” and “Comment tu t’appelles ?” People often also say where they come from, for example “I’m from Switzerland.”

When saying goodbye in English you say **“Goodbye”**, informally “Bye” or “See you!” In French it is “Au revoir”, or “Salut” among friends. If you will see someone again soon, you say “See you later!” or “À plus tard !” Good wishes such as “Have a nice day!” make a goodbye especially friendly.

In German-speaking Switzerland people say **“Grüezi”**, or “Grüessech” in Bern, and “Hoi” or “Sali” among friends. In French-speaking Switzerland people greet each other with “Bonjour” or “Salut”, in Ticino with “Buongiorno” or “Ciao”. In Romansh the typical greeting is **“Allegra”**. So within Switzerland you can already practise four languages when greeting people.

Greetings often include **gestures** too. In Switzerland adults often shake hands, and among friends in French-speaking Switzerland there are often three kisses on the cheek. In Britain and the USA a handshake or a wave is more usual than kisses. In Japan people bow when they greet each other.

begriffe.erklaerung: The words and gestures with which you welcome someone when you meet.
A fixed sentence that you say out of politeness without expecting a long answer.
A Romansh greeting that means something like “Be glad”.
When people shake hands to greet each other.

gewusst: The English “Goodbye” grew out of the old wish “God be with you”.
“Ciao” comes from Venetian and originally meant something like “your servant”.
In English there is no difference between the familiar “du” and the polite “Sie”; you say “you” to everyone.

teile.einleitung: In English some verbs are followed by the **gerund**, the ing form, and others by the **infinitive** with “to”. With some verbs the meaning even changes depending on which form you choose. If you know the most important rules, you make far fewer mistakes.
wichtigste: After “enjoy”, “avoid”, “finish” and “mind” comes the ing form.
After “decide”, “plan”, “hope” and “want” comes the infinitive with “to”.
“Would like” is followed by the infinitive with “to”.
After prepositions comes the ing form, also with “look forward to”.
With “stop” and “remember” the form changes the meaning.
After “make someone” and “let someone” comes the infinitive without “to”.

abschnitte.text: Some verbs are always followed by the **gerund**. They include **enjoy**, **avoid**, **finish** and **mind**. Examples: **I enjoy swimming in the lake in summer.** or **Do you mind opening the window?** The second one politely asks whether the other person would be willing to open the window. It is best to learn these verbs as a group.

Other verbs require the **infinitive with to**. They include **decide**, **plan**, **hope** and **want**: **She decided to study abroad.** The to-infinitive also follows **would like**, **would love** and **would prefer**: **I would like to order a coffee, please.** These verbs often look towards the future.

With **stop** and **remember** the form matters. **He stopped to rest** means that he stopped in order to rest. **He stopped running**, on the other hand, means that he no longer ran. **I remember locking the door** means that you remember something you have done. **Remember to lock the door** means not to forget to do it.

After a **preposition** there is always the ing form. In **look forward to**, “to” is a preposition, which is why you say **I'm looking forward to seeing you**. After **make** and **let** with an object comes the infinitive **without to**: **They made me write the whole text again.** In the passive, however, the “to” comes back: **I was made to write**.

gewusst: Many learners confuse “look forward to see” and “look forward to seeing”. Only the ing form is correct.
With verbs such as “like” and “love”, both forms are often possible in everyday life: “I like swimming” and “I like to swim”.

teile.einleitung: In English the word for a job is “job” or “profession”. Many job names are easy to remember because they are made of words you already know. Here you learn important jobs and what people do in them.
wichtigste: A “firefighter” works for the fire service.
The person who bakes bread is a “baker”, the one who sells meat a “butcher”.
A “plumber” repairs water pipes.
Someone who builds with wood is a “carpenter”.
A “nurse” cares for sick people; a doctor is called a “doctor”.
A “lawyer” gives legal advice, and a “vet” is an animal doctor.

abschnitte.text: A **firefighter** puts out fires and helps at accidents. The word is made of “fire” and “fighter”. A **police officer** works for the police. In hospital there are **doctors** and **nurses**. A “nurse” is a trained carer, a woman or a man, who looks after sick people.

The **baker** bakes bread and croissants (in Swiss German “Gipfeli”). Watch out, similar words: a **butcher** sells meat and a **barber** cuts men's hair. Someone who cooks in a restaurant is a **cook** or **chef**. The person who brings the food is called a **waiter** or **waitress**.

A **plumber** installs and repairs water pipes. He or she looks after pipes, washbasins and toilets. A **carpenter** works with wood, for example building roofs or making furniture. A **painter** paints walls and buildings, and an **electrician** puts in electric cables. A **mechanic** repairs cars and machines.

A **lawyer** advises people on legal questions and represents them in court. The word comes from **law**. A **teacher** teaches at school. If your pet is ill, you take it to the **vet**. This is short for “veterinarian” (American) or “veterinary surgeon” (British). A **hairdresser** cuts and styles hair; in Switzerland people say “Coiffeur”.

If you want to know what someone does for a living, you ask: **What do you do?** or **What's your job?** The answer might be **I'm a teacher**. Important: in English there is always **a** or **an** before the job, so “I'm an electrician”. In German, on the other hand, people simply say “Ich bin Elektriker”, without the article.

gewusst: The word “plumber” comes from the Latin “plumbum”, meaning lead, because water pipes used to be made of lead.
Many English job names end in “-er”, such as teacher, baker or painter.

teile.einleitung: You need colours every day, when drawing, shopping or describing clothes. Here you learn the most important colours in French and how they change.
wichtigste: “Rouge” is red, “bleu” is blue, “vert” is green.
“Jaune” is yellow, “noir” is black, “blanc” is white.
“Gris” is grey.
The Swiss flag is “rouge et blanc”, red and white.
In French, colours usually come after the noun.
With feminine words the ending often changes: “noir” becomes “noire”.

abschnitte.text: Red is **rouge**, blue is **bleu** and yellow is **jaune**. Green is **vert**, like the grass in the meadow: “L'herbe est verte”. On fine days the sky is “bleu”. A banana is “jaune”. Other colours are **orange** (orange), **rose** (pink) and **violet** (purple).

Black is **noir**, white is **blanc** and grey is **gris**. Snow is “blanc”, the night is “noire”. A mouse is often “grise”. These three colours change their ending with feminine nouns: noir becomes **noire**, gris becomes **grise** and blanc even becomes **blanche**.

The Swiss flag is red with a white cross. In French you say: “Le drapeau suisse est **rouge et blanc**.” The flag of France has three colours: **bleu, blanc, rouge**. That is why it is also called “le drapeau tricolore”, the three-coloured flag. This is a good way to practise colours with countries.

In French the colour almost always comes **after the noun**: “une voiture rouge” is a red car. The colour adapts to the noun. With feminine nouns an **e** is often added: “un pull vert” (a green jumper), but “une robe verte” (a green dress). In the plural you add an **s**: “des fleurs jaunes” (yellow flowers). To ask about the colour you say “De quelle couleur est …?” (What colour is …?).

gewusst: “La couleur”, the colour, is a feminine word in French.
The rainbow is called “l'arc-en-ciel” in French, literally “arch in the sky”.

teile.einleitung: Conditional sentences, also called if-clauses, describe conditions: if something happens, something else follows. In English there are several types, depending on how likely or real the condition is.
wichtigste: A conditional sentence consists of an if-clause and a main clause.
Type 0 is always true: If you heat ice, it melts.
Type 1 is quite possible: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.
Type 2 is unlikely or imagined: If I had more time, I would learn Japanese.
Type 3 is no longer possible because it concerns the past: If you had studied, you would have passed.
In formal English it is If I were and If he were.
Unless means if not.

abschnitte.text: **Type 0** describes things that are always true, for example laws of nature. Both parts of the sentence are in the **simple present**. “If you heat ice, it melts.” Here you can almost always replace if with when. It is not about a single situation but about a rule.

**Type 1** describes a condition that may well come true. The if-clause has the **simple present**, the main clause **will** and the basic form. “If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.” Important: there is no will after if. So you do not say “If it will rain”. With **unless** you say “if not”: “Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.”

**Type 2** describes something that is unlikely or only imagined. The if-clause has the **simple past**, the main clause **would** and the basic form. “If I had more time, I would learn Japanese.” With be, formal English uses **were** for all persons: “If he were here, he would help us.” For advice people often say **“If I were you, I would apologise.”**

**Type 3** concerns the past, which can no longer be changed. The if-clause has the **past perfect**, the main clause **would have** and the past participle. “If you had studied, you would have passed the exam.” Or: “If she had left earlier, she wouldn't have missed the train.” It is often used to express regret or criticism.

Sometimes a condition in the past has a result in the present. Then you mix type 3 and type 2. “If I had taken the job in New York, I **would be living** there now.” The if-clause is in the past perfect, the main clause has would with the basic form or the -ing form. These **mixed conditionals** show how the past changes the present.

gewusst: The if-clause can come first or last. If it comes first, you usually put a comma after it.
In everyday speech you also hear “If I was you”. In formal English and in exams, “If I were you” is considered correct.

teile.einleitung: In the classroom there are lots of things you need every day. Here you learn what the most important school things are called in English.
wichtigste: Bleistift is “pencil”.
Buch is “book”.
Schere is “scissors”.
Radiergummi is “eraser”, in Great Britain also “rubber”.
Lineal is “ruler”.
Leim is “glue”, an Etui is a “pencil case”.

abschnitte.text: With a **pencil** you write and draw. A Kugelschreiber is called a “pen”. Farbstifte are called “coloured pencils”. If something is wrong, the **eraser** helps. In Great Britain it is also called a “rubber”.
With a **ruler** you draw straight lines and measure lengths. **Scissors** are the Schere. The word is always plural, because scissors have two blades. With **glue** you stick paper together.
A **book** is a Buch. A Heft is called an “exercise book” or “notebook”. A Blatt Papier is “a sheet of paper”. At school you often read in a “textbook”.

The **schoolbag** is the Schultasche; in Switzerland it is also called a “Thek”. Inside it is the **pencil case**, the Etui. In the pencil case you keep pencils, a rubber and a sharpener. By the way, a Spitzer is called a “sharpener”.

gewusst: “Scissors” always needs the plural: you say “a pair of scissors”, even when it is only one tool.
In the USA “rubber” means something else, so people there prefer to say “eraser”.

teile.einleitung: In French you do not simply say “I eat bread”, but “Je mange du pain”. The little word in front is called the partitive article and shows an unspecified amount.
wichtigste: The partitive article stands for an unspecified amount of something.
Before masculine words it is “du”, before feminine ones “de la”.
Before a vowel it is “de l'”, for example “de l'eau”.
In the plural you use “des”: “des pâtes”.
After a negative and after quantities, only “de” is used.
After aimer, adorer or détester, the definite article is used: “J'aime le fromage”.

abschnitte.text: When you talk about an **unspecified amount**, French uses the **partitive article**. “Je mange du pain” means “I am eating bread” or “some bread”, so any piece, not the whole loaf. In English and German the article is usually left out in sentences like this. In French, however, it must not be missing.

With masculine words the partitive article is **du**: du pain (bread), du fromage (cheese). With feminine words it is **de la**: de la confiture (jam), de la viande (meat). If a word begins with a vowel or a silent h, you say **de l'**: de l'eau (water), de l'huile (oil). In the plural you use **des**: des pâtes (pasta), des frites (chips).

After a **negative** the partitive article becomes **de**. That is why you say “Je ne mange pas de viande.” (I don't eat meat.) After **quantities** such as un kilo, un litre, beaucoup or peu, only de is used too: “Je voudrais un kilo de pommes” (I would like a kilo of apples), “beaucoup de lait” (a lot of milk). Before a vowel, de becomes d': “pas d'eau” (no water).

After verbs of **liking** such as aimer, adorer, préférer or détester, the **definite article** le, la, l' or les is used. You then mean something in general. “J'aime le fromage” means “I like cheese”, cheese in general. But if you are eating some right now, you say: “Je mange du fromage.”

gewusst: “Du” is actually a merger of “de” and “le”.
Italian also has partitive articles, for example “del pane” for “bread”.

teile.einleitung: Intercultural communication means understanding each other well with people from other cultures. It involves more than language: greetings, rules of politeness, mealtimes and humour differ from country to country. In multilingual Switzerland especially, you come across such differences within your own country.
wichtigste: Culture shows in gestures, politeness, mealtimes and humour.
In France and the Romandy, acquaintances often greet each other with “la bise”, kisses on the cheek.
In French, you address adults you do not know with “vous”.
In western Switzerland, “le dîner” traditionally means the midday meal.
British “understatement” is a deliberate playing down.
The “Röstigraben” (rösti ditch) means the cultural border between German-speaking Switzerland and the Romandy.
Switzerland belongs to the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie.

abschnitte.text: **Intercultural communication** is understanding between people of different origins and cultures. Misunderstandings often arise not because words are missing, but because people have different **habits**. What is polite in one country can seem strange somewhere else. If you stay open, curious and respectful, you usually find a good way.

In France and western Switzerland, acquaintances often greet each other with **“la bise”**, kisses on the cheeks. In the Romandy there are usually three; in France, depending on the region, two to four. In French you address adults you do not know with “vous”, and friends and children with “tu”. In Britain people tend to shake hands or just greet each other with words.

There are differences with food too. In western Switzerland the midday meal is traditionally called “le dîner”, while in France that word means the evening meal. In the USA a **tip** of around 15 to 20 per cent is usual in restaurants (as of 2025), while in Switzerland service is included in the price. In France the fresh start after the summer holidays is called **“la rentrée”**; it affects school, work and politics.

The British are known for their **understatement**, a deliberate playing down. Someone who says “It’s a bit chilly” sometimes means it is freezing cold. In Britain people also drive on the left-hand side of the road, which you have to watch out for when crossing the street. Punctuality is considered very important in Switzerland, while in other countries people are often more relaxed about it.

Switzerland has four national languages and therefore different **language regions** too. The border between German-speaking Switzerland and the Romandy is jokingly called the **“Röstigraben”** (rösti ditch), because rösti is seen as typical of German-speaking Switzerland. It sometimes shows in popular votes or in habits. Towards Ticino, people speak of the “Polentagraben” (polenta ditch).

French connects people on several continents. In Canada, the province of **Quebec** has French as its only official language. The countries in which French plays an important role have joined together in the **Organisation internationale de la Francophonie**, to which Switzerland also belongs. It promotes the French language and cooperation between its members.

begriffe.erklaerung: Everything a group of people have in common, such as language, customs, food and values.
A greeting with kisses on the cheek in France and western Switzerland.
A deliberate playing down, typical of British humour.
A joking name for the cultural border between German-speaking Switzerland and the Romandy.
The community of French-speaking countries and people.

gewusst: In some places the Röstigraben roughly follows the course of the River Saane, which is called the Sarine in French.
In Japan it is considered impolite to give a tip.
In Bulgaria, nodding your head traditionally means no and not yes.

teile.einleitung: Politeness is very important in English. With a few words such as please, thank you and sorry you can get through almost any situation in a friendly way.
wichtigste: Please means bitte, thank you means danke.
Thank you very much means vielen Dank.
The polite answer to thank you is You're welcome.
When you hand someone something, you say Here you are.
You say Excuse me to speak to a stranger.
You say Sorry when you regret something.

abschnitte.text: The most important word is **please**. “Yes, please” means “Ja, bitte”, “No, thank you” means “Nein, danke”. To say thank you you say **thank you** or, for short, **thanks**. If you want to thank someone a lot, you say **thank you very much**. In English a request without please can easily seem rude.

When someone thanks you, you answer **“You're welcome”**. This means roughly “Gern geschehen”. You can also say “No problem” or “That's okay”. In German people often say “Bitte” in this situation. But in English, please is wrong as an answer to thank you.

When you hand someone something, you say **“Here you are”**. In German this corresponds to “Bitte schön” or “Hier, bitte”. It fits in a restaurant, in a shop or at school. “Here you go” is also common. The other person then usually answers “Thank you”.

If you want to speak to a stranger, you begin with **“Excuse me”**. For example: “Excuse me, where is the station?” If you are sorry about something, you say **“Sorry”** or “I'm sorry”. So if you bump into someone by accident, you say sorry. If you have not understood something, you politely ask “Sorry?” or “Pardon?”.

A request becomes friendly with **can** or **could** and please. “Can I have a glass of water, please?” is a polite way of asking. **“Could I have …, please?”** sounds even more polite. **“Would you like …?”** is also a polite question; it is how you offer someone something.

gewusst: English has no special word for the polite German “Sie”. You fits friends and adult strangers alike, which is why please and could show the politeness.
In Great Britain many people say sorry very often, even when they are the ones who have been bumped into.

teile.einleitung: A relative clause gives extra information about a person, a thing or a place. It begins with a relative pronoun such as who, which, that or whose.
wichtigste: Who is used for people, which for things and animals.
That can be used for people and things in defining relative clauses.
Whose shows possession: the boy whose bike was stolen.
Where is used for places, why after the reason.
After a preposition formal English uses whom.
If the pronoun is the object, it can be left out in defining relative clauses.
Non-defining relative clauses stand between commas and never use that.

abschnitte.text: The relative pronoun depends on what you are talking about. For **people** you use **who**: “The woman who lives next door is a doctor.” For **things and animals** you use **which**. **That** works for both, but only in defining relative clauses. After words such as **everything**, nothing or all you usually use that: “Everything **that** he said was true.”

With **whose** you show **possession**. “That's the boy **whose** bike was stolen.” Whose is used for people and sometimes for things. If a **preposition** comes before the pronoun, formal English uses **whom**: “The person to **whom** I spoke was very helpful.” In everyday speech people tend to say “The person I spoke to”.

For **places** you use **where**: “This is the town **where** I was born.” For **reasons** you use **why**, usually after the reason: “Do you know the reason **why** she left so early?” Similarly, **when** is used for points in time: “I remember the day when we met.” This lets you join sentences elegantly instead of making two short sentences.

In **defining** relative clauses you can often **leave out** the pronoun. This works when it is the **object** of the relative clause. “The book **that** I bought is great” can also be said more briefly: “The book I bought is great.” But if the pronoun is the subject, it must stay. “The woman lives next door” without who would be a completely different sentence.

A **defining relative clause** says exactly who or what is meant. It has no commas. A **non-defining relative clause** only gives extra information and stands between **commas**: “Bern, **which** is the federal city of Switzerland, lies on the Aare.” Here you must **not** use that. With which you can also refer to a whole sentence: “He passed the exam, which surprised everyone.”

gewusst: Officially Bern is not a capital but the federal city of Switzerland, which is why English often says federal city.
In German every relative clause has commas round it; in English only non-defining ones do.

teile.einleitung: With the present progressive you say in English what is happening right now. It is formed with a form of be and a verb ending in -ing.
wichtigste: The present progressive is formed with am, is or are and a verb ending in -ing.
It describes what is happening at the moment: Look! The baby is sleeping.
Typical signal words are now, at the moment and Look!
With swim the consonant is doubled: swimming.
With make the silent e disappears: making.
Ie becomes y: lie becomes lying.
Verbs such as know, like or want are not normally used in this form.

abschnitte.text: The **present progressive** is also called the present continuous. It has two parts: a form of **be** and the verb with **-ing**. I **am** reading, she **is** reading, we **are** reading. For a **question** you put the form of be at the front: “**Are** you listening to me?” For the negative you add not: “He isn't sleeping.”

You use this form for things that are happening **right now**. “Look! The baby is sleeping.” Typical **signal words** are **now**, **right now**, **at the moment** and exclamations such as **Look!** or **Listen!**. You also need the form for situations that are only temporary: “I'm staying with my grandmother this week.”

Usually you simply add -ing: read becomes reading. If a verb ends in a **silent e**, the e disappears: make becomes **making**, write becomes writing. With short verbs that end in one vowel and one consonant, the consonant is **doubled**: swim becomes **swimming**, run becomes running. **Ie** becomes **y**: lie becomes **lying**, die becomes dying.

Some verbs do not describe an action but a **state**. They are normally **not** used in the present progressive. They include **know**, believe, understand, like, love, want and need. You say “I **know** the answer”, not “I am knowing”. They are called **state verbs**.

The present progressive can also talk about the **near future** when something has been firmly arranged. “I'm meeting my friends tomorrow” means the meeting is already agreed. Usually there is a time expression such as tomorrow or on Saturday. In German people simply say “Ich treffe morgen meine Freunde” (I meet my friends tomorrow).

gewusst: German has no special progressive form. Instead people say “gerade” (just now) or “im Moment” (at the moment).
In informal speech you sometimes hear the progressive form with feelings anyway, for example “I'm loving this song”.

teile.einleitung: When you meet someone, you greet them. English has simple words for this, such as “Hello” or “Good morning”. With a few polite sentences you can already have a short conversation.
wichtigste: “Hello” means “Hallo” in German.
In the morning you say “Good morning”.
When you leave you say “Goodbye”.
With “How are you?” you ask how someone is.
“Thank you” means “Danke” and “please” means “bitte”.
When you introduce yourself, you say “My name is” followed by your name.

abschnitte.text: The most important greeting is **Hello**, “Hallo” in German. Among friends people also say the short **Hi**. There are special greetings for different times of day: **Good morning** in the morning, **Good afternoon** in the afternoon and **Good evening** in the evening. Before going to sleep you say **Good night**, “Gute Nacht” in German.

When you meet someone new, you say your name: **My name is Anna**. Literally this means “Mein Name ist Anna” in German. A shorter way is **I'm Anna**. The other person may ask **What's your name?**, “Wie heisst du?”. Afterwards people often say **Nice to meet you**, which means “Freut mich, dich kennenzulernen”.

With **How are you?** you ask how someone is. The usual answer is **I'm fine, thank you**, “Mir geht es gut, danke”. Then you politely ask back: **And you?** In England and America “How are you?” is often simply a friendly greeting. People then do not expect a long answer.

Polite words are very important in English. You say **please** when you ask for something, for example **Water, please**. **Thank you** means “Danke”; a shorter form is **Thanks**. If someone thanks you, you answer with **You're welcome**, “Gern geschehen”.

When you leave you say **Goodbye**, “Auf Wiedersehen”. **Bye** or **Bye-bye** sounds more casual. If you will see each other again soon, you say **See you** or **See you later**, “Bis später”. That way a conversation ends in a friendly way.

gewusst: “Goodbye” was originally a shortened form of “God be with you”.
In Australia people often casually say “G'day”, short for “Good day”.

teile.einleitung: A year has twelve months, and in French many of them sound similar to English and German. Here you learn all the names of the months and how to say a date.
wichtigste: The month is called “le mois” in French.
The months are called: janvier, février, mars, avril, mai, juin, juillet, août, septembre, octobre, novembre, décembre.
In French the names of the months are written with a small letter.
In French-speaking Switzerland the Swiss national holiday is called “le 1er août”.
“En janvier” means “in January”.
All the names of the months are masculine.

abschnitte.text: The year begins with **janvier**, January. Then comes **février**, February, the shortest month of the year. They are followed by **mars** (March), **avril** (April) and **mai** (May). “Avril” is the fourth month, “mai” the fifth. In French the names of the months are written with a **small letter**, unlike in English and German.

In summer come **juin** (June), **juillet** (July) and **août** (August). Most Swiss children have their summer holidays in July. On 1 August Switzerland celebrates its national holiday. In French-speaking Switzerland it is simply called **“le 1er août”**, pronounced “le premier août”. “Juin” and “juillet” sound similar, so you have to listen carefully.

In autumn come **septembre** (September), **octobre** (October) and **novembre** (November). “Septembre” is the ninth month of the year. The year ends with **décembre**, December. In December people celebrate Christmas, “Noël” in French. These four months are very similar to the German names.

The month is called **le mois**; a year has **douze mois**, twelve months. “In January” is **en janvier**. In a date, “le” comes before the number: “le 14 juillet” (14 July). Only for the first day do you say **premier**, shortened to “1er”. To ask the date you say “Quelle est la date aujourd'hui ?” (What is the date today?).

gewusst: “Septembre” comes from the Latin word for seven, because in ancient Rome the year originally began in March.
The days of the week are also written with a small letter in French, for example “lundi” for Monday.

teile.einleitung: The concordance des temps is the sequence of tenses in French. It decides which tense must be used in the subordinate clause, depending on what is in the main clause. The subjonctif and sentences with “si” and “quand” are especially important here.
wichtigste: Verbs such as vouloir que, douter que and craindre que require the subjonctif.
For things happening at the same time you use the subjonctif présent; for things that happened before, the subjonctif passé.
After the conditional “si” you use neither the future nor the conditionnel.
After “quand” referring to the future, you use the futur simple.
In the past, the futur antérieur becomes the conditionnel passé.
In literary language the subjonctif imparfait follows a past tense: “qu'il vînt”.

abschnitte.titel: Sequence of tenses with the subjonctif
abschnitte.text: After expressions of wishing, doubt or fear you use the **subjonctif**. If things happen **at the same time** or in the future, you use the subjonctif présent: “Je voudrais qu'il **vienne** demain.” (I would like him to come tomorrow.) This also applies when the main clause is in the conditionnel. If the action happened **before**, you use the subjonctif passé: “Je doute qu'il **soit venu** hier.” (I doubt that he came yesterday.) In “Je crains qu'il ne **soit** trop tard” (I fear it is too late), the “ne” is a **ne explétif** and does not make the sentence negative.

After the conditional “**si**” (if) you use **neither the future nor the conditionnel**. The present, imparfait and plus-que-parfait are possible. For a condition that can be fulfilled, the present follows “si” and the main clause usually has the **futur simple**: “Si tu viens, je **serai** content.” (If you come, I will be happy.) The main clause can also have a present tense or an imperative. So you should never get used to a mistake such as “si tu viendrais”.

Here French differs from German. In German you say “Wenn er ankommt, essen wir” (when he arrives, we eat), using the present tense. In French, after “**quand**” (when) referring to the future, you use the **futur simple**: “Quand il **arrivera**, nous mangerons.” Both actions lie in the future, so both are in the future tense.

abschnitte.titel: The future seen from the past
abschnitte.text: If the main clause is in the past, the tenses shift. The **futur antérieur** then becomes the **conditionnel passé**. “Il dit qu'il **aura fini** à midi” (he says he will have finished by midday) becomes “Il a dit qu'il **aurait fini** à midi” (he said he would have finished by midday). In classical, literary language the **subjonctif imparfait** follows a main clause in the past: “Je voulais qu'il **vînt**.” (I wanted him to come.) In everyday language today people usually use the subjonctif présent instead: “Je voulais qu'il vienne.”

gewusst: Today you find the subjonctif imparfait almost only in books; in conversation it sounds very old-fashioned.
The “ne explétif” after “craindre que” or “avant que” can be left out without changing the meaning.

teile.einleitung: In French lessons you need words for the things in your pencil case and school bag. Here you get to know the most important school things.
wichtigste: The pencil is called “le crayon”, a colouring pencil “le crayon de couleur”.
The rubber is called “la gomme”, the glue “la colle”.
The ruler is called “la règle”, the scissors “les ciseaux”.
The exercise book is called “le cahier”.
The school bag is called “le cartable”, the pencil case “la trousse”.
It is best to learn the article le or la together with every noun.

abschnitte.text: With **le crayon**, the pencil, you write in your exercise book. A colouring pencil is called **le crayon de couleur**. If a line is wrong, **la gomme**, the rubber, helps. With **la règle**, the ruler, you draw straight lines. By the way, a ballpoint pen is called “le stylo”, and the pencil sharpener “le taille-crayon”.

For crafts you need **les ciseaux**, the scissors. In French this word is **plural**, just like the English “scissors”. With **la colle**, the glue, you stick paper together. That way you can stick pictures into your exercise book, for example. Paper is called “le papier”.

abschnitte.titel: Bag, pencil case and exercise book
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland people often call the school bag a **Thek**. In French it is called **le cartable**. In it you carry books and exercise books to school. An exercise book is called **le cahier**, a book “le livre”. The pencils go in **la trousse**, the pencil case. The sharpener and rubber are in there too.

In French, nouns are either **masculine** (le) or **feminine** (la). This often does not match German. In German “die Schere” (the scissors) is feminine, but “les ciseaux” is masculine and plural. That is why it is best to learn every new word **together with its article**: le crayon, la gomme, le cahier, la trousse.

gewusst: The word “crayon” comes from the French “craie”, which means chalk.
In French “la trousse de toilette” means the washbag.

teile.einleitung: Basic French vocabulary covers the most important words you need in everyday life in French. They include numbers, colours, days of the week, animals, family and places such as “la gare”, the station. In western Switzerland there are some special features, such as “nonante” for the number 90.
wichtigste: “La gare” means the station, and “la fenêtre” means the window.
In western Switzerland people say “nonante” for 90.
Friday in French is “vendredi”.
Red is “rouge”, and the dog is “le chien”.
“Le frère” is the brother, “la sœur” the sister.
“La pomme de terre” means the potato.
It is best always to learn nouns together with their article, le or la.

abschnitte.text: The numbers from one to ten are un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix. From 70 it gets exciting: in France people say “soixante-dix” (sixty and ten), and for 90 “quatre-vingt-dix”. In Switzerland and Belgium people more simply say **“septante”** and **“nonante”**. For 80, people in the cantons of Vaud, Valais and Fribourg often say “huitante”.

The days of the week are lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, **vendredi**, samedi and dimanche. Vendredi is Friday. In French they are written with a small letter and are all masculine. Most of the names go back to Roman gods and heavenly bodies; lundi, for example, comes from the moon, in Latin “luna”.

In the house there are la porte (the door), **la fenêtre** (the window) and la cuisine (the kitchen). In town you find la gare (the station), l’école (the school) and le magasin (the shop). If you ask the way, you say “Où est la gare, s’il vous plaît ?” With these words you can already find your way around Lausanne or Geneva quite well.

The dog is **“le chien”** and the cat “le chat”. The horse is “le cheval”, the bird “l’oiseau”. The family includes la mère, le père, le frère (the brother) and la sœur (the sister). The grandparents are les grands-parents.

Bread is “le pain”, cheese “le fromage” and the potato **“la pomme de terre”**. The apple is “la pomme”, water “l’eau”. Important colours are rouge (red), bleu (blue), vert (green) and jaune (yellow). In French, colours usually come after the noun, as in “une pomme rouge” (a red apple).

It is best always to learn French nouns with their **article**, because the gender is often different from German. Index cards, learning apps or little notes stuck on things at home are helpful. Swiss German speakers already know many words, such as Velo, Trottoir or Glace. But you learn most in conversation, for example on a class exchange with the Romandy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The most important words that you need most often in everyday life.
The word for 90 in Switzerland and Belgium.
The little word before the noun; in French le, la, l’ or les.
A little card with the word on one side and the translation on the other.

gewusst: “Mercredi”, Wednesday, is named after the Roman god Mercury.
The Swiss German word “Glace” for ice cream comes straight from French.
Anyone who says “nonante” in Paris is immediately recognised as Swiss or Belgian.

teile.einleitung: The past perfect is the “past before the past” in English. You use it when you are telling a story in the past and want to show that something happened even earlier.
wichtigste: The past perfect is formed with had and the past participle.
It shows what happened before another event in the past.
Example: When we arrived, the train had already left.
The negative is had not or hadn't.
In questions had comes first: Had you ever been to London?
The past perfect progressive is formed with had been and -ing.
Typical words with it are after, before, already and by the time.

abschnitte.text: The **past perfect simple** consists of **had** and the **past participle**. With regular verbs the participle ends in -ed: finished, changed. Irregular ones have to be learnt: left, eaten, seen. Had stays the same for all persons: I had, she had, they had. The short form is **I'd** or **she'd**.

When you tell a story about the past, two things often happen one after the other.
