The earlier one is in the **past perfect**, the later one in the **simple past**. “When we arrived at the station, the train **had already left**.” First the train left, then we arrived. Likewise: “She realised that she **had left** her keys at home.”

The past perfect often appears with words such as **after**, **before**, **already** and **by the time**. “After she had finished her homework, she went out to play football.” “By the time the film started, we **had eaten** all the popcorn.” After because, too, it explains a reason: “I didn't recognise him because he **had changed** a lot.”

For the **negative** you put not after had: “I **had not seen** that film before.” The short form is **hadn't**. For a **question** you put had at the beginning: “**Had** you ever been to London before you moved there?” Short answers are “Yes, I had” or “No, I hadn't”.

The **past perfect progressive** stresses that something went on for a longer time before something else happened. It is formed with **had been** and the verb with **-ing**. “She was tired because she **had been working** all day.” Here the length of the work is what counts. This is often how you explain why someone was tired, wet or dirty.

gewusst: In German the corresponding tense is called the Plusquamperfekt, for example “Ich hatte gegessen” (I had eaten).
The short form he'd can mean he had or he would. If a participle follows, it means had.

teile.einleitung: If you are learning French, you need numbers almost every day: when shopping, telling the time or saying your age. The numbers from 1 to 20 are the basis for all bigger numbers.
wichtigste: The numbers from 1 to 10 are un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix.
The numbers from 11 to 16 have their own names: onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize.
From 17 onwards the number is made of “dix” and a unit, for example “dix-sept”.
Compound numbers such as “dix-neuf” are written with a hyphen.
Many final letters are not pronounced, or only softly.
In Switzerland people say “septante” and “nonante” for 70 and 90.

abschnitte.text: It is best to learn the first ten numbers by heart: **un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix**. “Trois” sounds roughly like “trwah”, “cinq” like “sank”. In “six” and “dix” the x at the end is pronounced like a sharp s: “seess” and “deess”. But if a word beginning with a consonant follows, this sound is often dropped.

The numbers from 11 to 16 have **their own words**, which you have to remember: **onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize**. “Onze” is pronounced roughly “onz”, “treize” roughly “trez”. These numbers all end in “-ze”. That helps you recognise them.

From 17 onwards it gets easier: you take “dix” and add a unit. That gives **dix-sept** (17), **dix-huit** (18) and **dix-neuf** (19). There is a **hyphen** between the parts. After that it continues with “vingt” (20), “trente” (30), “quarante” (40), “cinquante” (50) and “soixante” (60).

You can say sums in French too. **Plus** means plus, **moins** means minus. “Deux plus deux font quatre” means: two plus two makes four. If you do mental arithmetic in French, you practise the numbers especially well.

French is one of the **national languages of Switzerland** and is spoken mainly in western Switzerland. In France people say “soixante-dix” for 70, sixty and ten. In Switzerland and Belgium people say the simpler **septante** for 70 and **nonante** for 90. In some cantons of western Switzerland, such as Vaud, people also say **huitante** for 80.

gewusst: In France 80 is “quatre-vingts”, literally “four times twenty”.
The number 1 is “un” or “une”, depending on whether the noun is masculine or feminine.

teile.einleitung: Paris is the capital of France and one of the best-known cities in the world. Famous buildings such as the Eiffel Tower, the Louvre and Notre-Dame are here. You can reach Paris by direct train from several Swiss cities.
wichtigste: The Seine flows through Paris.
Paris is divided into 20 arrondissements (districts).
The “Mona Lisa” by Leonardo da Vinci hangs in the Louvre.
On the hill of Montmartre stands the white church of Sacré-Cœur.
Notre-Dame reopened in December 2024 after the fire of 2019.
In 2024 Paris hosted the Summer Olympic Games for the third time.

abschnitte.text: The **Seine** flows through Paris. It divides the city into the right bank, the **Rive droite**, and the left bank, the **Rive gauche**. The city is divided into **20 arrondissements**, or districts. They are numbered from the centre outwards like a **snail's shell**. In the middle of the Seine lies the island of Île de la Cité, where the city first began.

The best-known landmark is the **Eiffel Tower**. It was built for the World Exhibition of 1889 and is around 300 metres tall. At the top end of the grand avenue of the **Champs-Élysées** stands the **Arc de Triomphe**, the triumphal arch. It stands on the Place Charles-de-Gaulle. On the hill of **Montmartre**, one of the highest points in Paris, the white basilica of **Sacré-Cœur** rises above the city.

The **Louvre** is one of the most visited museums in the world. The **Mona Lisa** by Leonardo da Vinci hangs there. The Louvre used to be a royal palace; today a large glass pyramid stands in front of it. The cathedral of **Notre-Dame** on the Île de la Cité was badly damaged by fire in April 2019. After more than five years of rebuilding, it was ceremonially reopened at the beginning of **December 2024**.

Paris has hosted the **Summer Olympic Games** three times: in 1900, 1924 and **2024**. At the 2024 Games, events took place at many famous places in the city. For the first time the opening ceremony was held not in a stadium but on the **Seine**. The athletes travelled through the city on boats.

gewusst: The Paris Métro has been running since 1900; it opened in time for the World Exhibition of that year.
When it was built, the Eiffel Tower was the tallest structure in the world.

teile.einleitung: Idioms are fixed expressions that mean something different from what the words say. English has lots of funny images with cats, cake or the moon.
wichtigste: It's raining cats and dogs means: it is raining very hard.
Break a leg! wishes someone good luck before a performance.
It's a piece of cake means: it is very easy.
I'm over the moon means: I am extremely happy.
Once in a blue moon means very rarely.
To let the cat out of the bag means to give away a secret.
I'm all ears means: I am listening carefully.

abschnitte.text: “**It's raining cats and dogs**” does not mean that animals are falling from the sky. It means it is **raining very hard**. In German people say “Es regnet in Strömen” (it is raining in streams) or “Es schüttet” (it is pouring). Nobody knows for sure where the expression comes from. “**I'm feeling under the weather**”, on the other hand, means “I feel ill” or not quite well.

Before a performance on stage, people do not say “Good luck” but “**Break a leg!**”. This wishes someone **good luck**, just as people say “Toi, toi, toi” in German. If you are very happy, you say “**I'm over the moon**”. The joy is so great that you could jump over the moon.

If something is very easy, you say “**It's a piece of cake**”. In German this is roughly “Das ist ein Kinderspiel” (that is child's play). If something happens only **very rarely**, you say “**once in a blue moon**”. So “I go to the cinema once in a blue moon” means: I hardly ever go to the cinema.

abschnitte.titel: The cat out of the bag
abschnitte.text: Someone who “**lets the cat out of the bag**” gives away a **secret**. Funnily enough, German has exactly the same image: “die Katze aus dem Sack lassen”. Both expressions mean that something comes out that was really supposed to stay hidden. For example, when someone talks about the surprise before the party.

“**To hit the books**” literally means to strike the books. But it means **to study hard**, for example before an exam. “**I'm all ears**” means “I am listening carefully”. People say it when they are curious and someone is about to tell them something.

gewusst: A really blue moon hardly ever exists. But a second full moon in the same month is also called a blue moon, and that is rare.
Theatre people often avoid wishing each other luck directly, because it is thought to bring bad luck. That is why they say Break a leg.

teile.einleitung: In French there are several ways of asking a question. The easiest is the question with “est-ce que”, in which the word order stays the same. Here you learn the three most important forms.
wichtigste: You can form a question with your voice, with “est-ce que” or by changing the word order.
With “est-ce que” the word order stays the same as in a statement.
Question words such as “où”, “quand” or “pourquoi” come at the beginning.
“Qu'est-ce que” means “what”.
In inversion, verb and subject swap places.
In inversion, verb and subject are joined with a hyphen.

abschnitte.text: The simplest question is formed just with your **voice**. You say the normal sentence and let your voice go up at the end: “Tu aimes le foot ?” (Do you like football?). In writing there is a question mark at the end. This form is very common in conversation. However, it is rather casual and informal.

If you put **est-ce que** in front of a statement, it becomes a question. “Tu aimes le foot.” becomes “Est-ce que tu aimes le foot ?”. Nothing else changes, because the **word order stays** as in a statement: subject, verb, rest. That is why this form is especially easy to learn. Before a vowel it becomes **est-ce qu'**, for example “Est-ce qu'il vient ?” (Is he coming?).

If you want to ask about a place, a time or a reason, the **question word** comes first. Then come “est-ce que” and the normal sentence. “Where do you live?” is “**Où** est-ce que tu habites ?”. “When are you coming?” is “**Quand** est-ce que tu viens ?”. You ask about things with **qu'est-ce que**: “Qu'est-ce que tu fais ?” means “What are you doing?”. A question with “pourquoi” (why) is often answered with “parce que” (because).

In **inversion**, verb and subject swap places. “Tu parles anglais.” (You speak English.) becomes “**Parles-tu** anglais ?” (Do you speak English?). Verb and subject are joined with a **hyphen**. This form sounds rather formal and often appears in written texts. If the verb ends in a vowel, you insert a **t**: “A-t-il un chien ?” (Has he got a dog?).

gewusst: “Est-ce que” literally means “Is it that …”.
Inversion is also used for polite questions, for example “Pouvez-vous m'aider ?” (Can you help me?).

teile.einleitung: The present perfect links the past with the present. You use it when something happened earlier but still matters now, or when something has been going on until today.
wichtigste: The present perfect is formed with have or has and the past participle.
With he, she and it you use has: She has finished.
Typical signal words are already, yet, ever, never and just.
With since you give a point in time: since 2020.
With for you give a length of time: for ten years.
With exact time expressions such as yesterday you use the simple past: I saw him yesterday.

abschnitte.text: The **present perfect** consists of **have** or **has** and the **past participle**. With I, you, we and they you use have, with he, she and it **has**. Regular verbs end in -ed: “She has finished her homework.” Irregular ones have to be learnt: be becomes **been**, see becomes seen, go becomes gone. Short forms are I've and she's.

You use the present perfect when the **result** matters now, not the exact time. “She has already finished her homework” means: she is done now. Typical **signal words** are **already**, **just** (a moment ago), **ever** and **never**. “Have you ever been to London?” asks about experiences in your whole life.

If something is still going on today, you also use the present perfect. With **since** you name the **point in time** when it began: “I have lived here since 2020.” With **for** you name the **length of time**: “We have known each other for ten years.” In German you say “seit” in both cases and usually use the present tense. That is why this is a common mistake.

For the **negative** you add not to have or has: “I **haven't** seen that film yet.” The word **yet** is used in negative sentences and questions and means “so far” or “by now”. “Have you finished yet?” asks whether you are done already. Yet usually comes at the **end of the sentence**. Already, on the other hand, usually comes before the participle.

If you name an **exact time** in the past, you need the **simple past**. This includes words such as **yesterday**, last week, in 2019 or two days ago. So “I saw him yesterday” is correct, “I have seen him yesterday” is wrong. In German “Ich habe ihn gestern gesehen” is correct. That is exactly why you need to be careful in English.

gewusst: Been and gone are different: He has been to Paris means he was there and has come back. He has gone to Paris means he is there now.
In American English you sometimes hear the simple past with just and already: “I just ate.”

teile.einleitung: In the countries where French is spoken there are many special festivals. Some are celebrated all over France, others only in one region of French-speaking Switzerland. Here you get to know the best-known ones.
wichtigste: On 14 July France celebrates the storming of the Bastille in 1789.
The “Fête de la Musique” takes place every year on 21 June.
Inside the “Galette des Rois” there is a small figure, the “fève”.
At “Chandeleur” on 2 February people make crêpes.
The Bénichon in the canton of Fribourg is a harvest festival with a long menu.
The “Fête des Vignerons” takes place in Vevey only about every 20 to 25 years.

abschnitte.text: The French national holiday is on **14 July**. On this day in 1789, citizens of Paris stormed the **Bastille** prison. This is seen as the beginning of the **French Revolution**. Today there is a big parade in Paris and fireworks everywhere. Many people simply call the day “le 14 juillet”.

The **Fête de la Musique** was founded in France in 1982. It takes place on **21 June**, around the longest day of the year. On that day musicians play everywhere in streets and squares, usually for free. Today this festival is also held in many Swiss towns and cities. In Vevey on Lake Geneva the **Fête des Vignerons** takes place, a huge winegrowers' festival, most recently in 2019. It is part of the intangible cultural heritage of **UNESCO**.

At Epiphany people eat the **Galette des Rois**, a cake made of puff pastry. Inside it there is a small figure, **la fève**. Whoever finds it becomes king or queen and gets a crown. On 2 February it is **la Chandeleur**, Candlemas. Then people make **crêpes**, whose round golden shape is meant to remind you of the sun. On 1 November it is **la Toussaint**, All Saints' Day, a public holiday in France.

In the canton of Fribourg the **Bénichon** is celebrated in September or October. It is a harvest festival marking the end of harvest time. It includes a very long menu with **leg of lamb** and the sweet **cuchaule** bread, which is eaten with mustard. In Geneva the **Escalade** is celebrated in December. It recalls the year 1602, when the city fought off a night-time attack. It includes a chocolate cooking pot, the “marmite”.

gewusst: Easter is called “Pâques” in French, and children then look for “les œufs de Pâques” (Easter eggs).
The word “Toussaint” comes from “tous les saints”, meaning “all the saints”.

teile.einleitung: French cuisine is famous all over the world, from the croissant to the crêpe. Many of these specialities are eaten in Switzerland too. Here you learn the most important words to do with food.
wichtigste: “Croissant” means “crescent”, which is the shape of the pastry.
The baguette is a long, thin loaf of bread.
A “pain au chocolat” is a puff pastry with chocolate.
A crêpe is a very thin pancake.
“La confiture” is jam.
A “moitié-moitié” fondue is made of Gruyère and Vacherin fribourgeois.

abschnitte.text: The best-known French bread is the **baguette**. It is long and thin, and its name means “stick” or “little rod”. The **croissant** literally means “crescent”, because that is its shape. A **pain au chocolat** is made of puff pastry like a croissant, with sticks of chocolate inside. People like to eat pastries like these for breakfast.

For breakfast you spread **la confiture**, jam, on your bread. With it you might drink a **chocolat chaud**, a hot chocolate. “Chaud” means “warm” or “hot”, “froid” means “cold”. In French-speaking Switzerland breakfast is called **le déjeuner**, lunch **le dîner** and supper **le souper**. In France, on the other hand, people say “petit-déjeuner”, “déjeuner” and “dîner”.

A **crêpe** is a very thin pancake. You fill it with, for example, sugar, chocolate or jam. Crêpes originally come from Brittany, a region in the west of France. A **tarte** is a flat cake or tart (in Switzerland also called a Wähe). “Une tarte aux pommes” is an apple tart, because “aux pommes” means “with apples”.

In French-speaking Switzerland people love eating **fondue**. The **moitié-moitié** fondue from the canton of Fribourg is made half of **Gruyère** and half of **Vacherin fribourgeois**. “Moitié-moitié” means “half and half”. **Raclette** comes from Valais: melted cheese is scraped onto potatoes. France is also famous for its many kinds of cheese.

gewusst: UNESCO added the French gastronomic meal to its intangible cultural heritage list in 2010, and the craft of making baguettes in 2022.
Many German words to do with food come from French, for example “Menü”, “Dessert” and “Konfitüre”, and English has borrowed “menu” and “dessert” from French too.

teile.einleitung: French numbers are easy at first, but from 70 onwards they get tricky in France. French-speaking Switzerland and Belgium have more practical words for them. Here you learn the most important numbers.
wichtigste: “Dix” is 10, “vingt” is 20, “trente” is 30.
“Quarante” is 40, “cinquante” is 50, “soixante” is 60.
Numbers such as 18 are put together: “dix-huit”, so 10 + 8.
For 21, 31, 41, 51 and 61 you say “et un”, for example “vingt et un”.
In France 80 is “quatre-vingts”, in Vaud, Valais and Fribourg “huitante”.
“Cent” is 100, “mille” is 1,000.

abschnitte.text: The tens are **dix** (10), **vingt** (20), **trente** (30), **quarante** (40), **cinquante** (50) and **soixante** (60). Be careful not to mix them up: “trente” is 30, but “treize” is 13 and “trois” is 3. “Soixante” (60), “seize” (16) and “six” (6) also sound similar. Inside “cinquante” you can find “cinq”, five.

Many numbers are made of two parts joined with a hyphen. **Dix-huit** is 10 + 8, so 18. **Quarante-deux** is 40 + 2, so 42. For 21, 31, 41, 51 and 61 you say **et un**, meaning “and one”: “vingt et un”, “trente et un”. For 22 it is again without “et”: “vingt-deux”.

In France things get unusual from 70 onwards. 70 is **soixante-dix**, so 60 + 10. 80 is **quatre-vingts**, meaning “four twenties”. 90 is **quatre-vingt-dix**, so 4 × 20 + 10. So for 99 you say “quatre-vingt-dix-neuf”. This way of counting comes from an old system of counting in twenties.

In French-speaking Switzerland it is easier. For 70 you say **septante** and for 90 **nonante**. In the cantons of **Vaud, Valais and Fribourg** people usually say **huitante** for 80. In Belgium people also say “septante” and “nonante”. Bigger numbers are **cent** (100) and **mille** (1,000).

gewusst: “Quatre-vingts” only has an “s” at the end when no other number follows: “quatre-vingts”, but “quatre-vingt-un”.
In France 71 is “soixante et onze”, meaning 60 and 11.

teile.einleitung: The Romandie is the French-speaking part of Switzerland, also called western Switzerland. It stretches from Lake Geneva across the Jura to Valais.
wichtigste: The French-speaking part of Switzerland is called the Romandie or western Switzerland.
Geneva is the largest city in the Romandie, followed by Lausanne.
Lausanne is the capital of the canton of Vaud.
The landmark of Geneva is the Jet d'eau, which shoots water around 140 metres high.
Fribourg and Biel/Bienne lie on the language border.
The difference between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland is jokingly called the “Röstigraben”.

abschnitte.text: The **Romandie** includes the cantons of Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel and Jura, where almost only French is spoken. In addition there are the French-speaking parts of the bilingual cantons of **Bern**, **Fribourg** and **Valais**. The border with German-speaking Switzerland is jokingly called the **Röstigraben**, the “rösti ditch”. It means a border of language and culture, not a real ditch.

**Geneva** is the largest city in the Romandie. Its landmark is the **Jet d'eau**, a fountain in Lake Geneva that shoots water around 140 metres high. In Geneva the **Rhone** leaves the lake and flows on into France. **Lausanne** lies on the northern shore of the lake and is the capital of Vaud. Further east lies **Montreux**, known for the Montreux Jazz Festival, which has taken place every summer since 1967.

The Jura is the home of **watchmaking**. The towns of **La Chaux-de-Fonds** and **Le Locle** in the canton of Neuchâtel have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since 2009. Their streets and houses were planned entirely around the work of the watchmakers. The town of **Neuchâtel** lies right on the shore of Lake Neuchâtel.

Some towns lie exactly where German and French meet. In **Fribourg** the majority speak French, but many also speak German. **Biel/Bienne** is officially bilingual, and the street signs are written in both languages. In towns like these, many people switch quite naturally between the languages in everyday life.

gewusst: The International Olympic Committee has its headquarters in Lausanne.
The Jet d'eau is switched off in strong winds so that the spectators on the shore do not get wet.

teile.einleitung: The **Commonwealth of Nations** is a voluntary association of countries on every continent. Most of them used to belong to the **British Empire**. Today the countries work together as equals, for example in education, sport and trade.
wichtigste: In 2024 the Commonwealth had 56 member countries.
Since 2022 its head has been King Charles III; the role is symbolic.
The Statute of Westminster of 1931 made the dominions independent.
The Secretariat has its headquarters at Marlborough House in London.
In 1995 Mozambique became the first country without a British colonial past to join.
Commonwealth Day is on the second Monday in March.

abschnitte.text: Great Britain used to rule a huge **empire** with colonies on every continent. Countries such as Canada and Australia became so-called **dominions** with their own governments. The **Statute of Westminster** of 1931 made them equal to the United Kingdom: the British Parliament could no longer impose laws on them without their consent. Gradually many colonies also became independent and joined the community.

The Commonwealth has a symbolic head, the **Head of the Commonwealth**. After the death of Queen **Elizabeth II** in September 2022, **Charles III** took on this role. He has no power over the member countries. The organisation is run by the **Secretariat** at **Marlborough House** in London, which is led by a Secretary-General.

The members include large countries such as India and small island states in the Pacific and the Caribbean. Some have the British monarch as their head of state, for example Canada, Australia or Jamaica. Others are **republics**. **Barbados** became a republic on 30 November 2021 and remained a member. **Mozambique**, formerly a Portuguese colony, joined in 1995, and **Rwanda** followed in 2009.

Every four years the **Commonwealth Games** take place, a big sporting festival of the member countries. In 2022 Birmingham was the host. The 2026 Games were held in summer in **Glasgow**, on a smaller scale than before. As well as well-known sports, there are also competitions such as **lawn bowls** or **netball**, which are popular mainly in Commonwealth countries.

**Commonwealth Day** is celebrated every year on the **second Monday in March**. There used to be **Empire Day** on 24 May, Queen Victoria's birthday. Today the day stands for cooperation, peace and shared values. Switzerland was never part of the British Empire and does not belong to the Commonwealth.

gewusst: English is the common working language of the Commonwealth, although hundreds of languages are spoken in the member countries.
India is the member of the Commonwealth with the largest population.

teile.einleitung: With negation you say that something is not true or does not happen. In French it usually consists of two parts that go round the verb.
wichtigste: The simple negative is “ne … pas”: “Je ne mange pas.”
“Ne” comes before the conjugated verb, “pas” after it.
Before a vowel “ne” becomes “n'”: “Je n'aime pas le café.”
After a negative, “un”, “une” or “des” becomes “de”: “Je n'ai pas de frère.”
In the passé composé the negative goes round the auxiliary verb only: “Il n'a pas mangé.”
Other forms are “ne … jamais” (never), “ne … plus” (no longer), “ne … rien” (nothing) and “ne … personne” (nobody).

abschnitte.text: The most common negative is **ne … pas**. It goes round the conjugated verb like a **sandwich**: “Je ne mange pas.” (I am not eating.) “Ne” comes before it, “pas” after it. If the verb begins with a vowel or a silent h, ne becomes **n'**: “Je n'aime pas le café” (I don't like coffee), “Je n'habite pas à Zurich” (I don't live in Zurich).

After a negative the articles **un**, **une** and **des** become **de**. “J'ai un frère” (I have a brother) becomes “Je n'ai pas **de** frère” (I haven't got a brother). The partitive article changes too: “Je mange du pain” becomes “Je ne mange pas de pain”. Before a vowel you use d': “Je n'ai pas d'amis.” (I have no friends.) The definite article le, la, les, on the other hand, stays the same.

In the **passé composé** there are two verb parts, the auxiliary and the participle. The negative goes round the **auxiliary** only. That is why you say “Il n'a pas mangé” (he hasn't eaten) and “Je ne suis pas venu” (I didn't come). The participle comes afterwards. Similar rules apply to questions and orders: “Ne mange pas !” (Don't eat!)

Instead of “pas” another word can be used. **Ne … jamais** means never: “Je ne mange jamais de viande.” (I never eat meat.) **Ne … plus** means no longer: “Il ne pleut plus.” (It isn't raining any more.) **Ne … rien** means nothing: “Je ne vois rien.” (I can't see anything.) **Ne … personne** means nobody: “Je ne vois personne.” (I can't see anyone.) By the way, without ne, “personne” means “the person”.

In everyday spoken language many people simply leave out the **ne**. Instead of “Je ne sais pas” (I don't know) you often hear “Je sais pas” or even “Chais pas”. At school and in writing, however, ne always belongs there. If you know both, you understand conversations better and still write correctly.

gewusst: “Pas” originally meant “step”: “je ne marche pas” meant something like “I don't walk a single step”.
“Ne … que” does not express a negative but “only”: “Je n'ai qu'un frère” means “I have only one brother”.

teile.einleitung: Colours are called **colours** in English, or **colors** in America. You need the names of colours all the time to describe things. Some sound almost like German, others have to be learnt from scratch.
wichtigste: Rot is “red”, Blau is “blue”.
Grün is “green”, Gelb is “yellow”.
“Black” means schwarz, “white” means weiss.
“Brown” means braun.
Grau is “grey”, in America also “gray”.
“Purple” means violett.

abschnitte.text: Rot is **red**, pronounced roughly like “räd” in German spelling. Gelb is **yellow**, roughly like “jello”. Grün is **green**, Blau is **blue**, pronounced like “bluu”. Violett is **purple**. Orange is also **orange** in English. A Regenbogen is called a **rainbow**.

**Black** means schwarz: the night is black. **White** means weiss: snow is white. Grau is **grey**; in America it is also spelt **gray**. An elephant is grey. Together with **brown**, braun, these colours describe many things in nature.

In English the colour comes before the thing, as in German: **a red apple** (ein roter Apfel), **a blue sky** (ein blauer Himmel). But the colour does not change, whether it is about one thing or several. To ask about the colour you say **What colour is it?** The answer might be **It's green**.

If you want to be more precise, you say **light** for hell and **dark** for dunkel. **Light blue** is hellblau, **dark green** is dunkelgrün. Rosa is **pink**. Gold and Silber are called **gold** and **silver**. That way you can describe almost any colour.

gewusst: The British write “colour” with a u, Americans “color” without a u.
If you are “feeling blue” in English, you are sad.

teile.einleitung: Food is one of the first topics you learn in a foreign language, because people have to eat and drink everywhere. For German speakers learning English, the German “Apfel” is an “apple”, “Brot” is “bread” and “Käse” is “cheese”. With these words you can go shopping on your travels, order in a restaurant and talk about your favourite food.
wichtigste: The German “Apfel” is “apple” in English, and “Banane” is “banana”.
“Brot” is “bread”, “Käse” is “cheese” and “Kuchen” is “cake”.
“Milk” means “Milch”, and “water” means “Wasser”.
The German “Ei” is an “egg” in English.
In French, bread is “le pain” and cheese is “le fromage”.
In English the meals are called breakfast, lunch and dinner.
Many food words in English are related to German words.

abschnitte.text: In English the German “Obst” is **“fruit”**, and “Gemüse” is “vegetables”. An apple is an “apple”, a banana a “banana” and the German “Erdbeere” a “strawberry”. The Swiss “Rüebli” is a “carrot”, and the potato a “potato”. In French the apple is “la pomme” and the potato “la pomme de terre”, literally “earth apple”.

For **breakfast** there is often “bread”, “butter” and “cheese”. People drink “milk”, “water” or “orange juice” with it. In French these things are called le pain, le beurre, le fromage and le lait. Swiss cheeses such as Emmental or Gruyère are well known abroad too.

An egg is an **“egg”** in English, and several are “eggs”. A fried egg is a “fried egg”, and scrambled egg is “scrambled eggs”. Sweet things such as cake are called “cake”; biscuits are called “biscuits” in Britain and “cookies” in the USA. Chocolate is “chocolate”, in French “le chocolat”.

In English the first meal of the day is **“breakfast”**, the midday meal “lunch” and the evening meal “dinner”. In France people say petit-déjeuner, déjeuner and dîner. In French-speaking Switzerland, however, “déjeuner” traditionally means breakfast, “dîner” the midday meal and **“souper”** the evening meal. So if you are invited to “dîner” in Geneva, you should turn up at midday.

In a shop you ask “How much is the cheese?” and in a restaurant you say “I would like a sandwich, please.” If you are hungry, you say **“I’m hungry.”**, and if you are thirsty, “I’m thirsty.” In French that is “J’ai faim.” and “J’ai soif.” At the table, people wish each other “Bon appétit !” in French, and in Switzerland people often say it in German too.

English has **countable** and **uncountable** nouns. You can count one apple and two apples, so “an apple” and “two apples”. Water, milk and bread, on the other hand, are not counted: you say “some water” or “a glass of milk”. “Bread” does not get an “s” either; you say “a slice of bread”.

begriffe.erklaerung: The English word for “Gemüse”.
The English word for “Frühstück”, literally breaking the fast after the night.
A word such as “water”, which you cannot simply put “a” or a number in front of.
In French-speaking Switzerland, the word for the evening meal.

gewusst: The English word “breakfast” literally means “to break the fast”.
In French the potato is called “pomme de terre”, literally “apple of the earth”.
The English word “cheese” and the German “Käse” both come from the Latin word “caseus”.

teile.einleitung: French-speaking Switzerland has produced many important writers. Their books are read throughout the French-speaking world.
wichtigste: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was born in Geneva in 1712.
His novel in letters “Julie ou la Nouvelle Héloïse” from 1761 is set near Vevey and Clarens.
Blaise Cendrars's real name was Frédéric-Louis Sauser, and he came from La Chaux-de-Fonds.
Nicolas Bouvier from Geneva wrote the travel book “L'Usage du monde”.
Philippe Jaccottet from Moudon was included in the Bibliothèque de la Pléiade in 2014, while still alive.
Joël Dicker from Geneva received a major prize in 2012 for “La Vérité sur l'affaire Harry Quebert”.

abschnitte.text: **Jean-Jacques Rousseau** was born in Geneva in 1712 and became one of the most important thinkers of his time. His novel in letters **“Julie ou la Nouvelle Héloïse”** appeared in 1761. It is set in the countryside around **Vevey** and **Clarens** on Lake Geneva. The book made this area famous among travellers all over Europe. Afterwards many came to the lake to see the places from the novel.

**Blaise Cendrars**'s real name was Frédéric-Louis Sauser, and he was born in **La Chaux-de-Fonds**. He became known for the poem “La Prose du Transsibérien” of 1913. Later he took French citizenship. In 1953 to 1954 **Nicolas Bouvier** from Geneva travelled with the painter Thierry Vernet in a small Fiat Topolino from Geneva to the Khyber Pass. This became **“L'Usage du monde”** (The Way of the World, 1963), a classic of travel writing.

**Philippe Jaccottet** came from **Moudon** in the canton of Vaud. He wrote quiet, precise poems about nature and was also an important **translator**. In 2014 his works were included in the **Bibliothèque de la Pléiade**. This series of books is regarded as the highest honour in French publishing. It is very rare for an author to be included during their lifetime.

**Joël Dicker** from Geneva received the **Grand Prix du roman de l'Académie française** in 2012 for “La Vérité sur l'affaire Harry Quebert” (The Truth About the Harry Quebert Affair). The crime novel is set in the USA and has been translated into many languages. With this prize Dicker became internationally known. It shows that literature from French-speaking Switzerland is still read worldwide today.

gewusst: The Vaud writer Charles-Ferdinand Ramuz is also very well known; his portrait appeared on a former 200-franc note.
The books of the Bibliothèque de la Pléiade are printed on very thin paper and bound in leather.

teile.einleitung: Family is a topic that comes up early in every foreign language, because people like to talk about themselves and the people they love. For German speakers learning English, the German “Mutter” is “mother”, “Vater” is “father” and the whole family is the “family”. With these words you can introduce yourself and describe photos or family trees.
wichtigste: The German “Familie” is “family” in English.
“Mutter” is “mother” and “Vater” is “father”; informally people say “mum” and “dad”.
“My sister” is “meine Schwester”, and “brother” is “Bruder”.
“Grossmutter” is “grandmother”, and “my grandfather” is “mein Grossvater”.
The German “Tante” is “aunt” in English, and “Onkel” is “uncle”.
In French, the mother is “la mère” and the father “le père”.
A family tree is a good way to practise family words.

abschnitte.text: In English the German “Eltern” are **“parents”**, the mother is “mother” and the father “father”. At home children usually say “mum” or “mom” and “dad”. A son is a “son”, and a daughter a “daughter”. In French the parents are “les parents”, the mother “la mère” and the father “le père”.

In English, brothers and sisters together are called **“siblings”**. The sister is the “sister” and the brother the “brother”. So you say, for example, “My sister is ten years old.” In French, sister and brother are “la sœur” and “le frère”.

In English the grandparents are called **“grandparents”**. The grandmother is the “grandmother”, lovingly “granny” or “grandma”. The grandfather is the “grandfather”, also called “grandpa”. In French people say “la grand-mère” and “le grand-père”, and children often say “mamie” and “papi”.

Other relatives include the aunt, in English **“aunt”**, and the uncle, “uncle”. Male and female cousins are both simply called “cousin”. The niece is the “niece” and the nephew the “nephew”. In French, on the other hand, there are “le cousin” and “la cousine”.

A **family tree** shows who is related to whom. At the top are the grandparents, below them parents, aunts and uncles, and right at the bottom the children. With a family tree you practise sentences such as “Lisa is my mother’s sister.” In English the “’s” shows who something belongs to or who someone belongs to.

Families look very different. Some children live with both parents, others with one parent, in a **blended family** or with foster parents. In English a stepmother is a “stepmother” and a half-brother a “half-brother”. What matters in every family is being there for each other.

begriffe.erklaerung: The English word for mother and father, not for relatives in general.
The English word for brothers and sisters together.
A drawing that shows how people in a family are related to each other.
A family in which children from the parents’ earlier relationships live together.

gewusst: The English word “parents” is a false friend for speakers of some languages, because it means mother and father and not relatives, who are called “relatives”.
In English there is only one single word for a male and a female cousin: “cousin”.
The mother-in-law is called “mother-in-law” in English, that is mother by law.

teile.einleitung: Molière is the most famous writer of comedies in France. He lived in the 17th century, at the time of King Louis XIV. His plays are still performed all over the world today.
wichtigste: Molière's real name was Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, and he was born in Paris in 1622.
He was an actor, a theatre manager and a writer all at once.
Famous plays are “Tartuffe”, “L'Avare”, “Le Misanthrope” and “Le Malade imaginaire”.
In 1673 he fell ill during a performance of “Le Malade imaginaire” and died the same evening.
The Comédie-Française is still called “la maison de Molière” today.
“La langue de Molière” is another name for the French language.

abschnitte.text: Molière was born in Paris in **1622** as **Jean-Baptiste Poquelin**. Later he took the stage name Molière. With a theatre company he travelled for many years through the French provinces. Afterwards he performed in Paris and won the favour of King **Louis XIV**. He was an actor, the manager of his company and the author of his plays all at once.

In his **comedies** Molière makes fun of people's weaknesses. In **“L'Avare”** (The Miser, 1668) **Harpagon** guards his money box more closely than his children. Today his name stands for a miser in French. In **“Tartuffe”** a man pretends to be pious in order to take advantage of the trusting Orgon. In this way Molière attacks **religious hypocrisy**. Because of protests from religious circles, the play was banned for years after its first performance in 1664.

In **“Le Misanthrope”** **Alceste** demands total honesty from everyone. This brings him into conflict with court society, while his friend Philinte takes a more moderate view. In **“Le Bourgeois gentilhomme”** (The Would-Be Gentleman) the rich middle-class man **Monsieur Jourdain** wants to become a nobleman. He takes lessons and is amazed to learn that he has been speaking prose for more than forty years without knowing it. His teacher explains to him that everything that is not verse is prose.

In his last play, **“Le Malade imaginaire”** (The Imaginary Invalid), Molière himself played the main role of Argan. At the fourth performance in **1673** he fell ill on stage and died a few hours later. In 1680 the **Comédie-Française** was founded on the orders of Louis XIV, partly from Molière's former company. That is why it is still called **“la maison de Molière”** (the house of Molière) today. And just as German is called the language of Goethe, **“la langue de Molière”** stands for French.

gewusst: Of all things, in the play about an imaginary invalid Molière himself was really ill.
France's best-known theatre awards are named after him: the “Molières”.

teile.einleitung: Colours are among the first words you learn in a new language, because they are all around us. For German speakers learning English, the German “rot” is “red”, “blau” is “blue” and “grün” is “green”. With colours you can describe clothes, animals and pictures and even express feelings.
wichtigste: The German “rot” is “red”, “blau” is “blue”, “grün” is “green” and “gelb” is “yellow”.
“Black” is “schwarz” and “white” is “weiss”.
“Brown” means “braun” and “grey” means “grau”.
The German “violett” is “purple” in English.
In the USA grey is spelt “gray”, in Britain “grey”.
In French, red is “rouge” and blue is “bleu”.
In English the colour comes before the noun; in French it usually comes after.

abschnitte.text: The most important colours in English are **red**, blue, green and yellow. Then there are black, white, brown and grey. Orange is simply “orange”, and the German “rosa” is “pink”. The German “violett” is **“purple”**; the word “violet” exists too, but it means a lighter bluish purple.

With some colour words, the **spelling** is different. In Britain people write “grey” and “colour”, in the USA “gray” and “color”. Both spellings are correct. At school in Switzerland pupils usually learn the British form, but you should stick to one form within a text.

In French the colours are rouge, bleu, vert, jaune, noir, blanc, gris and marron. French colour adjectives usually come **after the noun**: “une voiture rouge” is a red car. They often adapt to the noun: with feminine nouns “vert” becomes “verte”. So it is “un pull vert” (a green jumper), but “une pomme verte” (a green apple).

In English the colour comes before the noun and stays **unchanged**: “a red car”, “two red cars”. You ask about the colour with “What colour is it?” Lighter and darker shades are described with “light” and “dark”, for example “light blue”. The colour word itself never gets a plural s.

Colours appear in many **idioms**. Someone who is “feeling blue” is sad. Someone who is “green with envy” is very jealous, and “to see red” means to get angry. In German, on the other hand, people say “gelb vor Neid” (yellow with envy), so every language has its own images.

In a paintbox you can mix lots of new colours from the basic colours. Blue and yellow make green, and red and yellow make orange. In English you say: “Blue and yellow make green.” In art lessons people talk about **primary colours** and mixed colours, in English “primary colours” and “secondary colours”.

begriffe.erklaerung: The English word for “Farbe”, spelt “color” in the USA.
Basic colours from which other colours can be mixed.
A describing word; colours, for example, are adjectives.
A fixed expression with a figurative meaning, for example “feeling blue”.

gewusst: The colour orange is named after the fruit, not the other way round.
If someone is “feeling blue” in English, they have not been painted blue; they are sad.
Before the orange fruit was known in Europe, English had no word of its own for this colour.

teile.einleitung: If you go shopping in England or America, you need a few important words and sentences. With them you can ask about prices, try on clothes and pay at the till. Many words are easy to learn.
wichtigste: With “How much is it?” you ask about the price.
In the supermarket you pay at the “checkout”.
The “receipt” is the slip you get after paying; a “recipe” is a cooking recipe.
With “Can I try it on?” you ask whether you may try something on.
When paying, “change” is the money you get back.
In a “SALE” the prices are reduced.

abschnitte.text: In the supermarket you take a **basket** or push a **trolley**, which is what the shopping cart is called in Great Britain. In America people say **shopping cart**. The goods are on a **shelf**, and between the shelves there is an **aisle**. You pay at the **checkout**, the till.

With **How much is it?** or **How much does it cost?** you ask what something costs. For several things you say **How much are they?** In Great Britain people pay with **pounds** and **pence**, in the USA with **dollars** and **cents**. A big **SALE** sign means that many goods are cheaper than usual.

In a clothes shop you ask **Can I try it on?** You can do this in the **changing room**. If something does not fit, you ask for another size: **Do you have this in a smaller size?** If you like it, you say **I'll take it**.

The shop assistant may ask **Cash or card?** If you hand over too much money, you get **change**, the money back: **Here's your change**. After that you receive the **receipt**. Careful: a cooking recipe is called a **recipe**; it sounds similar, but it is something different.

Many foods have their own words for amounts. A whole bread is called **a loaf of bread**. Chocolate goes with **a bar of chocolate**, bananas or flowers with **a bunch**. You buy toothpaste as **a tube of toothpaste** and milk as **a carton of milk**. To order politely you say **I'd like ..., please**.

gewusst: In Great Britain people usually say “shop”, in America usually “store”.
In Great Britain price labels show the sign £ for pounds.

teile.einleitung: Prepositions are little words such as in, on, at or under. They show where something is, when something happens or how you travel. In English they are often used differently from German.
wichtigste: In is used with months, years, towns and countries: in May, in Zurich.
On is used with days and dates: on Monday, on the 1st of August.
At is used with clock times: at 8 o'clock.
At is also used with particular points: at the bus stop.
On is used with surfaces: on the wall, on the table.
Under means below, and by bike means travelling on a bicycle.

abschnitte.text: There are three important prepositions for time. **In** is used with longer periods such as months, seasons and years: in May, in winter, in 2025. **On** is used with days and dates: on Monday, “Swiss National Day is **on** the 1st of August”. **At** is used with exact clock times: “The lesson starts **at** 8 o'clock.” A memory trick: from big to small, you go from in to on to at.

For towns, countries and enclosed spaces you use **in**. “I live **in** Zurich”, “She lives in Switzerland”, “The cat is in the box”. Here in means that something is inside something else. With streets, too, British English often uses in: in Main Street.

**At** is used for a particular **point** or meeting place: “She is waiting **at** the bus stop”, at the door, at school. **On** is used for **surfaces**: “The picture hangs **on** the wall”, on the table, on the floor. In German it is “an der Wand” (at the wall) and “auf dem Tisch” (on the table), but in English both are on.

Other prepositions show the exact position. **Under** means below: “The cat is under the table.” **Next to**, **behind** and **in front of** describe what is beside, behind or before something. **Between** and **above** are useful too. With these words you can describe a room precisely.

For means of transport you use **by**: “He goes to school **by** bike.” Likewise: by bus, by train, by car. Walking is an exception, because you say **on foot**. If you are talking about a particular vehicle, this changes: “I'm **on** the bus” or “She is **in** the car”. In Switzerland many children go to school by bike or by bus.

gewusst: Morning is in the morning, but night is at night.
Prepositions are among the hardest words when learning a language, because every language uses them a little differently.

teile.einleitung: French grammar covers the rules for verbs, nouns, pronouns and sentence structure in French. Typical features are the many verb forms, the matching of words to gender and number, and special moods such as the subjunctive (subjonctif). In the upper years and at grammar school these rules are learnt in depth, so that you can speak and write with confidence.
wichtigste: After “il faut que” comes the subjunctive: “Il faut que tu viennes demain.” (You have to come tomorrow.)
The subjunctive also follows “bien que”, as in “Bien qu’il soit malade, il travaille.” (Although he is ill, he is working.)
According to the French standard, “après que” is followed by the indicative.
With “si” and the imperfect comes the conditional: “Si j’avais de l’argent, j’achèterais une voiture.” (If I had money, I would buy a car.)
The participle agrees when the direct object comes before it: “Les lettres que j’ai écrites” (The letters I wrote).
Pronouns come before the verb, for example “Je le lui donne.” (I give it to him or her.)
“Le cheval” (the horse) forms the plural “les chevaux”.

abschnitte.text: French **verbs** change a lot depending on person and tense. They are divided into groups; most end in -er, like “parler” (to speak). Important tenses are the présent, the **passé composé**, the imparfait and the futur. Common verbs such as être, avoir, aller and faire are irregular and have to be learnt by heart.

The **subjunctive** (subjonctif) expresses wishes, necessity and doubt. It comes, for example, after “il faut que”, as in “Il faut que tu viennes demain.”, and after “bien que”, as in “Bien qu’il soit malade, il travaille.” After “après que”, on the other hand, the standard requires the indicative, even though many people use the subjunctive in everyday life. The **conditional** (conditionnel) is used in conditional sentences: “Si j’avais de l’argent, j’achèterais une voiture.”

In the passé composé with “avoir”, the participle agrees when the **direct object** comes before it. That is why you write “Les lettres que j’ai écrites” with -es, because “les lettres” is feminine and plural. There is a special rule for reflexive verbs such as “se laver” (to wash). In “Elle s’est lavé les mains.” (She washed her hands), “les mains” is the direct object and comes after the verb, so “lavé” stays unchanged.

French **object pronouns** come before the conjugated verb. “Je donne le livre à Marie.” (I give the book to Marie) becomes “Je le lui donne.”, where “le” replaces the book and “lui” replaces Marie. The pronoun **“en”** replaces amounts: “Tu as des frères ? Oui, j’en ai deux.” (Have you got brothers? Yes, I have two.) The pronoun “y”, on the other hand, usually replaces a place, as in “J’y vais.” (I’m going there.)

Most French nouns form the plural with a silent -s. Words ending in -al often form it with **-aux**, as in “le cheval, les chevaux” (horse, horses) or “le journal, les journaux” (newspaper, newspapers). Nouns and adjectives agree in gender and number. So it is “un petit chat” (a little cat) and “une petite maison” (a little house).

French **negation** usually has two parts, “ne” and “pas”, which go round the verb. “Je ne sais pas” means “I don’t know”. With “ne ... que” you express “only”: “Je n’ai que dix francs.” means “I only have ten francs.” In spoken French many people leave out the “ne” and simply say “Je sais pas”.

begriffe.erklaerung: A verb form for wishes, feelings, doubt and necessity.
The form for possibility; it matches the English “would”.
A compound past tense, such as “j’ai mangé” (I ate, I have eaten).
A short word that replaces an object, for example le, la, lui or en.
The French term for making a word match in gender and number.

gewusst: The rules for the agreement of the participle are considered so difficult that even native French speakers make mistakes with them.
In France and Belgium there are dictation competitions in which you have to master exactly these grammar rules.
The word “oiseau” (bird) contains all five vowel letters a, e, i, o and u.

teile.einleitung: France is Switzerland's largest neighbour and very varied. Each region has its own landscape, food and history.
wichtigste: Because of its shape, the French often call their country “l'Hexagone”, the hexagon.
Brittany in the north-west is known for crêpes and the Celtic language Breton.
Provence in the south is famous for its lavender fields.
Strasbourg in Alsace lies on the Rhine on the border with Germany.
Many magnificent châteaux such as Chambord and Chenonceau stand along the Loire.
Marseille is the second-largest city in France after Paris.

abschnitte.text: The outline of mainland France looks like a hexagon. That is why the French like to call their country **l'Hexagone**. France borders several countries, including **Switzerland**, Germany, Italy, Spain and Belgium. To the west lies the Atlantic, to the south the Mediterranean. The country is divided into **regions**, a bit like Switzerland into cantons, though with fewer rights of their own.

**Brittany** lies on a peninsula in the north-west on the Atlantic. It is known for its crêpes and Celtic traditions. It even has its own Celtic language, **Breton**. Right next to it is **Normandy**. On a tidal island there stands the famous abbey mount of **Mont-Saint-Michel**. At high tide it is surrounded by the sea.

In **Provence** huge **lavender fields** bloom in summer. The lavender is used for scents and soaps. The Mediterranean coast in the south-east is called the **Côte d'Azur**; the largest city there is Nice. The port city of **Marseille** is the second-largest city in France after Paris and has the country's biggest port. Off the coast lies the island of **Corsica**, where Napoleon Bonaparte was born in Ajaccio in 1769.

At around 1,000 kilometres, the **Loire** is the longest river that flows entirely within France. In the Loire Valley there are many magnificent **Renaissance châteaux**, for example Chambord and Chenonceau. In the east lies **Alsace** with the city of **Strasbourg**. It lies on the Rhine, right on the border with Germany. The European Parliament also meets in Strasbourg.

gewusst: The Château de Chenonceau is built on arches over the River Cher.
Some islands far away, for example in the Caribbean and the Indian Ocean, also belong to France.

teile.einleitung: An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning you cannot guess from the individual words. English has a great many of them, and they make the language lively.
wichtigste: An idiom is a fixed expression with a figurative meaning.
You must not translate an idiom word for word.
To pull someone's leg means to tease someone.
To spill the beans means to give away a secret.
To bite the bullet corresponds to the German “in den sauren Apfel beissen”.
The elephant in the room is a problem everyone can see but nobody mentions.

abschnitte.text: An **idiom** is a fixed group of words with a **figurative meaning**. If you translate “to spill the beans” literally, it is about beans being knocked over. What it really means is: to give away a secret. That is why idioms have to be learnt like vocabulary. German has lots of them too, for example “Tomaten auf den Augen haben” (to have tomatoes on your eyes), which means not to notice something obvious.

**To pull someone's leg** literally means to tug at someone's leg. But it means to **tease** someone or make a fool of them in fun. So “Are you pulling my leg?” means “Are you joking with me?” Someone who **spills the beans** gives away a secret. “Come on, spill the beans!” means “Come on, tell me!”

Some idioms have a German equivalent with completely different images. **To bite the bullet** corresponds to “in den sauren Apfel beissen” (to bite into the sour apple), meaning to have to do something unpleasant. **To beat around the bush** is “um den heissen Brei herumreden” (to talk around the hot porridge) in German. If something **costs an arm and a leg**, it is very expensive. In German people say something like “Das kostet ein Vermögen” (that costs a fortune).

**To feel under the weather** means to feel unwell or slightly ill. The expression **to kick the bucket** is a casual way of saying “to die”, similar to the German “den Löffel abgeben” (to hand in the spoon). Because it sounds so casual, it does not fit serious conversations. Idioms often have a particular **tone**, so you need to know when you can use them.

**The elephant in the room** is an obvious problem that nobody wants to talk about. An elephant in a room cannot be overlooked, and yet everyone pretends it is not there. Today the expression is used in German too. This is how idioms sometimes travel from one language to another.

gewusst: Many English idioms come from books and plays by William Shakespeare.
For people learning a language, idioms are among the hardest things, because logic alone does not help.

teile.einleitung: With the going-to future you talk about the future in English. It is used mainly for firm plans and for things you can already see coming.
wichtigste: The going-to future is formed with am, is or are, then going to and the basic form of the verb.
You need it for plans and intentions that are already decided.
You also need it for predictions when you can see clear signs.
The negative is formed with not after the form of be: They aren't going to play.
In questions the form of be comes first: Is she going to buy a bike?
In spoken language going to is often shortened to gonna.

abschnitte.text: The going-to future has three parts. First comes a form of **be**: I am, you are, he, she or it is, we and they are. Then comes **going to** and finally the **basic form** of the verb, the verb without any ending. An example: “I am going to visit my aunt.” The short forms I'm, she's or we're are quite normal in conversation.

If you have already decided on something, you use going to. “We are going to travel to Geneva next week” means: the trip is planned. Often you already know what you need to do for it. This is called an **intention**, something you have firmly made up your mind to do. New Year's resolutions often sound like this too: “I'm going to read more books.”

You also use going to when you can see something coming. When there are dark clouds, you say: “It is going to rain.” When someone trips, you shout: “Careful! You are going to fall!” The **signs** are already there, so you are fairly sure. Without such signs, people tend to use **will** for guesses.

For the **negative** you add not to the form of be: “I'm not going to come”, “They aren't going to play.” For a **question** you put the form of be at the beginning: “Are you going to help me?” or “Is she going to buy a new bike?” Short answers are, for example, “Yes, I am” or “No, she isn't”. Going to and the basic form always stay the same.

In conversation and in songs you often hear **gonna** instead of going to. “I'm gonna call you” means the same as “I'm going to call you”. But gonna is **informal language**. That is why you always write going to in essays and exams. Gonna only stands for going to with a verb, not for “I'm going to school”, which is about movement.

gewusst: The sentence “I'm going to go” is correct: the first go belongs to going to, the second is the verb.
Many well-known pop songs have gonna in their title, because it sounds shorter and smoother when singing.

teile.einleitung: In a child's bedroom there are lots of things you see every day. Here you learn what the furniture and objects are called in French. With little words such as “sur” and “sous” you can also say where something is.
wichtigste: “La chambre” is the room, “ma chambre” means “my room”.
“Le lit” is the bed, “la table” the table, “la chaise” the chair.
“La fenêtre” is the window, “la porte” the door.
“La lampe” is the lamp.
“Sur” means “on”, “sous” means “under”.
Before feminine words you say “ma”, before masculine ones “mon”.

abschnitte.text: In the room there is **le lit**, the bed, where you sleep. At the table, **la table**, you sit on the chair, **la chaise**. The word “table” is the same as in English and reminds German speakers of the word “Tablett” (tray). A desk is called **le bureau**, a wardrobe **l'armoire**. Toys are **les jouets**.

You go into the room through **la porte**, the door. Light comes in through **la fenêtre**, the window. In “fenêtre” you can hear the similarity to the German word “Fenster”. In the evening you switch on **la lampe**. Many words in the room are feminine and therefore have the article “la”.

The room is called **la chambre**, especially the bedroom. If you want to say “my room”, it is **ma chambre**. Before feminine words you say **ma**, before masculine ones **mon**: “mon lit”, “ma lampe”. In the plural it is **mes**: “mes jouets”. This way you can describe your room: “Dans ma chambre, il y a un lit et une table.” (In my room there is a bed and a table.)

With little words you say where something is. **Sur** means “on”: “La lampe est sur la table”, the lamp is on the table. **Sous** means “under”: “Le chat est sous le lit”, the cat is under the bed. **Dans** means “in”, **devant** “in front of” and **derrière** “behind”. **À côté de** means “next to”.

gewusst: “Il y a” means “there is” or “there are” and is one of the most common expressions in French.
The German word “Büro” comes from the French “bureau”, and English uses “bureau” too.

teile.einleitung: In French the past participle (participe passé) can change: sometimes it gets an e for feminine or an s for plural. Whether this is needed depends on the auxiliary verb and on where the direct object stands. With a few rules you can find the right form.
wichtigste: With être the participe passé agrees with the subject: “Elles sont parties.”
With avoir it usually stays unchanged: “J'ai mangé les pommes.”
With avoir it agrees if the direct object comes before it: “Les fleurs que j'ai achetées.”
With reflexive verbs, what matters is whether “se” is the direct or the indirect object.
Impersonal verbs such as falloir always stay unchanged.
Feminine adds an e, plural an s, feminine plural es.

abschnitte.titel: With être: look at the subject
abschnitte.text: Verbs such as **partir**, venir, aller or arriver form the passé composé with **être**. Then the participe passé agrees with the **subject**, like an adjective. You say “il est parti”, but “elle est partie”. In the plural it is “ils sont partis” and “**elles sont parties**”. So ask yourself: who has gone, and is it masculine or feminine, singular or plural?

abschnitte.titel: With avoir: where is the object?
abschnitte.text: With **avoir** the participe passé usually stays **unchanged**: “J'ai **mangé** les pommes.” (I ate the apples.) Here the direct object “les pommes” comes after the verb. If the **direct object comes first**, the participe passé agrees with it. In “Les fleurs que j'ai **achetées** sont belles” (the flowers I bought are beautiful), “que” stands for “les fleurs”, which is feminine plural. In the same way you write “Combien de livres as-tu **lus** ?” (how many books have you read?), because “combien de livres” comes first and is masculine plural.

Reflexive verbs such as **se laver** (to wash oneself) form the passé composé with être. Even so, you have to look closely here: is “se” the **direct** object? In “Ce matin, elle s'est **lavée**” (this morning she washed herself), she washes herself, so “se” is the direct object and comes first. That is why there is an e. In “Elle s'est **lavé** les mains” (she washed her hands), “les mains” is the direct object and comes afterwards; “se” is only the indirect object. In “Ils se sont **parlé**” (they spoke to each other) the form stays the same, because you say “parler **à** quelqu'un” (to speak to someone).

Some verbs never have a real direct object. One example is the impersonal verb **falloir** (to be necessary). Its participe passé **fallu** always stays the same: “Les efforts qu'il a **fallu** étaient énormes.” (The efforts that were needed were enormous.) Even though “que” comes first here, nothing changes. A good tip: ask for the direct object with “quoi ?” (what?) or “qui ?” (whom?). If you cannot find one, the form stays unchanged.

gewusst: You cannot hear many of the endings at all: “acheté” and “achetées” sound the same, and you only see the difference in writing.
With some verbs you can hear the agreement, for example in “la lettre qu'il a écrite”, where the t becomes audible.

teile.einleitung: The Parliament of the United Kingdom makes the laws for England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. It meets in the Palace of Westminster in London and has two chambers: the House of Commons and the House of Lords.
wichtigste: Parliament consists of the monarch, the House of Lords and the House of Commons.
Only the House of Commons is directly elected by the people.
In 2026 the House of Commons has 650 seats.
Elections use first past the post in single-member constituencies.
The Speaker chairs the debates and keeps order impartially.
Since the Parliament Act of 1911 the House of Lords can only delay laws.
Prime Minister's Questions take place every Wednesday when Parliament is sitting.

abschnitte.text: The British Parliament has two chambers. The **House of Commons**, the lower house, is elected by the people and is today the more important chamber. The **House of Lords**, the upper house, is not elected. Its members are mostly appointed for life, and some are bishops of the Church of England. Formally the **monarch** is also part of Parliament and signs the laws.

The country is divided into **constituencies**; in 2026 there are 650. In each constituency exactly one person is elected. Whoever has the most votes wins the seat, even without an absolute majority. This is called **first past the post**. The party with the most seats usually forms the government and provides the **Prime Minister**. In Switzerland, by contrast, the National Council is mostly elected by proportional representation.

The debates in the House of Commons are chaired by the **Speaker**. He or she is elected by the MPs and must be **impartial**. That is why the Speaker gives up party membership. The Speaker calls on the speakers and keeps order, often with a loud cry of “Order!”. The benches of the government and the opposition face each other directly.

The House of Lords used to be able to block laws completely. The **Parliament Act of 1911** changed this: since then the upper house can only **delay** many laws, but no longer stop them for good. Another act in 1949 shortened this time even further. So in the end the elected lower house gets its way.

Parliament meets in the **Palace of Westminster** on the Thames. Since 2012 the famous clock tower has been called the **Elizabeth Tower**; the bell **Big Ben** hangs inside it. At the State Opening of Parliament the monarch gives the **King's Speech**, reading out the government's programme. Every **Wednesday** MPs put questions to the head of government at **Prime Minister's Questions**.

gewusst: The monarch is not allowed to enter the House of Commons. This tradition dates back to the 17th century.
The benches in the House of Commons are green, those in the House of Lords red.

teile.einleitung: If you are looking for your way in a strange town, you need to be able to ask and understand the answer. With a few important words you can find your way around Lausanne, Geneva or Paris too.
wichtigste: “À gauche” means left, “à droite” means right.
“Tout droit” means straight on.
To ask the way you say, for example: “Où est la gare ?”
“En face de” means opposite, “à côté de” means next to.
“Au coin de la rue” means on the street corner.
“Le carrefour” is the crossroads, “le pont” the bridge.

abschnitte.text: First you greet the person politely: “Excusez-moi, madame” or “Pardon, monsieur”. Then you ask: “**Où est la gare ?**” That means “Where is the station?”. You can also ask: “Pour aller à la poste, s'il vous plaît ?” (How do I get to the post office, please?) The airport is called “l'aéroport”, the post office “la poste” and the cinema “le cinéma”. At the end you say thank you with “Merci beaucoup !”

The most important words are **à gauche** (left), **à droite** (right) and **tout droit** (straight on). Careful: “droite” and “droit” look similar, but here they mean different things. “Tournez à gauche” means “Turn left”. “Allez tout droit” means “Go straight on”. You hear this command form with -ez very often in directions.

To describe a place exactly, you need little place words. **En face de** means opposite: “en face de la poste” (opposite the post office). **À côté de** means next to, and **derrière** means behind. “De le” becomes **du**: “à côté du cinéma” (next to the cinema). **Au coin de la rue** means on the street corner, because “le coin” is the corner and “la rue” the street.

At a **crossroads**, “le carrefour” in French, you often have to decide which way to go. The roundabout is called “le giratoire” or “le rond-point”. The traffic light is called “le feu”. **Le pont**, the bridge, crosses a river. “Traversez le pont” means “Cross the bridge”. By the way, there are many bridges in Lausanne, because the town lies on a steep slope.

gewusst: In French the traffic light is called “le feu”, literally “the fire”.
Instead of “Where is …?” you can also say: “Je cherche la gare”, I am looking for the station.

teile.einleitung: In a restaurant you need a few special words to order and to pay. A French menu usually has a fixed order of courses. Here you learn how to find your way around a restaurant.
wichtigste: “La carte” is the menu.
“L'entrée” is the starter, “le plat principal” the main course, “le dessert” the pudding.
“Le serveur” is the waiter, “la serveuse” the waitress.
“Vous avez choisi ?” means “Have you chosen?”.
To pay you say “L'addition, s'il vous plaît”.
“Une carafe d'eau” is a jug of tap water.

abschnitte.text: In a restaurant you first ask for **la carte**, the menu. The dishes are listed on it. You can order **à la carte**, which means choosing individual dishes. Or you take **le menu**, a fixed set of several courses for one price. The waiter is called **le serveur**, the waitress **la serveuse**. In the kitchen works **le cuisinier**, the cook.

A meal starts with **l'entrée**, the starter. The word literally means “entrance”, because it is the first course. Then comes **le plat principal**, the main course, for example meat or fish with a side dish. At the end there is **le dessert**, the pudding. That might be a crème brûlée or an ice cream.

The waiter often asks **“Vous avez choisi ?”**. “Choisir” means to choose, so he wants to know whether you have already chosen. Then you say, for example, “Je voudrais le poulet, s'il vous plaît” (I would like the chicken, please). If you want water, you order **une carafe d'eau**. This is a jug of tap water, which in France is usually free in restaurants. Before eating people wish each other **Bon appétit !**.

If you want to pay, you say **“L'addition, s'il vous plaît”**. “L'addition” is the bill in a restaurant. In France people pay in euros, in French-speaking Switzerland in francs. The tip is called **le pourboire**, literally “for drinking”. When you leave you say “Merci, au revoir !”.

gewusst: The word “restaurant” came into German, and into English, from French.
In French “l'entrée” is the starter, whereas in American English “entrée” usually means the main course.

teile.einleitung: The passé simple is a past tense found mainly in books. In fairy tales, novels and history books it tells what once happened.
wichtigste: The passé simple is a tense of the written language.
It is found mainly in novels, fairy tales and historical narratives.
In conversation people almost always use the passé composé instead.
Verbs ending in -er have the endings -ai, -as, -a, -âmes, -âtes, -èrent.
Regular verbs ending in -ir end in -is, -is, -it, -îmes, -îtes, -irent.
Important irregular forms are “il fut”, “ils eurent”, “je fis” and “ils vinrent”.

abschnitte.text: **Passé simple** means “simple past”, because it consists of just one word. In everyday life you hardly ever hear it. But if you read a French fairy tale or novel, you meet it all the time. A fairy tale might go on like this, for example: “Le roi fut très content.” (The king was very pleased.) That is why it is important to **recognise** the forms, even if you rarely write them yourself.

When you talk about completed events, you use the **passé composé**. Instead of “il parla” you say “il a parlé” in conversation. Both forms mean the same thing (he spoke), but they belong to different areas of the language. The passé simple sounds solemn and literary. It still sometimes appears in newspapers and news reports, especially in the 3rd person.

Verbs ending in **-er** such as “parler” get the endings -ai, -as, -a, -âmes, -âtes, -èrent. This gives: je parlai, tu parlas, il parla, nous parlâmes, vous parlâtes, ils parlèrent. You most often read the **3rd person**, that is “il parla” and “ils parlèrent”. The forms with nous and vous carry a **circumflex** (^) on the vowel.

Regular verbs ending in **-ir** such as “finir” have the endings -is, -is, -it, -îmes, -îtes, -irent. So: je finis, il finit, nous finîmes, ils finirent. Careful: “je finis” and “il finit” look the same as in the present tense. Whether the present or the past is meant can then be seen from the **context** of the story.

Some important verbs have a special stem. **Être** has the stem “fu-”: je fus, il fut, ils furent. **Avoir** has “eu-”: j'eus, il eut, ils eurent. **Faire** forms its endings with “fi-”: je fis, il fit, nous fîmes. **Venir** has “vin-”: je vins, il vint, ils vinrent. Similar-looking forms such as “fût” or “ils eussent” belong to another tense, the subjonctif imparfait.

gewusst: Many French children first get to know the passé simple by reading fairy tales.
The forms “il fut” (he was) and “il fit” (he did) differ by just one letter.

teile.einleitung: The plural is the form of a noun for more than one. In English it is usually simple: you add an s. But there are a few rules and some exceptions you have to learn by heart.
wichtigste: Most nouns get an s in the plural: cat becomes cats, book becomes books.
After s, x, ch and sh you add es: box becomes boxes, bus becomes buses.
If a word ends in a consonant and y, the y becomes ies: baby becomes babies.
Some words are irregular: child becomes children, mouse becomes mice.
Foot becomes feet, tooth becomes teeth.
Some words stay the same, for example sheep.

abschnitte.text: With most nouns the **plural** is formed with **s**. One cat becomes two **cats**, one book becomes three **books**. Likewise: one apple, two **apples**. In English this is much simpler than in German, where there are many different endings. Depending on the word, the s is pronounced like s or like a soft z.

If a noun ends in **s, ss, x, ch** or **sh**, you add **es**. Otherwise the plural would be almost impossible to pronounce. Box becomes **boxes**, bus becomes **buses**, glass becomes glasses. Likewise: watch becomes watches, dish becomes dishes. The es is pronounced as a syllable of its own.

abschnitte.titel: Words ending in y and f
abschnitte.text: If a word ends in a **consonant and y**, the y becomes **ies**: baby becomes babies, city becomes cities. If there is a vowel before the y, it stays: boy becomes boys, day becomes days. Some words ending in **f** or **fe** change to **ves**: leaf becomes leaves, knife becomes knives. It is best to learn these words one by one.

Some words have a plural all of their own. **Child** becomes **children**, **mouse** becomes **mice** and **foot** becomes **feet**. Likewise man becomes men, woman becomes women and tooth becomes teeth. These forms are very old and come from earlier stages of the English language. Because they are used so often, they have survived to this day.

With some words the singular and plural are the same. Examples are **sheep**, **fish** and **deer**. So you say “one sheep, ten sheep”. Other words exist only in the plural, for example **trousers**, **glasses** for spectacles and **scissors**.

gewusst: The plural of person is usually people, not persons.
German also has a vowel change in Maus and Mäuse, very similar to mouse and mice.

teile.einleitung: You need the parts of the body when you describe yourself or say where something hurts. Here you learn the most important words from head to toe. Some of them have a special plural.
wichtigste: “La tête” is the head, and on it grow “les cheveux”, the hair.
“L'œil” is the eye; several eyes are called “les yeux”.
“Le nez” is the nose, “la bouche” the mouth, “l'oreille” the ear.
“La main” is the hand, “le bras” the arm.
“Le pied” is the foot, “la jambe” the leg.
In “pied” and “bras” the last letter is not pronounced.

abschnitte.text: The head is called **la tête**. On your head grow **les cheveux**, your hair. On your face are **le nez**, the nose, and **la bouche**, the mouth. You smell with your nose, and you eat and speak with your mouth. Inside your mouth are **les dents**, your teeth.

The eye is called **l'œil**. Several eyes are called something completely different: **les yeux**. This is one of the strangest plural forms in French. The ear is called **l'oreille**; you hear with your ears. Before a vowel, “le” or “la” becomes **l'**, which is why you say “l'œil” and “l'oreille”.

The arm is called **le bras**. The “s” at the end is not pronounced. The hand is called **la main**; a hand has five fingers, **les doigts**. You write, paint and grab things with your hands. The back is called **le dos**, the tummy **le ventre**.

The leg is called **la jambe**, the foot **le pied**. In “pied” the “d” at the end is not pronounced. To go on foot is **aller à pied**. If something hurts, you say **J'ai mal à …**: “J'ai mal à la tête” means “I have a headache”. With masculine words it is “J'ai mal au pied” (my foot hurts).

gewusst: The word “œil” is pronounced roughly like “uhy”.
“La main” gives the expression “à la main”, meaning “by hand”.

teile.einleitung: “Être” means “to be” and “avoir” means “to have”. These two verbs are among the most important in French. They are irregular, so it is best to learn their forms by heart.
wichtigste: “Être” means “to be”: je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont.
“Avoir” means “to have”: j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont.
Before a vowel, “je” becomes “j'”, which is why it is “j'ai”.
Age is given with “avoir”: “J'ai douze ans”.
Do not mix up “ils ont” (they have) and “ils sont” (they are).
“Est” from “être” and “et” (and) sound the same but mean different things.

abschnitte.text: With **être** you say who someone is or what they are like. The forms are **je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont**. “Tu es” and “il est” sound the same. “Vous êtes” is written with an **accent circonflexe**, the little roof on the first e. An example: “Je suis suisse.” (I am Swiss.) Nationalities are written with a small letter here, because they are adjectives.

With **avoir** you say what someone has. The forms are **j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont**. Because “ai” begins with a vowel, “je” becomes **j'**. The forms “nous avons” and “vous avez” have the usual endings -ons and -ez. “Ils ont un chien” means: They have a dog.

Sometimes French uses **avoir** where English and German use “to be”. For age you say “J'ai douze ans”, literally “I have twelve years”. For feelings, too, you say “have”: **avoir faim** (to be hungry), **avoir soif** (to be thirsty), **avoir froid** (to be cold). So “Tu as douze ans” means “You are twelve”.
