Some forms look alike. **Ils ont** (they have) is linked with a soft s sound like a z, **ils sont** (they are) with a sharp s. **Est** and **et** also sound the same: “Elle est contente” means “She is pleased”, while “et” simply means “and”. If you read aloud and listen carefully, you will learn the differences quickly.

“Être” and “avoir” are also **auxiliary verbs**. You use them to form the **passé composé**, a past tense. Most verbs need “avoir”, for example “J'ai mangé” (I have eaten). Some verbs of movement need “être”, for example “Je suis allé” (I have gone).

gewusst: “Être” and “avoir” are among the verbs that occur most often in French.
In German, too, “sein” (to be) and “haben” (to have) are auxiliary verbs for the past, just as “have” is in English.

teile.einleitung: People like talking about hobbies when they get to know someone. In French you need a few verbs and little words such as “au” or “du” for this. Here you learn how to say what you like doing.
wichtigste: “J'aime” means “I like” or “I love”, and it is followed by a verb in the infinitive.
“J'aime nager” means “I like swimming”.
For sports you say “jouer au”: “Je joue au football”.
For musical instruments you say “jouer du”: “Je joue du piano”.
Many sports are formed with “faire du”: “faire du ski”.
With “ne … pas” you say what you do not like doing.

abschnitte.text: With **J'aime** you say what you like doing. It is followed by a verb in the **infinitive**: “J'aime **nager**” means “I like swimming”. “J'aime **danser**” means “I like dancing”. With **ne … pas** you make it negative: “Je n'aime pas chanter” means “I don't like singing”. To ask about someone's hobby you say “Qu'est-ce que tu aimes faire ?” (What do you like doing?).

For games and ball sports you say **jouer au**. “Je joue au football” means “I play football”. In the same way you say “jouer au tennis” or “jouer au basket”. With feminine words it is **jouer à la**, in the plural **jouer aux**, for example “jouer aux cartes”, to play cards. “Je joue” means “I play”.

For **musical instruments** you say **jouer du** or **jouer de la**. “Je joue du piano” means “I play the piano”. For the guitar it is “Je joue de la guitare”. So the difference is: sport with “au”, instruments with “du”. That way you can tell straight away whether someone is playing a game or making music.

Many sports are formed with **faire du** or **faire de la**. “Faire du ski” means “to go skiing”, a very popular hobby in Switzerland. You also say “faire du vélo” (to cycle) or “faire de la natation” (to swim). Other hobbies are **lire** (reading) and **dessiner** (drawing). To read a book is “lire un livre”, and a drawing is “un dessin”.

gewusst: A hobby is called “un loisir” or “un passe-temps” in French, literally “pastime”.
In French-speaking Switzerland a bicycle is usually called “le vélo”; in France people also say “la bicyclette”.

teile.einleitung: Polite words open many doors, in French too. With “merci”, “s'il vous plaît” and the right form of address you will make a good impression in French-speaking Switzerland and in France. Here you learn the most important polite expressions.
wichtigste: “Merci beaucoup” means “Thank you very much”.
To answer “Merci !” you say “De rien !”.
“Excusez-moi” is a polite apology; “Pardon !” is said after an accident.
Adults you do not know are addressed with “vous”, like the German “Sie”.
A woman is addressed as “Madame”, a man as “Monsieur”.
“Je voudrais” means “I would like” and sounds polite.

abschnitte.text: “Thank you” is **merci**, “thank you very much” is **merci beaucoup**, because “beaucoup” means “a lot”. When someone answers your thanks, they often say **De rien !**, meaning “You're welcome” or literally “For nothing”. “Please” is **s'il vous plaît** to adults and **s'il te plaît** among friends. If you are happy to do something, you say **Avec plaisir !**, “with pleasure”.

If you bump into someone by accident, you say **Pardon !**. To adults you politely say **Excusez-moi**, “Excuse me”. You also need this when you want to ask someone something: “Excusez-moi, où est la gare ?” (Excuse me, where is the station?). Among friends it is **Excuse-moi**. For a bigger mistake you say “Je suis désolé”, meaning “I'm sorry”.

In French there are two ways of addressing someone. You say **tu** to friends, family and children. **Vous** is the polite form, like the German “Sie”. You use it with adults you do not know, for example in a shop, or with a teacher. A woman is addressed as **Madame**, a man as **Monsieur**. So you say “Bonjour Madame” or “Bonjour Monsieur”.

If you would like something, you say **Je voudrais**, “I would like”. That sounds friendlier than “Je veux”, “I want”. “Je voudrais un verre d'eau, s'il vous plaît” means “I would like a glass of water, please”. When saying goodbye, people often wish you **Bonne journée !**, have a nice day. In the evening they say **Bonne soirée !**.

gewusst: “S'il vous plaît” literally means “if it pleases you”.
In French-speaking Switzerland and in France people usually say “Bonjour” when they go into a small shop.

teile.einleitung: When you go shopping in French, you need a few important words and sentences. You have to know where to buy what, how to ask what something costs and how to pay. In French-speaking Switzerland you can try it out straight away.
wichtigste: “Combien ça coûte ?” means: How much does it cost?
In the “boulangerie” you buy bread, in the “boucherie” meat.
“Je voudrais ...” is the polite way to say what you would like.
You pay at the “caisse”.
“C'est trop cher” means: That's too expensive.
“La monnaie” is the change or small coins.
“Le marché” is the market.

abschnitte.text: Bread, baguettes and croissants are bought in the “**boulangerie**”, the bakery. Meat is sold in the “**boucherie**”, the butcher's. The butcher is called “le boucher”. You find fresh vegetables and fruit at the “**marché**”, the market. Careful: “la marche” without an accent means walking or a step. Many things are also bought in the “supermarché”, the supermarket.

If you want to buy something, you politely say “**Je voudrais ...**”, which means “I would like ...”. For example: “Je voudrais un kilo de **pommes**, s'il vous plaît.” Then you get a kilo of apples. Watch out: the potato is called “la pomme de terre”, literally “earth apple”. To greet someone you say “Bonjour, Madame” or “Bonjour, Monsieur”, and when you leave, “Merci, au revoir”.

If you want to know what something costs, you ask “**Combien ça coûte ?**”. “Combien” means how much, “coûter” means to cost. If something is too expensive for you, you say “**C'est trop cher**”. “Cher” means expensive, “trop” means too. In French-speaking Switzerland, as in the whole of Switzerland, people pay in **francs** and centimes; in France they pay in euros.

You pay at the “**caisse**”, the till. The female cashier is called “la caissière”, the male cashier “le caissier”. If you hand over a large note, you get “**la monnaie**” back. That is the **change** or small coins. The receipt is called “le ticket de caisse”.

gewusst: In French-speaking Switzerland the Rappen (the hundredth part of a franc) is called “le centime” in French.
The word “monnaie” also means currency: the franc is “la monnaie suisse”.

teile.einleitung: Possessive determiners show whom something belongs to: my book, your sister, our class. In French they agree with the noun that comes after them.
wichtigste: For “my” you say mon, ma or mes.
For “your” you say ton, ta or tes; for “his” or “her” son, sa or ses.
For “our” it is notre and nos, for “your” (plural) votre and vos.
If something belongs to several people, you say leur or leurs.
The determiner agrees with the noun, not with the owner.
Before a vowel you use mon, ton or son, even with feminine words: “mon école”.

abschnitte.text: A **possessive determiner** stands in front of a noun and shows who owns something. In English these are words like my, your, his, her, our and their. In French the form depends on whether the noun is **masculine** or **feminine** and whether it is **singular** or **plural**. That is why there are three forms for “my”: mon vélo (my bike), ma maison (my house), mes livres (my books).

If something belongs to one person, these forms apply: **mon, ma, mes** for I, **ton, ta, tes** for you and **son, sa, ses** for he or she. Examples: ta sœur (your sister), son vélo, sa maison. Important: “son” and “sa” agree with the thing. “C'est la maison de Léa” (it is Léa's house) becomes “sa maison”, and “le vélo de Paul” becomes “son vélo”. Whether the owner is a boy or a girl makes no difference.

If something belongs to several people, there are only two forms per person. For “our” it is **notre** in the singular and **nos** in the plural: notre classe (our class), nos amis (our friends). For “your” (plural) you say **votre** and **vos**: vos cahiers (your exercise books). For “their” you say **leur** and **leurs**: leur maison (their house), leurs enfants (their children). Careful: “vous” is a pronoun and not a determiner.

If a feminine word begins with a **vowel** or a silent h, you still use mon, ton or son. That makes the word easier to pronounce. So you say “mon école” instead of “ma école” and “ton amie” instead of “ta amie”. When speaking, the two words are run together: “mo-nécole”. This link is called a **liaison**.

gewusst: German, like English, distinguishes “sein” (his) and “ihr” (her) according to the owner; in French there is no such difference with son and sa.
“Mon amie” and “mon ami” sound exactly the same when spoken; you can only see the difference in writing.

teile.einleitung: The passé composé is the most important past tense in spoken French. You use it to tell what happened yesterday, last week or in the holidays.
wichtigste: The passé composé has two parts: an auxiliary verb and the past participle.
Most verbs form it with “avoir”, for example “j'ai mangé”.
Verbs of movement such as “aller”, “venir”, “partir” and “arriver” take “être”.
Verbs ending in -er have a participle ending in -é; verbs like “finir” have one ending in -i.
Many common verbs have an irregular participle: “pris”, “fait”, “eu”.
With “être” the participle agrees with the subject: “Marie est arrivée”.

abschnitte.text: Passé composé literally means “compound past”. It consists of an **auxiliary verb** in the present and the **past participle**. The auxiliary is either “avoir” or “être”. In the sentence “Nous avons regardé un film” (we watched a film), “avons” is the auxiliary and “regardé” the participle. This is similar to English and German: “We have watched a film”, “Wir haben einen Film geschaut”.

The vast majority of verbs form the passé composé with **avoir**. So you say “j'ai mangé” (I ate), “tu as joué” (you played) or “ils ont travaillé” (they worked). “Avoir” itself and “être” also take avoir: “j'ai eu”, “j'ai été”. With avoir the participle stays unchanged in simple sentences. That is why it is “nous avons regardé” with no extra ending.

A small group of verbs takes **être**. They are mainly verbs of movement and change: aller, venir, partir, arriver, entrer, sortir, monter, descendre, naître and mourir. So you say “je suis venu” (I came) and “Paul est allé au marché” (Paul went to the market). With être the participle agrees with the subject. For a woman an **e** is added, in the plural an **s**: “Marie est arrivée”, “ils sont partis”.

With verbs ending in **-er** the participle ends in -é: parler becomes parlé, manger becomes mangé. Verbs like “finir” form it with **-i**: “j'ai fini”. Many common verbs are **irregular**. It is best to learn them by heart: prendre becomes pris, faire becomes fait, avoir becomes eu, être becomes été, voir becomes vu. “Apprendre” and “comprendre” also follow the pattern of prendre: appris, compris.

With the passé composé you tell about **completed events**. Typical signal words are “hier” (yesterday), “la semaine dernière” (last week) or “il y a deux jours” (two days ago). In everyday life, in letters and in conversations it is the usual past tense. For descriptions and habits in the past, on the other hand, people often use the **imparfait**.

gewusst: French has a memory aid for the être verbs: you picture a house that you go into, climb up, go down and come out of again.
All reflexive verbs such as “se lever” (to get up) form the passé composé with être: “je me suis levé”.

teile.einleitung: Food and drink are among the first words you learn in a new language. In English the word for “Essen” is “food”. Many words sound similar to German and are therefore easy to remember.
wichtigste: An “Apfel” is called an “apple” in English.
“Bread” means Brot, “milk” means Milch.
“Cheese” is the English word for Käse.
An “Ei” is called an “egg”, “Wasser” is called “water”.
A “Rüebli” (Swiss German for carrot) is called a “carrot” in English.
A “pear” is a Birne.

abschnitte.text: Fruit (in German “Früchte”) is called **fruit** in English. An Apfel is an **apple**, a Birne a **pear**. You pronounce “pear” roughly like “pair”. The banana is called a **banana** and the orange an **orange**. Erdbeeren are **strawberries**, and Trauben are called **grapes**.

Gemüse is called **vegetables**. The Karotte, in Switzerland the **Rüebli**, is a **carrot** in English. Kartoffeln are called **potatoes** and Tomaten **tomatoes**. A salad for eating is called a **salad**. Vegetables contain lots of vitamins and are healthy.

For breakfast, **breakfast** in English, there is often **bread**, **butter** and **jam**. You pronounce “bread” like “bred”. With it people drink **milk**. Hens lay **eggs**. Switzerland is famous for its **cheese**.

Getränke are called **drinks**. The best drink when you are thirsty is **water**. Fruit juice is called **juice**, for example **apple juice**. Adults often drink **tea** or **coffee**. If you are thirsty, you say **I'm thirsty**.

If you are hungry, you say **I'm hungry**. If you would like something, you ask politely: **Can I have an apple, please?** The meals are called **breakfast**, **lunch** (the midday meal) and **dinner** (the evening meal). Before eating, people in English sometimes say **Enjoy your meal**, like “En Guete” in Swiss German.

gewusst: Many English food words are related to German: “milk” and Milch, “bread” and Brot, “water” and Wasser.
The English word “orange” means both the fruit and the colour.

teile.einleitung: Formal English texts such as job applications, business letters or enquiries follow their own rules. They are polite, factual and precise. They include fixed forms of address, certain abbreviations and an elevated choice of words.
wichtigste: “To Whom It May Concern” addresses readers you do not know.
“Ms” is the neutral form of address for women.
In formal texts, short forms such as “don't” are written out in full.
Instead of “ask for”, formal writing uses “request”.
“Encl.” points to an enclosure, and with “p.p.” you sign on someone's behalf.
Americans write the month before the day in dates.

abschnitte.text: If the recipient is completely unknown, for example in a reference or a job testimonial, you traditionally write **To Whom It May Concern**. For a woman you use **Ms** if her marital status is unknown or unimportant. **Mrs** traditionally refers to married women, **Miss** to unmarried women. For men there is only **Mr**.

Formal texts avoid **short forms** such as “don't” or “we're”. They are correct, but they sound informal. So you write **do not** and **we are**. Instead of phrasal verbs such as “ask for”, single verbs of Latin origin are often preferred, for example **request**. A sentence like “We request further information” sounds polite and factual.

**Encl.** stands for “enclosure” or “enclosed” and points to documents included with the letter. **p.p.** before a signature comes from the Latin “per procurationem”. It shows that someone is signing on another person's behalf. A copy to other people is marked with **cc**, an afterthought with **P.S.**. Invitations often say **RSVP**, from the French “répondez s'il vous plaît”, meaning “please reply”.

British and American English differ when it comes to dates. In the USA the **month comes before the day**, followed by a comma and the year: **October 11, 2026**. In Great Britain people write **11 October 2026**. With numbers only, such as 10/11/2026, this can lead to confusion. That is why it is best to write out the month in formal letters.

gewusst: The form of address “Ms” became widespread mainly from the 1970s onwards.
Today many companies write a bit more casually even in formal emails, but job applications usually stay strictly formal.

teile.einleitung: Letters and emails in English follow fixed rules. Depending on whether you are writing to a company or to a friend, you choose a different **greeting** and a different **closing**. The fields of an email also have English names.
wichtigste: Without a name, a formal letter begins with “Dear Sir or Madam”.
In British English this is followed by the closing “Yours faithfully”.
If you know the name, you end with “Yours sincerely”.
To friends you write casually, for example “Love” or “Best wishes”.
The “Subject” field contains what the email is about.
With “cc” you send a copy; an “attachment” is a file you add.

abschnitte.text: A formal letter begins with **Dear**. If you know the name, you write, for example, **Dear Ms Brown** or **Dear Mr Smith**. If you do not know it, the usual greeting is **Dear Sir or Madam**. After the greeting comes a comma. Among people who know each other, a casual **Hi** or **Hello** is enough.

In British English the closing depends on the greeting. “Dear Sir or Madam” is followed by **Yours faithfully**. If there is a name in the greeting, you end with **Yours sincerely**. In American letters “Sincerely” or “Sincerely yours” is common. **Kind regards** or **Best regards** are neutral and often suitable too.

To friends and family you write in a casual, personal way. You begin with **Dear Tom** or **Hi Tom** and end with **Love**, **Best wishes** or **See you**. Formal closings such as “Yours faithfully” do not fit here. Often you ask at the beginning how the person is and then tell your news.

The **Subject** line says briefly what it is about. By the way, the word can also mean a school subject. **Cc** comes from “carbon copy”: everyone can see who gets a copy. With **bcc** this stays hidden. An **attachment** is a file attached to the email, for example a photo. People then often write “Please find attached ...”.

Formal letters often end with **I look forward to hearing from you**. “To look forward to” means to be pleased about something that is coming. At the beginning you might write **I am writing to ...** to give the reason for writing. If you are asking for something, **Could you please ...** is polite.

gewusst: A “carbon copy” used to be a second copy made with carbon paper while typing on a typewriter.
In English, Ms, Mr and Mrs are usually written without a full stop in British letters and with one in American letters.

teile.einleitung: The “Röstigraben” (rösti ditch) is a joking expression for the border between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland. It refers to differences in language, attitudes and voting behaviour.
wichtigste: The Röstigraben is not a real ditch, but a border of culture and attitudes.
Rösti is seen as a typical dish of German-speaking Switzerland, hence the name.
The River Saane (Sarine in French) is often named as its symbolic course.
Bern, Fribourg and Valais are officially bilingual in German and French.
Biel/Bienne is considered the largest bilingual town in Switzerland.
The Röstigraben showed especially clearly in the vote on the EEA on 6 December 1992.

abschnitte.text: **Rösti**, a dish of fried grated potatoes, is seen as a typical dish of German-speaking Switzerland. That is why people jokingly speak of the **Röstigraben** when talking about differences between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland. In the Romandie it is called the “barrière de rösti” or “rideau de rösti”, the rösti barrier or rösti curtain. It refers to differences in **attitudes**, in habits and above all in **voting behaviour**.

The **Saane** is often named as its symbolic course. It flows through the canton of Fribourg and the town of Fribourg, near where the language border lies. In Valais the stream **Raspille** between Salgesch and Sierre is seen as the border: above it most people speak German, below it French. The cantons of **Bern**, **Fribourg** and **Valais** are officially bilingual in German and French.

The Röstigraben became especially visible on **6 December 1992**. On that day Switzerland voted on joining the **European Economic Area** (EEA). All the French-speaking cantons said yes, most German-speaking cantons said no. The people narrowly rejected it with 50.3 per cent voting no, and the majority of the cantons also said no. Since then experts have watched many votes to see whether the language regions differ.

There are places where both languages live together quite naturally. **Biel/Bienne** is considered the largest bilingual town in Switzerland. German and French are official languages there with equal rights, and the street signs are bilingual. At school, too, children all over Switzerland learn a second national language. This helps the regions get to know each other better.

Based on the Röstigraben, people also speak of the **Polentagraben**, the polenta ditch. It is a joking name for the border between German-speaking Switzerland and **Ticino**, because polenta is seen as a typical Ticino dish. Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. The canton of **the Grisons** is even trilingual, with German, Romansh and Italian.

gewusst: Although rösti is seen as German-Swiss, people in the Romandie enjoy eating it too.
The expression “Röstigraben” is so well known that French-language newspapers often simply use it in German.

teile.einleitung: The chanson is the French-language song in which the lyrics are especially important. Famous singers from France, Belgium and Canada made it known all over the world. There are also children's songs that are sung in Swiss schools too.
wichtigste: Édith Piaf became world-famous with “Non, je ne regrette rien”.
The French national anthem is called “La Marseillaise”.
Jacques Brel came from Belgium and wrote “Ne me quitte pas” in 1959.
Céline Dion won the Eurovision Song Contest for Switzerland in 1988.
Stromae (“Alors on danse”) comes from Belgium.
Well-known children's songs are “Frère Jacques”, “Sur le pont d'Avignon” and “Alouette”.

abschnitte.text: **Édith Piaf** was one of the best-known chanson singers in France. Her nickname was “the Sparrow of Paris”, and she became world-famous with “**Non, je ne regrette rien**”. After 1945 **Juliette Gréco** was seen as the muse of the existentialists in the Paris quarter of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. She sang lyrics by Jean-Paul Sartre, Raymond Queneau and Jacques Prévert. Her trademark was her black dress.

Not all chanson singers come from France. **Jacques Brel** was born in 1929 in Schaerbeek near Brussels in **Belgium**. In 1959 he wrote “**Ne me quitte pas**”, one of the most famous chansons of all. Later he lived in Paris and in Polynesia. The singer **Stromae** also comes from Belgium. He was born in Brussels in 1985 and became famous with “Alors on danse”.

In 1988 the **Eurovision Song Contest** took place in Dublin. The Canadian singer **Céline Dion** competed for **Switzerland**. With the song “Ne partez pas sans moi” she won by a narrow margin. Afterwards she became one of the most successful singers in the world. For Switzerland it was the second win in the contest after 1956; in 2024 Nemo brought the third.

The French national anthem is called “**La Marseillaise**”. Rouget de Lisle wrote it in 1792, and soldiers from Marseille made it known in Paris. Many children know “**Frère Jacques, dormez-vous ?**”: Brother John is asleep and is supposed to ring the morning bells. In “**Sur le pont d'Avignon**” people dance on the medieval Saint-Bénézet bridge over the Rhone. The song “**Alouette, gentille alouette**” is about a lark, a songbird.

gewusst: The bridge at Avignon has not survived complete: only four of its original more than twenty arches are still standing.
The Rhone, which the bridge at Avignon crosses, rises at the Rhone Glacier in the canton of Valais.

teile.einleitung: In the discours indirect, reported speech, you tell what someone has said or asked without quoting them word for word. The pronouns change, and often the tenses and time expressions too. What matters most is the tense of the introducing verb.
wichtigste: If the introducing verb is in the present, the tense stays the same.
If it is in the past, the present becomes the imparfait.
The passé composé becomes the plus-que-parfait.
The futur simple becomes the conditionnel présent.
Yes-no questions are introduced with “si”.
“Qu'est-ce que” becomes “ce que”, “qu'est-ce qui” becomes “ce qui”.
An imperative becomes “de” plus infinitive.

abschnitte.text: If the introducing verb, such as “dire” (to say), is in the **present**, the tense in reported speech stays **unchanged**. Only the pronouns change. “Il dit : ‘Je suis fatigué.’” (He says: ‘I am tired.’) becomes “**Il dit qu'il est fatigué.**” (He says that he is tired.) “Je” becomes “il”, because now someone else is telling it. Reported speech is introduced with “**que**”.

If the introducing verb is in the **past**, the tenses shift. The **present** becomes the **imparfait**: “Il a dit qu'il **était** fatigué.” (He said he was tired.) The **passé composé** becomes the **plus-que-parfait**: “Elle a dit qu'elle **avait fini**.” (She said she had finished.) The **futur simple** becomes the **conditionnel présent**: “Il a dit qu'il **viendrait**.” (He said he would come.) This form is also called “futur dans le passé”.

Questions can also be reported indirectly. **Yes-no questions**, which you answer with yes or no, are introduced with “**si**” (whether): “Il demande **si** tu viens.” (He asks whether you are coming.) “**Qu'est-ce que**” asks about the object and becomes “**ce que**”: “Elle demande ce que tu fais.” (She asks what you are doing.) “**Qu'est-ce qui**” asks about the subject and becomes “**ce qui**”: “Il demande ce qui se passe.” (He asks what is happening.)

An **order** in the imperative is reported with “**de**” and the **infinitive**. “Il m'a dit : ‘Ferme la porte !’” (He said to me: ‘Shut the door!’) becomes “Il m'a dit **de fermer** la porte.” (He told me to shut the door.) Time expressions change too, because the moment of telling has moved. “Demain” (tomorrow) becomes “**le lendemain**”, the next day. “Hier” (yesterday) becomes “**la veille**” (the day before), “aujourd'hui” (today) becomes “ce jour-là” (that day).

gewusst: In German reported speech often uses the subjunctive (“er sagt, er sei müde”, he says he is tired); French has no special verb form for this.
With “si” and “il” the words merge: you write “s'il”, but “si elle”.

teile.einleitung: Common verbs are the doing words that you need again and again in a language, such as be, have, go, make and want. In English they include “to buy” and “to understand”, and in French “aller” (to go) and “faire” (to make or do). If you have a sure grasp of these verbs, you can already make a great many sentences.
wichtigste: The English verb “to buy” means “kaufen” in German.
“To forget” means “vergessen” and “to understand” means “verstehen”.
The French “aller” means to go and “venir” means to come.
“Faire” means to make or do, and “prendre” means to take.
“Vouloir” means to want.
The most common verbs are almost always irregular.
In English the little word “to” often comes before the basic form of a verb.

abschnitte.text: **Verbs** are the heart of a sentence, because without a verb there is hardly ever a complete sentence. A few verbs come up especially often in every language, such as be, have, go and make. In English these are “to be”, “to have”, “to do” and “to go”. If you learn these first, you can hold simple conversations very quickly.

In English the little word **“to”** comes before the basic form, for example “to buy” or “to forget”. In the present the verb hardly changes; only with he, she and it is an -s added: “she buys”. Many common verbs are **irregular**, such as buy, bought, bought or forget, forgot, forgotten. Another important verb is “to understand”, with the past form “understood”.

French verbs are divided into groups according to their ending: -er, -ir and -re. Most end in **-er**, like “parler” (to speak), and are regular. But the most common verbs, such as aller (to go), faire (to make or do), prendre (to take), vouloir (to want) and venir (to come), are irregular. With “aller”, for example, it is je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont.

The verbs “be” and “have” are also **auxiliary verbs**, which are used to form tenses. In English you say “I have finished”. In French the passé composé is formed with avoir or être: “j’ai mangé” (I have eaten) and “je suis venu” (I have come). Verbs of movement such as aller and venir usually take être.

In both English and French you can express the **near future** with the verb go. In English you say “I’m going to buy a new bike.” In French it is “Je vais acheter un vélo.”, literally “I go to buy a bike”. This form is very handy, because you only have to conjugate one verb.

Verbs are best learnt with their **principal parts** or in small tables. It helps to say them aloud or put them into sentences, for example “I forgot my homework.” Many learners practise with index cards or learning apps. If you practise for a few minutes every day, you remember the forms better than with one long learning marathon.

begriffe.erklaerung: A doing word that says what someone does or what happens.
A verb whose forms do not follow a fixed rule and have to be learnt by heart.
The change of a verb according to person and tense.
A verb such as have or be that helps to form other tenses.

gewusst: With be, am, is, are, was, were and been, the English “to be” has a particularly large number of different forms.
Most French verbs end in -er and are regular, but the most important ones are not.
The past of “go” is “went”, which originally came from a completely different verb.

teile.einleitung: A question is a sentence you use when you want to know something, and it ends with a question mark. English and French have their own rules for questions, which are different from German. If you can ask questions correctly, you can hold conversations, find out new things and make friends.
wichtigste: Question words such as “Where”, “What” or “How” introduce wh- questions.
“Where” asks about the place.
In English many questions are formed with “do” or “does”, for example “Do you like pizza?”
With he, she and it you need “does”: “Does she play tennis?”
You ask about the price with “How much is this T-shirt?”
In French you can introduce yes/no questions with “Est-ce que”.
“Comment tu t’appelles ?” means “What’s your name?”

abschnitte.text: There are two main kinds of question. **Yes/no questions** can be answered with yes or no, for example “Do you like pizza?” **Wh- questions** begin with a question word and ask for a more precise answer, such as “Where do you live?” In English they are called “wh-questions” because most question words begin with “wh”.

The most important English question words are **who**, what, where, when, why and how. “Where” asks about the place, “when” about the time. With “How much” you ask about price or amount, for example “How much is this T-shirt?” “How old are you?” asks about someone’s age.

In English you usually need an **auxiliary verb** for questions. With ordinary verbs it is “do”, and with he, she and it “does”: “Does she play tennis?” The main verb then stays in the basic form, so “play” and not “plays”. With “to be” and with auxiliary verbs such as “can”, you just change the order: “Are you ready?” or “Can you swim?”

In French there are three ways of asking a question. You can simply **raise your voice**: “Tu viens ?” You can put **“Est-ce que”** in front: “Est-ce que tu viens ?” In polite written language you swap the verb and the pronoun: “Viens-tu ?” (Are you coming?)

You ask someone’s name with “Comment tu t’appelles ?” and their age with **“Quel âge as-tu ?”**. “Pourquoi” means why, “où” means where and “quand” means when. You ask about the price with “Combien ça coûte ?” In written French there is a small space before the question mark.

With questions the **intonation**, the melody of the sentence, often changes. With yes/no questions the voice usually goes up at the end. With wh- questions in English it often falls again at the end. So if you listen carefully, you can recognise a question even without a question mark.

begriffe.erklaerung: The punctuation mark ? that comes at the end of a question.
A word that introduces a question, for example where, why or pourquoi.
A verb that helps another verb form questions or tenses, such as do or have.
How the voice goes up or down when speaking.

gewusst: In Spanish an upside-down question mark also comes at the beginning of a question.
In English almost all question words begin with “wh”; only “how” is the odd one out.
A question mark with no text, just “?”, can already be a whole question in a chat.

teile.einleitung: **Etymology** studies where words come from and how they have changed. The English language has an especially eventful history. It has taken in words from Germanic, from French and from many other languages of the world.
wichtigste: English is named after the Angles, a Germanic tribe.
The Norman Conquest of 1066 brought many French words.
The word “beef” comes from French, while “cow” is Germanic.
“Kindergarten” is a German loanword in English.
“Robot” comes from Czech, “shampoo” from Hindi.
The Great Vowel Shift separated pronunciation from spelling.

abschnitte.text: In the 5th century Germanic tribes came to Britain: the **Angles**, the **Saxons** and the **Jutes**. Their language is called **Old English**. The word “English” goes back to the Angles, and “England” originally meant “land of the Angles”. That is why many simple English words are related to German, for example “house” and Haus or “water” and Wasser.

In 1066 **William the Conqueror** won at **Hastings**. After that, the English upper class spoke **Anglo-Norman**, a form of French, for a long time. Thousands of words from law, government and cooking came into English this way. A nice example: the Anglo-Saxon farmers looked after the **cow**, while the Norman upper class ate the **beef**, from the Old French “boeuf”. It is similar with “pig” and “pork”.

abschnitte.titel: Words from all over the world
abschnitte.text: English has borrowed words from a great many languages. **Kindergarten** comes from German. The term goes back to **Friedrich Fröbel**, who founded the first kindergarten in 1840. **Robot** comes from Czech and became known through Karel Čapek's play “R.U.R.” of 1920. **Shampoo** comes from **Hindi** and came into English in the 18th century by way of British India.

Between about 1400 and 1700 the pronunciation of the long vowels changed a great deal. This sound change is called the **Great Vowel Shift**. The spelling, however, stayed largely the same, partly because it began to become fixed through **printing**. That is why “name” is no longer pronounced like “nahme”. And that is why English words often sound different from the way they are written.

gewusst: The word “etymology” comes from Greek: “etymos” means “true”.
The Oxford English Dictionary shows for every word since when it has been recorded.

teile.einleitung: Idioms are fixed expressions that you must not understand word for word. French has lots of funny images with animals, vegetables and parts of the body.
wichtigste: An idiom has a figurative meaning that must not be taken literally.
“Poser un lapin à quelqu'un” means to stand someone up.
“Coûter les yeux de la tête” means that something is very expensive.
Someone who is hoarse has “un chat dans la gorge” in French, but a frog in the throat in German and English.
“Tomber dans les pommes” means to faint.
“Il pleut des cordes” describes heavy rain.

abschnitte.text: Many French expressions play with **animals**. If you put down “un lapin”, a rabbit, for someone, you do not turn up for the meeting. In English this is called **standing someone up**. Originally the expression meant not paying for a service. Someone who is hoarse has a **cat in the throat** in French: “avoir un chat dans la gorge”. So similar images are drawn with different animals in different languages.

**Food** often comes up too. “Tomber dans les pommes” literally means “to fall into the apples”. It means **to faint**. Where the expression comes from is disputed. “Les carottes sont cuites” means “the carrots are cooked”: nothing can be changed any more. People say it when a situation is **lost** and nothing more can be done.

In German, someone who gives an opinion nobody asked for adds **their mustard** (“seinen Senf dazugeben”); in English they put in their two pennies' worth. In French you sprinkle a grain of salt instead: “mettre son grain de sel”. Another expression is “mettre de l'huile sur le feu”, to pour oil on the fire. It means making a quarrel even worse. This expression exists in almost the same form in German too.

When it is raining very hard, people say “il pleut des cordes”, it is raining ropes. The drops then look like **ropes** hanging from the sky. In English it is raining cats and dogs. Someone who is “dans la lune”, on the moon, has their mind elsewhere and is **daydreaming**. A related expression is “avoir la tête dans les nuages”, to have your head in the clouds.

“Coûter les yeux de la tête” literally means something costs “the eyes out of your head”. The eyes are seen as something very precious. It means that something **costs a fortune**. Images like these make a language lively. If you know idioms, you understand conversations, films and comics much better.

gewusst: For “not being quite right in the head”, French sometimes says “avoir une araignée au plafond”, to have a spider on the ceiling.
Many idioms cannot be translated literally, so it is best to learn them as whole expressions.

teile.einleitung: **English literature** goes back more than a thousand years. From ancient heroic epics to Shakespeare and modern novels, many works are world-famous. Some stories even have a connection with Switzerland.
wichtigste: Beowulf is the most famous work of Old English literature.
In the 14th century Geoffrey Chaucer wrote “The Canterbury Tales”.
Defoe's “Robinson Crusoe” from 1719 is seen as one of the earliest English novels.
Jane Austen published “Pride and Prejudice” in 1813.
Mary Shelley came up with “Frankenstein” on Lake Geneva in 1816.
In “Nineteen Eighty-Four” George Orwell invented “Big Brother”.

abschnitte.text: The oldest known heroic epic is **Beowulf**. It is written in **Old English** and has come down to us in a manuscript from around the year 1000. The hero fights the monster **Grendel**, Grendel's mother and a dragon. In the 14th century **Geoffrey Chaucer** wrote **The Canterbury Tales** in Middle English. In it, pilgrims on their way to Canterbury tell each other stories.

The best-known English poet is **William Shakespeare** (1564 to 1616). He wrote plays such as “Romeo and Juliet”, “Hamlet” and “Macbeth”, which are still performed everywhere today. In 1719 **Robinson Crusoe** by **Daniel Defoe** appeared. It tells of a shipwrecked man surviving on an island and is seen as a milestone in the development of the English **novel**.

**Jane Austen** published **Pride and Prejudice** in 1813, about Elizabeth Bennet and Mr Darcy. In 1843 **Charles Dickens** created the mean **Ebenezer Scrooge** in “A Christmas Carol”; three ghosts at Christmas make him change his ways. The **Brontë** sisters also wrote classics: **Emily Brontë** wrote “Wuthering Heights” (1847), at first under the name Ellis Bell, and **Charlotte Brontë** “Jane Eyre”.

In the rainy summer of 1816 **Lord Byron** was staying at the **Villa Diodati** in Cologny near Geneva. He challenged his guests to write ghost stories. From this **Mary Shelley** developed **Frankenstein**, which appeared in 1818. In the story “The Final Problem” (1893) **Arthur Conan Doyle** has his detective **Sherlock Holmes** fight Professor Moriarty at the **Reichenbach Falls** near Meiringen. Today there is a Sherlock Holmes Museum in Meiringen.

In **Nineteen Eighty-Four** (1949) **George Orwell** describes a state in which the leader **Big Brother** watches everyone. Since then the expression “Big Brother” has stood for surveillance. Before that Orwell wrote the fable **Animal Farm**, in which animals take over a farm. Children's books from England are also world-famous, for example “Alice's Adventures in Wonderland” by Lewis Carroll.

gewusst: Holmes survived the fall at the Reichenbach Falls: because readers missed him, Conan Doyle later brought him back.
“Wuthering Heights” is Emily Brontë's only novel.

teile.einleitung: Charles Ferdinand Ramuz was one of the most important writers of French-speaking Switzerland. He wrote in French about farmers, herdsmen and life in the mountains of Vaud and Valais. Many people know his face from the former 200-franc note.
wichtigste: Ramuz was born in Lausanne in the canton of Vaud in 1878 and died in Pully in 1947.
He was pictured on the 200-franc note of the eighth banknote series.
For Igor Stravinsky he wrote the text of “L'Histoire du soldat” (1918).
At the centre of the novel “Derborence” is a rockslide in Valais.
“La Grande Peur dans la montagne” (1926) is about an alpine pasture with a bad reputation.

abschnitte.text: **Charles Ferdinand Ramuz** was born in **Lausanne** in 1878 and came from the canton of **Vaud**. Before the First World War he lived in Paris for some years, but then returned home. He died in 1947 in **Pully** on Lake Geneva. Many of his novels are set in the mountains of Valais and Vaud. He tells of simple people, of farmers and herdsmen, and of the power of nature. His language often sounds like the spoken French of the region.

Together with the Russian composer **Igor Stravinsky**, who was living in Vaud at the time, Ramuz created **“L'Histoire du soldat”** (The Soldier's Tale). Ramuz wrote the text and Stravinsky the music. It is about a soldier who sells his **violin** to the devil. The piece was first performed in **Lausanne** in 1918 and is still often performed today.

In the novel **“Derborence”** a **rockslide** buries an alpine pasture in Valais. A herdsman whom everyone believes to be dead returns after several weeks. It is based on the rockslides of the Diablerets in the 18th century. In **“La Grande Peur dans la montagne”** (Terror on the Mountain) from 1926, young farmers want to use an alpine pasture that is said to have been under a curse for years. In the end, illness and disasters confirm the old fears.

The **eighth banknote series** of the Swiss National Bank honoured people from the world of culture. Ramuz was pictured on the **200-franc note**. The 10-franc note showed the architect Le Corbusier. These notes have now been replaced by a new series.

gewusst: The Derborence valley in Valais was formed by the rockslides, and today there is a small lake there with an ancient, untouched forest.
The rockslides on the Diablerets that inspired Ramuz to write “Derborence” happened in 1714 and 1749.

teile.einleitung: In English-speaking countries there are many special **festivals**. Some are celebrated in Switzerland too, such as Christmas or Halloween. Others, such as Thanksgiving, Bonfire Night or Burns Night, exist only in certain countries.
wichtigste: Americans celebrate Thanksgiving on the fourth Thursday in November.
On 4 July the USA celebrates Independence Day.
On Bonfire Night, 5 November, people in England remember Guy Fawkes.
Boxing Day is on 26 December.
On St Patrick's Day, 17 March, people wear green.
Australia Day is on 26 January.

abschnitte.text: **Thanksgiving** is a harvest festival. In the USA it is celebrated on the **fourth Thursday in November**. The family gets together, and a big **turkey** is typical. On **4 July** it is **Independence Day**. It recalls the Declaration of Independence of 1776. People celebrate with parades and fireworks, a bit like Switzerland on 1 August.

On 5 November it is **Bonfire Night**. In 1605 **Guy Fawkes** and others wanted to blow up Parliament in London, but he was arrested. Since then there have been big bonfires and fireworks on this evening. On **Shrove Tuesday**, the carnival Tuesday before Lent, people make pancakes. That is why the day is also called **Pancake Day**, and there are even pancake races.

At **Christmas** many families in Great Britain open their presents on the morning of 25 December. The day after, **26 December**, is called **Boxing Day**. In Switzerland this is St Stephen's Day. The name probably comes from the fact that servants used to receive a box of presents on this day.

**St Patrick's Day** on 17 March honours the patron saint of Ireland. People wear **green**, the colour of Ireland, the “Emerald Isle”, and the **shamrock** is an important symbol. In Scotland the poet **Robert Burns** is honoured on **25 January**. On **Burns Night** people eat **haggis**, a dish made of sheep's offal and oats, and recite poems.

Australia's national day is **Australia Day** on **26 January**. It recalls the arrival of the first British fleet in 1788. Many people celebrate in summer with barbecues and fireworks. For many **Aboriginal people**, however, the day is controversial, because it marked the beginning of a hard time for them.

gewusst: Halloween on 31 October has its roots in an old festival in the British Isles and became especially popular in America.
In pancake races the runners carry a frying pan and toss the pancake into the air as they go.

tbvnynm.t: False friends between German and English

teile.einleitung: A **false friend** is a word that looks the same or similar in two languages but means something different. There are many of them between German and English. If you know them, you avoid funny or embarrassing misunderstandings.
wichtigste: An English “chef” is a cook; the German word “Chef” means the person in charge, which is “boss” in English.
“To become” means “werden”, not “bekommen” (to get).
A “gift” is a present; the German word “Gift” means “poison”.
“Handy” means practical and is not a telephone.
“Sensible” means reasonable; the German “sensibel” is “sensitive” in English.
“Actually” means in fact, and “brave” means courageous.

abschnitte.text: The technical term in linguistics is the French **faux amis**, meaning “false friends”. The words look familiar and tempt people to translate them wrongly. They often have a common origin but have developed differently in the two languages. That is why it is best to learn them on purpose, with example sentences.

A common mistake is **become**. “I become a teacher” means “Ich werde Lehrer”, not “Ich bekomme einen Lehrer” (I get a teacher). The German “bekommen” is **to get** in English. **Gift** is also a false friend: a “gift” is a **present** and gives pleasure. The German word “Gift” is **poison** in English.

An English **chef** stands in the kitchen; he or she is a cook or head cook. The German “Chef”, the person in charge, is a **boss**. **Sensible** means reasonable, while the German “empfindlich” or “sensibel” is **sensitive**. **Brave** means courageous. The German “brav”, meaning well-behaved, is **good** or **well-behaved** in English.

abschnitte.titel: Small words with a big effect
abschnitte.text: In English **handy** means practical or useful. The mobile phone, which Germans call a “Handy”, is a “mobile phone”. **Actually** means in fact or really, while the German “aktuell” is **current**. English **also** means “auch” (too). The German “also”, meaning therefore, is **so** or **therefore**. And **mist** is a light, damp fog, while German “Mist” means manure or rubbish.

gewusst: There are false friends between German and Italian too: “caldo” means warm and not cold (“kalt”).
The English word “gift” and the German word “Gift” both come from the verb meaning “to give”.

teile.einleitung: The **future perfect** is an English tense for the future. You use it for things that will be **completed** by a certain point in the future. In German it corresponds to the Futur II, for example “Ich werde fertig geworden sein”.
wichtigste: The future perfect is formed with “will have” and the past participle.
It shows what will be completed by a point in the future.
Typical signal words are “by next June” or “by then”.
The negative is “won't have” with the past participle.
Questions begin with “will”: “Will you have finished?”
The future perfect can also express a guess.

abschnitte.text: The future perfect consists of three parts: **will**, **have** and the **past participle**, the third form of the verb. Examples are **will have finished**, **will have sold** or **will have done**. The form is the same for all persons. After “will” there is always **have**, never “had” and never “has”.

You use the future perfect for something that will be **done** by a point in the future. **By next June, I will have finished school** means: next June, school will be over. **Call me at nine. I will have done my homework by then.** So at nine o'clock the homework will be finished.

Typical **signals** are expressions with **by** and a point in the future. They include **by the end of the week**, **by Friday**, **by 2030** or **by then**. They mean “up to” or “at the latest”. For comparison: **since** belongs to the present perfect and **last week** to the simple past.

The negative is **will not have**, **won't have** for short, with the past participle. **Don't come at six. We won't have finished dinner by then.** So at six the meal will not be over yet. For questions you put **will** before the subject: **Will you have finished the report by Friday?**

If you want to stress the **duration** up to a point in the future, you use the **future perfect progressive** with “will have been” and the ing form: **By 2030, she will have been teaching here for 20 years.** The future perfect can also express a **guess**: **He will have arrived home by now** means “He has probably already got home”.

gewusst: In everyday life you hear the future perfect fairly rarely, but it is common in reports and plans.
In German, too, the Futur II can express a guess: “Er wird den Zug verpasst haben.” (He will have missed the train.)

tdamlmz.t: Days of the week in French

teile.einleitung: You need the seven days of the week all the time, for example for your timetable or for making arrangements. In French many of them sound similar, because almost all of them end in -di.
wichtigste: The days of the week are lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi and dimanche.
Lundi is Monday; the school week begins with it.
Wednesday is mercredi, Thursday jeudi.
Samedi and dimanche make up the weekend.
In French the days of the week are written with a small letter.
The week is called “la semaine” and has seven days.

abschnitte.text: The week is called **la semaine**. It begins with **lundi** (Monday), followed by **mardi** (Tuesday), **mercredi** (Wednesday) and **jeudi** (Thursday). On **vendredi** (Friday) the school week ends. Then comes the weekend, “le week-end” in French, with **samedi** (Saturday) and **dimanche** (Sunday).

Unlike in English and German, the days of the week are written with a **small letter** in French: lundi, mardi, mercredi. All the days of the week are **masculine**: le lundi, le samedi. If you say “lundi”, you mean next Monday. If you say “le lundi”, you mean **every Monday**: “Le mercredi, je joue au foot” means “On Wednesdays I play football”.

Most of the names go back to **Latin**. Lundi is the day of the moon (lune), mardi the day of Mars, mercredi the day of Mercury, jeudi the day of Jupiter and vendredi the day of Venus. The ending **-di** comes from the Latin word for day, “dies”. Dimanche means “the Lord's day”, and samedi goes back to the Sabbath.

In many Swiss schools there is no school on **mercredi après-midi**, Wednesday afternoon. You often need the days of the week for making arrangements: “On se voit jeudi ?” means “Shall we meet on Thursday?”. To ask what day it is, you say: “Quel jour sommes-nous ?” The answer might be “Nous sommes vendredi” (It is Friday).

gewusst: The moon is also hidden in the word “Monday”, and in the German “Montag”.
In France Wednesday is completely or partly free of school for many children.

teile.einleitung: The Académie française is a famous society of scholars in Paris. For almost 400 years it has looked after the French language. Its 40 members are called “les Immortels”, the Immortals.
wichtigste: Cardinal Richelieu founded the Académie française in 1635.
It has 40 members who are elected for life.
The members are called “les Immortels”.
Its main task is a dictionary of the French language, the “Dictionnaire”.
In 1980 Marguerite Yourcenar was elected as the first woman.
The Academy meets in the Institut de France in Paris.

abschnitte.text: **Cardinal Richelieu** was the chief minister of King Louis XIII. In 1635 he gave a small circle of scholars an official status. This is how the **Académie française** came into being. Its job was to **cultivate** the French language and make it **uniform**. To this day it gives recommendations on how to use French correctly. In French-speaking Switzerland these recommendations are not binding, but they are often followed.

The Academy's main task is a **dictionary** of the French language, the **“Dictionnaire de l'Académie française”**. The first edition appeared in 1694. Since then it has been revised several times. The work moves forward very slowly, because the members discuss it word by word. Besides this, the Academy awards numerous literary prizes every year.

The Academy has exactly **40 members**. They are called **“les Immortels”**, the Immortals. The name goes back to the motto “À l'immortalité” (to immortality), which refers to the language. Each member has a numbered seat for life, the **fauteuil**. A new member is only elected when a fauteuil becomes free through death. The newcomer then gives a speech in praise of his or her predecessor. The work is led by the **Secrétaire perpétuel** (permanent secretary), since 2023 the writer **Amin Maalouf**.

abschnitte.titel: Green coat and the first woman
abschnitte.text: At formal sessions the members wear the **“habit vert”**. This is a dark tailcoat embroidered with green olive branches. Traditionally it comes with a **sword**, which friends give to the new member as a present. For a long time the Academy was open only to men. In 1980 **Marguerite Yourcenar** was elected as the first woman; she is known for her novel “Mémoires d'Hadrien”. Simone Veil became a member in 2008.

The Academy meets in the **Institut de France** on the Quai de Conti in Paris. The building stands on the Seine, opposite the **Louvre**. It houses five academies in total. Its **dome** is the symbol of the Académie française. That is why people in France sometimes say “sous la Coupole” (under the dome) when they talk about the Academy.

gewusst: In 2023 Amin Maalouf succeeded Hélène Carrère d'Encausse, who had held the post of Secrétaire perpétuel for a long time.
Almost 60 years passed between the founding in 1635 and the first edition of the dictionary in 1694.

teile.einleitung: The conditionnel is a French verb form that roughly corresponds to the English “would”. You need it for wishes, polite requests, conditions and unconfirmed news. There is the conditionnel présent and the conditionnel passé.
wichtigste: The conditionnel présent is formed from the future stem and the endings of the imparfait.
“je serais” is conditionnel, whereas “je serai” is futur simple.
Polite wishes are expressed with “je voudrais”.
In an unreal conditional sentence, the imparfait follows “si” and the main clause has the conditionnel.
The conditionnel passé consists of avoir or être in the conditionnel and the participe passé.
In newspaper reports the conditionnel shows that information is unconfirmed.

abschnitte.titel: How to form the conditionnel présent
abschnitte.text: You take the **stem of the futur simple** and add the **endings of the imparfait**: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. So “parler” (to speak) becomes **je parlerais** (I would speak). Irregular verbs keep their special future stem. “Être” becomes **je serais**, “pouvoir” becomes **vous pourriez**, “vouloir” becomes **je voudrais**. Careful: “je serai” without an s is futur simple, “je serais” with an s is conditionnel.

The conditionnel makes requests **more polite**. Instead of “Je veux un café” (I want a coffee), in a restaurant it is better to say “**Je voudrais** un café, s'il vous plaît” (I would like a coffee, please). “**Pourriez-vous** m'aider ?” (Could you help me?) also sounds much friendlier than an order. These forms are very useful in everyday life, in Paris just as much as in Lausanne or Geneva.

The conditionnel is used in **unreal conditional sentences**. For the present: after “si” comes the imparfait, and the main clause has the conditionnel présent. “Si j'avais le temps, je **voyagerais** plus souvent.” (If I had the time, I would travel more often.) For the past: after “si” comes the plus-que-parfait, and the main clause has the conditionnel passé. “Si tu étais venu, tu **aurais vu** ce film.” (If you had come, you would have seen this film.)

The **conditionnel passé** consists of avoir or être in the conditionnel présent and the **participe passé**: “j'aurais chanté” (I would have sung), “elle serait partie” (she would have left). The conditionnel has a special job in **journalism**. “Le ministre **serait** malade” means that the news is not confirmed. In English you would say something like “The minister is said to be ill”.

gewusst: The verbs pouvoir, voir, envoyer and mourir have a double r in the conditionnel: pourrais, verrais, enverrais, mourrais.
The conditionnel is sometimes also called “futur dans le passé” (future in the past), because in reported speech it expresses the future as seen from the past.

teile.einleitung: With the futur proche you talk about things that will happen soon or are firmly planned. It is very easy to form and very common in everyday life. All you need is the verb “aller” and an infinitive.
wichtigste: “Futur proche” means “near future”.
It is formed with “aller” in the present and an infinitive.
Example: “je vais manger”, “I am going to eat”.
The forms of “aller” are: vais, vas, va, allons, allez, vont.
The second verb always stays in the infinitive.
In the negative, “ne … pas” goes round the form of “aller”.

abschnitte.text: **Futur proche** means “near future”. You use it to describe what is **happening soon** or is **firmly planned**. “Ce soir, je vais regarder un film” means “This evening I am going to watch a film”. In German people often just use the present: “Heute Abend schaue ich einen Film”. French speakers use this form very often in conversation.

The futur proche has two parts: the **present tense of aller** and the **infinitive** of the second verb. The forms of “aller” are: **je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont**. Then comes the verb in its basic form: “tu vas finir”, “nous allons partir”, “vous allez prendre le train”. The second verb never changes. So “They are about to eat” is “Ils vont manger”.

If you want to make it negative, you put **ne … pas** round the form of “aller”. “Je vais venir” (I am going to come) becomes “Je **ne** vais **pas** venir”. The infinitive only follows afterwards. Before a vowel, “ne” becomes **n'**. That is why it is “nous **n'**allons pas partir” and “vous **n'**allez pas venir”. With “je”, “tu” and “il”, “ne” stays unchanged: “Il ne va pas pleuvoir” (It is not going to rain).

There is a second future form, the **futur simple**, for example “je mangerai” (I will eat). The futur simple is used more for things further away or less certain, and in written texts. The futur proche sounds closer and more everyday. The **passé récent** with “venir de” is built in a very similar way: “Je viens de manger” means “I have just eaten”.

gewusst: English has a similar form: “I am going to eat”.
Because you only have to conjugate “aller”, many children learn the futur proche before the futur simple.

teile.einleitung: In English many questions are formed with the auxiliary verb **do** or **does**. This applies in the **simple present**, the simple present tense. With a few rules you can easily form questions like these yourself.
wichtigste: With I, you, we and they the question begins with “do”.
With he, she and it the question begins with “does”.
After “does” the verb has no -s.
After a question word comes “do” or “does”.
In a short answer you repeat the auxiliary verb from the question.
Auxiliary verbs such as “can” do not need “do” in questions.

abschnitte.text: In German you simply put the verb at the front: “Spielst du?” (Do you play?). In English you need an **auxiliary verb** for this. With **I, you, we** and **they** it is **do**: **Do they live in Bern?** With **he, she** and **it** it is **does**: **Does your sister like pizza?** After all, “your sister” is a “she”.

In a statement you say “He plays tennis” with an **-s**. In the question, however, the -s is already contained in **does**. That is why the verb after it is in its basic form: **Does he play tennis?** “Does he plays tennis?” would be wrong. The rule also applies to things: “the film” is an “it”, so **What time does the film start?**

If the question begins with a **question word** such as where, what or when, **do** or **does** comes straight after it. Then come the person and the verb. Examples: **Where do you go to school?** and **What time does the film start?** So the order is question word, auxiliary, person, verb.

Questions like these are often answered briefly. You repeat the auxiliary verb from the question. To **Do you speak German?** you say **Yes, I do** or **No, I don't**. To **Does Anna have a cat?** you answer **Yes, she does** or **No, she doesn't**. Just saying “Yes” or “No” can sometimes sound a little rude.

Some verbs are **auxiliary verbs** themselves, for example **can**, **must** or **will**. You simply put them at the beginning: **Can you swim?** The verb **to be** does not need do either: **Are you tired?** or **Is she at home?** Only with all the other verbs do you need the help of do or does.

gewusst: Negative sentences are formed in a very similar way: “I don't like fish” and “She doesn't like fish”.
In the past, do and does simply become “did”: “Did you see the film?”

teile.einleitung: In French many letters have small marks above them, the accents. They show how a letter is pronounced, or they tell apart words that would otherwise look the same. If you know them, you read and write French much more confidently.
wichtigste: The accent aigu (é) appears only on the e, for example in “été”.
The accent grave (è, à, ù) is pronounced open or tells words apart.
The accent circonflexe (ê) is often found where there used to be an s.
“à” is a preposition, “a” is a form of avoir.
“où” means where, “ou” means or.
The cédille (ç) turns the c before a, o and u into an s sound.
The tréma (ë) shows that two vowels are pronounced separately.

abschnitte.text: The **accent aigu** is a small stroke slanting up to the right. It appears **only on the e**: “é”. It is pronounced closed, a bit like the vowel in “say”. Examples are “été” (summer) and “**école**” (school). In “école” only the first e has an accent; the last e is silent.

The **accent grave** is a stroke slanting up to the left. On the e it shows an **open** è, as in “mère” (mother). On a and u it tells words apart. “**À**” is a preposition and means, for example, “to” or “in”, as in “à Lausanne”. Without an accent, “a” is a form of avoir: “il a” (he has). In the same way “**où**” means where, but “ou” without an accent means or.

The **accent circonflexe** looks like a little roof: “ê”. It can sit on a, e, i, o and u. It is often found where Old French had an **s**. Compare “fête” with the German word “Fest” (English “feast”) or “forêt” with “Forst” (English “forest”). This way you can understand some words more easily.

The **cédille** is a small hook under the c: “ç”. It shows that the c before a, o and u sounds **like s**, for example in “garçon” (boy) or “français”. The **tréma** is two dots above a vowel. It shows that two vowels are pronounced **separately**. So in “Noël” (Christmas) you hear the o and the e one after the other.

gewusst: The word “où” carries the only accent grave on a u in the whole French language.
You can see accents on Swiss place-name signs too, for example on “Genève” or “Neuchâtel”.

teile.einleitung: In inversion, the usual English word order is turned round: the auxiliary verb comes before the subject, as in a question. This sounds formal and gives a statement especially strong emphasis.
wichtigste: Inversion means: auxiliary before the subject, although the sentence is not a question.
It often follows negative expressions such as never, hardly or not only at the start of a sentence.
Example: Never have I seen such a beautiful sunset.
If there is no auxiliary, you need do, does or did: Only then did I realise the truth.
No sooner is followed by than, hardly by when.
In conditional sentences if can be dropped: Had I known, Should you need help.
Inversion sounds formal and is found mainly in written texts.

abschnitte.text: Normally an English statement has the **subject** first, then the verb: I have seen. In **inversion** this is turned round: **have I seen**. It looks like a question, but it is a statement. Inversion is used to **emphasise** something. It sounds elevated and is found in speeches, books and newspapers.

Inversion often follows words with a negative meaning at the start of a sentence. Examples are **never**, **rarely**, **seldom**, **hardly** and **under no circumstances**. “Never have I seen such a beautiful sunset” is more emphatic than “I have never seen”. Likewise: “Under no circumstances should you open the door.” **Not only** belongs here too: “Not only was he late, but he also forgot his books.”

If you want to say that two things happened almost at the same time, you use **hardly** or **no sooner** with the past perfect. “Hardly had I arrived when the phone rang” means that the phone rang almost as soon as I arrived. Hardly is followed by **when**, no sooner by **than**. “No sooner had we left than it started to rain.”

If the sentence has no auxiliary verb, you insert **do**, **does** or **did**, just as in questions. “I realised the truth only then” becomes “**Only then did I realise** the truth.” The main verb then follows in its basic form. The same applies after only after or only when. With be you do not need do: “Not only was he late.”

In formal conditional sentences you can leave out **if** and put the auxiliary at the front. “If I had known” becomes “**Had** I known, I would have helped”. “If you should need help” becomes “**Should** you need any help, please call me”. This form is often found in letters and emails. “Were I you” for “If I were you” also occurs, but it sounds very elevated.

gewusst: In German it is quite normal for the verb to come before the subject, for example “Gestern habe ich” (yesterday have I). In English it is the exception.
Inversion is often found in poems and old songs, because it makes rhythm and rhyme easier to achieve.

teile.einleitung: The plus-que-parfait is the past perfect. It shows that something happened even earlier than another event in the past.
wichtigste: The plus-que-parfait corresponds to the English past perfect: “we had eaten”.
It is formed with avoir or être in the imparfait and the participe passé.
Examples are “nous avions mangé” and “il était parti”.
Verbs that form the passé composé with être also take être here.
With être the participe passé agrees with the subject.
After “si”, the plus-que-parfait is used for a condition in the past that was not fulfilled.

abschnitte.text: Sometimes you tell about two things that happened one after the other. The earlier event is then in the **plus-que-parfait**. An example: “Quand je suis arrivé à la gare, le train était parti.” The train left first, then I arrived. That is why “était parti” is in the past perfect. In English you say: “The train had already left.”

The plus-que-parfait consists of the **auxiliary verb in the imparfait** and the **participe passé**. Avoir in the imparfait is: j'avais, tu avais, il avait, nous avions, vous aviez, ils avaient. Être is: j'étais, tu étais, il était, nous étions, vous étiez, ils étaient. This gives forms such as “nous avions mangé” (we had eaten) or “nous avions fait” (we had done).

The choice of auxiliary follows the same rules as in the **passé composé**. Most verbs take avoir. Verbs of movement such as partir or venir and all **reflexive verbs** take être. With être the participe passé agrees with the subject: “ils étaient venus” (they had come), “Marie s'était levée” (Marie had got up). Être itself forms its compound tenses with avoir: “tu avais été” (you had been).

The plus-que-parfait also appears in **conditional sentences**. If something did not happen in the past, the plus-que-parfait follows “si”. The main clause has the **conditionnel passé**. A well-known example: “Si j'avais su, je serais venu.” That means: “If I had known, I would have come.”

gewusst: There is another similar, rare tense, the passé antérieur: “nous eûmes mangé”. It is found almost only in books.
The name “plus-que-parfait” literally means “more than perfect”.

teile.einleitung: The German word “Familie” is **family** in English. There are special words for mother, father, brothers and sisters and grandparents. Many of them sound similar to German and are therefore easy to learn.
wichtigste: The Mutter is called “mother”; children often say “mum” or “mom”.
The Vater is called “father”; children often say “dad”.
A Bruder is a “brother”, a Schwester a “sister”.
The “grandma” is the Grossmutter.
The Onkel is called “uncle”, the Tante “aunt”.
“Meine Familie” is “my family” in English.

abschnitte.text: The Mutter is called **mother** in English, the Vater **father**. Together they are the **parents**, “die Eltern”. Children often call their mother **mum** (British) or **mom** (American). They call their father **dad** or **daddy**.

A Bruder is a **brother**, a Schwester a **sister**. Both words are related to German. Brothers and sisters together are called **siblings**, “Geschwister”. If someone asks you **Do you have any brothers or sisters?**, you can say, for example: **I have one sister**.

The Grossmutter is called **grandmother**, **grandma** for short. In Switzerland people often say “Grosi”. The Grossvater is called **grandfather** or **grandpa**. Together they are the **grandparents**. From your grandparents' point of view you are a **grandchild**, “ein Enkelkind”.

The Onkel is called **uncle**; the word sounds similar to “Onkel”. The Tante is called **aunt**, and it is spelt with “au”. A male or female cousin is called **cousin** in English in both cases. All of them together make up the **family**. When you talk about your family, you say **my family**.

gewusst: In English there is only one word for a male and a female cousin: “cousin”.
The word “family” comes from the Latin “familia”.

teile.einleitung: The imparfait is a past tense. You need it for descriptions, states and habits from the past. It is formed very regularly.
wichtigste: The stem comes from the nous form in the present without “-ons”.
The endings are: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.
Only “être” has an irregular stem: “ét-”.
The imparfait describes states, background and habits.
Single completed events are in the passé composé.
With verbs ending in -ger an “e” stays before “a”: “mangeait”.

abschnitte.text: For the imparfait you take the **nous form in the present** and remove the ending **-ons**. “Nous finissons” gives the stem **finiss-**, “nous faisons” gives **fais-**. “Nous avons” gives **av-**, which produces “j'avais” (I had). This rule works for almost all verbs, including many irregular ones. The only exception is **être**: it has the stem **ét-**, so “j'étais” (I was).

You add the endings **-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient** to the stem. So it is: je chantais, tu chantais, il chantait, nous chantions, vous chantiez, ils chantaient. The forms for je, tu, il and ils **sound the same**, although they are spelt differently. With “nous” it is, for example, “nous jouions”, with “ils” “ils parlaient”.

With verbs ending in **-ger**, an **e** stays before the “a” so that the g sounds soft. That is why it is “elle **mangeait**” (she was eating), but “nous mangions”. With verbs ending in **-cer**, the c gets a cédille before the “a”: “je commençais” (I was beginning). Before “i” this help is not needed, which is why it is “nous commencions”. This way the pronunciation stays the same.

The imparfait describes **states** and **background** in the past: “Il faisait beau.” (The weather was fine.) It also shows **habits**: “Quand j'étais petit, j'avais un chat.” (When I was little, I had a cat.) For single, **completed events** you need the **passé composé**. Often both appear together: “Elle mangeait une pomme quand le téléphone a sonné.” (She was eating an apple when the phone rang.) The ongoing action is in the imparfait, the sudden event in the passé composé.

gewusst: “Imparfait” means “unfinished”, because the action is described without a clear beginning or end.
With “si” and the imparfait you make suggestions: “Si on allait au cinéma ?” means “How about going to the cinema?”.

teile.einleitung: Anyone learning French usually starts with greetings. With just a few words you can say “hello”, ask how someone is and say a friendly goodbye. In French-speaking Switzerland you hear these words every day.
wichtigste: “Bonjour” is said during the day, “Bonsoir” in the evening.
Among friends people casually say “Salut” or “Coucou”.
You politely address an adult man as “Monsieur” and a woman as “Madame”.
“Ça va très bien” means: I'm very well.
“Comme ci, comme ça” means: so-so.
“À bientôt” means see you soon, “À tout à l'heure” see you later the same day.
“Bienvenue” means welcome.

abschnitte.text: During the day you greet people with “**Bonjour**”, in the evening with “**Bonsoir**”. It is polite to add the form of address: “Bonjour, **Monsieur**” for a man, “Bonjour, **Madame**” for a woman. Among friends people say the more casual “**Salut**”. Even more casual is “**Coucou**”, which you only say to friends and family. Guests are greeted with “**Bienvenue**”, which you often see on signs in French-speaking Switzerland.

The simplest question is “**Ça va ?**”. If you are very well, you answer “**Ça va très bien**”. If you are neither especially good nor especially bad, you say “**Comme ci, comme ça**”, meaning “so-so”. Then you ask back: “**Et toi ?**”, which means “And you?”. With adults you address formally, you say “Et vous ?”.

To say goodbye you say “**Au revoir**”. If you will see each other again soon, you say “**À bientôt**”, because “bientôt” means soon. If you meet again later the same day, you say “**À tout à l'heure**”, meaning “See you later”. In the morning or at midday you wish someone “**Bonne journée**”, a nice day. In the evening you wish “**Bonne soirée**”, a nice evening.

In French-speaking Switzerland friends and relatives often greet each other with **kisses on the cheek**, “la bise”. Usually people give three little kisses on the cheeks. Adults who do not know each other tend to shake hands. The difference between **tu** and **vous** is also important: you say tu to friends and children, and vous to adults you do not know.

gewusst: How many kisses on the cheek people give varies from region to region in France; in French-speaking Switzerland it is usually three.
“Salut” can be used both to say hello and to say goodbye.

teile.einleitung: The gérondif is a verb form that links two actions done by the same person. It shows, for example, that something is happening at the same time or how something is achieved. It consists of “en” and the participe présent.
wichtigste: The gérondif consists of “en” and the participe présent, for example “en chantant”.
The participe présent is formed from the stem of the nous form with the ending “-ant”.
“Étant” (être), “ayant” (avoir) and “sachant” (savoir) are irregular.
The gérondif always refers to the subject of the main clause.
It can express things happening at the same time, the means or the manner.
With “tout en” you stress that things happen at the same time or that there is a contrast.

abschnitte.text: The gérondif has two parts: the preposition **en** and the **participe présent**. The participe présent is formed from the **nous form in the present tense**. You remove “-ons” and add **-ant**. “Nous chantons” (we sing) gives “chantant”, so “en chantant” (while singing). “Nous faisons” (we do) gives “faisant”, so **en faisant**. The gérondif never changes; it has no feminine or plural form.

Three verbs have an **irregular** participe présent. “Être” becomes **étant**, “avoir” becomes **ayant** and “savoir” becomes **sachant**. This gives “en étant”, “en ayant” and “en sachant”. With verbs ending in **-ger**, an “e” stays before the “a” so that the g sounds soft: **en mangeant**. With verbs ending in **-cer**, the c gets a cédille: “en commençant”.

The gérondif always refers to the **subject of the main clause**. In “Il lit en mangeant” (he reads while eating), the same person is reading and eating. So you have to be careful: in “Je l'ai vu en sortant” (I saw him as I was going out), I am the one going out. If you want to talk about another person, you need a subordinate clause. For example: “Je l'ai vu quand il sortait.” (I saw him when he was going out.)

Often the gérondif shows that two actions happen **at the same time**: “Elle chante en cuisinant.” (She sings while cooking.) It can also name the **means**, that is how something happens. The proverb “C'est **en forgeant** qu'on devient forgeron” means “You become a blacksmith by forging”, in English “Practice makes perfect”. With **tout en** you stress that things happen at the same time or that there is a contrast: “Tout en étant riche, il est malheureux” (Although he is rich, he is unhappy).

gewusst: German has no gérondif; it is usually translated with “indem” (by), “während” (while) or “beim” (when).
The gérondif can also express a condition: “En travaillant, tu réussiras” means “If you work, you will succeed”.

teile.einleitung: When you meet someone new, you want to introduce yourself: your name, age, where you live and your hobbies. With a few simple sentences you can do this in French too.
wichtigste: You ask a child's name with “Comment tu t'appelles ?”.
You can answer with “Je m'appelle …”, meaning “My name is …”.
You ask someone's age with “Quel âge as-tu ?”.
“J'habite à Berne” means “I live in Bern”, “Je viens de Lausanne” means “I come from Lausanne”.
“Enchanté !” is said at a first meeting; it means “Pleased to meet you!”.
With “Voici …” you introduce someone else.
