abschnitte.text: First you say **Bonjour** or, among children, simply **Salut**. To ask someone's name you say: “**Comment tu t'appelles ?**” That means “What's your name?”. The answer is: “Je m'appelle Lena.” (My name is Lena.) When you meet someone for the first time, people like to say “**Enchanté !**”, which means “Pleased to meet you!”. A girl writes it with an extra e: “Enchantée”.

To ask someone's age you say: “**Quel âge as-tu ?**” Literally this means “What age have you?”. That is why you also answer with “avoir”: “J'ai dix ans.” (I am ten.) So in French you **have** your age. You say where you live with “**J'habite à Berne**”, I live in Bern. You say where you come from with “**Je viens de Lausanne**”. “Je viens” comes from the verb “venir”, to come.

With “**Je parle allemand**” you say that you speak German. In French, languages are written with a small letter: allemand, français, italien. You talk about hobbies and things you like with “**J'aime**”, I like. “J'aime les animaux” means “I like animals”, “J'aime le foot” means “I like football”. What you do not like, you say with “Je n'aime pas …”.

If you want to introduce someone else, you say “**Voici** mon amie Mia”. That means “This is my friend Mia”. You talk about a boy with **il** (he) and about a girl with **elle** (she). So the sentence “Il s'appelle Noah” is about a boy called Noah. “Elle s'appelle Mia” means “Her name is Mia”.

gewusst: In the Romandie and in France friends often greet each other with kisses on the cheek, la bise. How many there are varies from region to region.
Adults you do not know are asked more politely: “Comment vous appelez-vous ?”

teile.einleitung: Belgium and France are famous for their comics. Characters such as Tintin, Asterix, Lucky Luke or the Smurfs are known all over the world. French-speaking Switzerland has also contributed a lot to the history of comics.
wichtigste: In French a comic is called “bande dessinée”, “BD” for short.
Hergé from Belgium created “Tintin”, known in German as “Tim und Struppi”.
The Smurfs were created in 1958 by the Belgian artist Peyo.
Lucky Luke comes from the Belgian artist Morris.
Rodolphe Töpffer from Geneva is seen as a forerunner of the comic.
Titeuf comes from the Geneva artist Zep.

abschnitte.text: In French a comic is called **bande dessinée**, **BD** for short. Literally this means “drawn strip”. People speak of **Franco-Belgian comics** because many famous series come from France and Belgium. Large hardback albums are typical. In France and Belgium children and adults alike read comics.

Belgium is regarded as a centre of comics. The artist **Hergé**, whose real name was Georges Remi, lived in Brussels and created the reporter **Tintin**. In German the stories are called “Tim und Struppi”; Struppi is the German name of his white dog, Snowy. The Belgian **Morris** created **Lucky Luke**, the cowboy who draws faster than his shadow. His horse is called Jolly Jumper. **Peyo** created the little blue **Schtroumpfs**, the Smurfs.

From France comes **Asterix**, the little Gaul. He lives with his friend Obelix in a village that resists the Romans. The druid **Getafix**, called Panoramix in French, brews the magic potion that makes the Gauls invincibly strong. In the French town of **Angoulême** the biggest comics festival in France has taken place every year since 1974. Important comics prizes are awarded there.

From the 1820s, **Rodolphe Töpffer** from Geneva drew picture stories with text under the pictures. He is therefore seen as one of the inventors of the picture story and as a **forerunner of the modern comic**. The artist **Zep** also comes from the Geneva area. He created **Titeuf**, a cheeky primary-school boy with a yellow quiff. Titeuf is very popular in French-speaking Switzerland and in France.

gewusst: In Brussels many house walls are painted with large pictures of comic characters.
Hergé is a pen name: his initials G. R. were turned round to R. G., and in French this is pronounced “Hergé”.

teile.einleitung: French is one of the four national languages of Switzerland and is spoken mainly in western Switzerland, the Romandy. Around 300 million people speak it worldwide, for example in France, Belgium, Canada and many countries in Africa. For children in German-speaking Switzerland, French is often the first foreign language, and with it they can understand neighbours in their own country.
wichtigste: French is a Romance language and comes from Latin.
In Switzerland just under a quarter of the population speak French as their main language.
“Bonjour” means “Hello” or “Good day”, “Merci” means “Thank you” and “Au revoir” means “Goodbye”.
“Oui” means yes and “non” means no.
The cat is “le chat”, the mother “la mère” and bread “le pain”.
The first numbers are un, deux, trois.
French nouns are either masculine (le) or feminine (la).

abschnitte.text: French is an **official language** in around 30 countries, including France, Belgium, Luxembourg, Canada and many countries in West and Central Africa. In Switzerland it is spoken in the **Romandy**, that is in the cantons of Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel and Jura and in parts of the cantons of Fribourg, Valais and Bern. French is also important internationally, for example at the United Nations and the Olympic Games. The organisation of French-speaking countries is called the Francophonie.

French developed from the **Latin** of the Romans that was spoken in Gaul. That is why it is related to Italian, Spanish and Romansh. Later, words from the Germanic Franks were added; they gave the country of France its name. Since 1635 the **Académie française** in Paris has looked after the French language.

When you learn French, you start with greetings such as **“Bonjour”** (Good day), “Salut” (Hi) and “Au revoir” (Goodbye). You are polite with “Merci” (Thank you) and “s’il vous plaît” (please). Yes is “oui”, no is “non”. The numbers begin with un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq.

Every French noun has a **gender**, masculine or feminine; there is no neuter. Masculine nouns have the article “le”, feminine ones the article “la”, for example “le chat” (the cat) or “la mère” (the mother). Before a vowel this becomes “l’”, as in “l’école” (the school). The gender often does not match German, so you always learn the article along with the word.

In French many letters at the end of a word are not pronounced, such as the t in “chat” or the s in “trois”. There are **accents** such as é, è and ê, which change the pronunciation, and the ç with a little cedilla. Also typical are the **nasal sounds**, as in “pain” or “bonjour”. A song or a film in French helps you get a feel for the sound.

The French of the Romandy is almost the same as in France, but it has some **special features**. For 70 people say “septante” and for 90 “nonante”, while in France they say “soixante-dix” and “quatre-vingt-dix”. Instead of “déjeuner” for the midday meal, people traditionally say “dîner”. If you learn French, you can talk to lots of people in Lausanne, Geneva or Neuchâtel.

begriffe.erklaerung: The French-speaking part of Switzerland, also called western Switzerland.
A language that comes from Latin, such as French or Italian.
A small mark above a letter that changes the pronunciation, as in é.
A sound in which air also flows through the nose, as in “bonjour”.

gewusst: Many German words come from French, for example Trottoir (pavement), Portemonnaie (purse), Velo (bike) or Glace (ice cream).
In France, 80 is “quatre-vingts”, literally “four twenties”.
For a long time French was the most important language of diplomacy in Europe.

teile.einleitung: People talk about the weather every day. In French you mainly need two kinds of sentence for this: ones with “il fait” and ones with a weather verb.
wichtigste: “Il pleut” means “It is raining”, “Il neige” means “It is snowing”.
“Il fait chaud” means “It is hot”, “Il fait froid” means “It is cold”.
“Il fait beau” means “The weather is nice”.
The sun is called “le soleil”, the cloud “le nuage”.
The wind is called “le vent”, and when it is windy you say “Il y a du vent”.
Snow is called “la neige”.

abschnitte.text: There are special **verbs** for rain and snow. “**Il pleut**” means “It is raining”. Then you need an umbrella, “un parapluie” in French. “**Il neige**” means “It is snowing”. Snow is called **la neige**. These verbs are only used with “il”, just as in English they are only used with “it”.

Many weather sentences begin with **il fait**, literally “it makes”. “**Il fait chaud**” means “It is hot” or “It is warm”. “**Il fait froid**” means “It is cold”. “**Il fait beau**” means “The weather is nice”, and “Il fait mauvais” means “The weather is bad”. In English you say “it is” here, not “it makes”.

**Le soleil** is the sun. It shines during the day. When the sun is shining, you say “Il y a du soleil” (it is sunny). **Le nuage** is the cloud. Rain or snow falls from clouds. **Le vent** is the wind. When it is windy you say “**Il y a du vent**”. So here you need “il y a” with the partitive article “du”.

On the radio and television the weather forecast is called **la météo**. You ask: “Quel temps fait-il ?”, meaning “What is the weather like?”. For a thunderstorm you say “Il y a de l'orage”, for fog “Il y a du brouillard”. In the Romandie people also know the **bise**, a cold north-east wind that can blow strongly, especially on Lake Geneva.

gewusst: The word “la météo” is short for “la météorologie”, the science of weather.
In German-speaking Switzerland people also say “Bise” for the cold north-east wind.

teile.einleitung: London is the capital of the United Kingdom and one of the best-known cities in the world. It lies on the Thames and is famous for its sights, red buses and the underground.
wichtigste: London is the capital of the United Kingdom.
The city lies on the River Thames.
Big Ben is actually the name of the great bell in the clock tower.
The typical double-decker buses are red.
The underground is called the Tube.
The big wheel is called the London Eye.
Buckingham Palace is the King's official residence.

abschnitte.text: London is the **capital** of the United Kingdom, which is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The city lies on the **Thames**. The Romans founded a settlement here almost 2,000 years ago called **Londinium**. Today London is a huge city with people from all over the world and an important centre of trade and culture.

Many people think that **Big Ben** is the clock tower of Parliament. Actually, though, it is the name of the great **bell** inside the tower. Since 2012 the tower itself has been called the **Elizabeth Tower**. It is part of the **Palace of Westminster**, where the British Parliament meets. Very close by stands **Westminster Abbey**, a famous church where kings and queens are crowned.

**Buckingham Palace** is the British King's official residence in London. In front of the palace the famous **Changing of the Guard** takes place. The guards wear red jackets and tall black bearskin hats. Other royal places include the **Tower of London**, where the Crown Jewels are kept.

The London underground is called **the Tube**. It opened in 1863 and is considered the oldest underground railway in the world. Above ground run the red **double-decker buses**. The **black cabs**, the black taxis, are also typical. Anyone who wants to drive one of these taxis must pass a difficult exam about the city's streets, called **The Knowledge**.

On the bank of the Thames stands the **London Eye**, a huge **big wheel**. It was built for the year 2000 and is 135 metres tall. From the glass pods you have a wide view over the city. In clear weather you can see Big Ben, Buckingham Palace and many bridges, for example **Tower Bridge**.

gewusst: London has hosted the Summer Olympic Games three times: in 1908, 1948 and 2012.
In London people drive on the left-hand side of the road, as in the whole of the United Kingdom.

teile.einleitung: In the passive, the focus is not on who does something but on what happens to something. In English the passive is formed with a form of be and the past participle.
wichtigste: The passive is formed with be and the past participle: is spoken, was opened.
It is used when the action is more important than the person doing it.
The form of be shows the tense: is built, was built, has been built.
For the passive in progress you say is being repaired.
After modal verbs come be and the participle: must be filled in.
The person doing the action is introduced with by.
With is said to you say what people say about someone.

abschnitte.text: In the **active**, the person doing the action is in the foreground: “They opened the tunnel.” In the **passive**, the result is the focus: “The tunnel was opened.” The passive is formed with a form of **be** and the **past participle**. With regular verbs it ends in -ed; irregular ones have to be learnt, for example spoken or built.

You can tell the tense from the form of be. **Simple present**: “English **is spoken** in many countries.” **Simple past**: “The Gotthard Base Tunnel **was opened** in June 2016.” **Present perfect**: “The new bridge **has been built** recently.” The participle always stays the same. Only be changes.

If something is happening right now, you use the passive in the **present progressive**. For this you need is or are, then **being** and the participle. “The road **is being repaired** at the moment, so we have to take a detour.” In the simple past it is was being repaired.

If there is a **modal verb** such as must, can or should in the sentence, it is followed by **be** and the participle. “This form must **be filled in** in ink.” Other examples are “It can be done” and “It should be checked”. This form is often found on signs and in instructions.

If you want to say **who** did something, you use **by**: “The picture was painted by my sister.” Often, though, this is left out because it is unimportant or unknown. With verbs that have two objects, the person can become the subject: “**Anna was given a prize.**” With **is said to** you say what people say about someone: “He is said to be very rich.”

gewusst: The Gotthard Base Tunnel opened in June 2016 and, at around 57 kilometres, is the longest railway tunnel in the world.
The passive is especially common in newspapers and scientific texts.

teile.einleitung: You begin questions with **question words** when you want to know something specific. In English many of them start with “wh”. That is why they are also called **wh-questions**.
wichtigste: “Who?” means Wer? and asks about people.
“Where?” means Wo? and asks about places.
“When?” means Wann? and asks about time.
“Why?” means Warum? and asks about the reason.
“How?” means Wie?, “How many?” means Wie viele?
“What is your name?” means Wie heisst du?

abschnitte.text: With **Who?** you ask about a person: **Who is that?** means “Wer ist das?”. With **What?** you ask about a thing: **What is this?** means “Was ist das?”. The question **What is your name?** means “Wie heisst du?”. You answer, for example, **My name is Lea**.

With **Where?** you ask about a place: **Where is my bag?** means “Wo ist meine Tasche?”. With **When?** you ask about time: **When is your birthday?** means “Wann hast du Geburtstag?”. The answer to a “when” question gives a day, a month or a time.

With **Why?** you ask about the **reason**. For example: **Why are you sad?** means “Warum bist du traurig?”. The answer often begins with **because**, which means “weil”: **Because my cat is ill**. That way you can explain reasons.

With **How?** you ask what something is like or how it works, for example **How are you?**. With **How many?** you ask about a number: **How many apples?** means “Wie viele Äpfel?”. **How old are you?** means “Wie alt bist du?”, because “old” means alt. You answer, for example, **I am eight**.

gewusst: In English almost all question words begin with “wh”. Only “how” is different, but it also contains a w and an h.
With “Which?” you ask which of several things is meant.

teile.einleitung: Modal verbs such as can, must, should or may change the meaning of another verb. With them you express whether something is possible, necessary, forbidden or allowed.
wichtigste: Modal verbs come before the basic form of a verb and do not get an s with he, she and it.
Mustn't means: it is forbidden.
Don't have to means: it is not necessary.
Must can express a confident conclusion, can't the opposite.
Should have with a participle expresses criticism or regret.
For can in the future you say will be able to.
May I …? is a polite request for permission.

abschnitte.text: **Modal verbs** are auxiliary verbs that give another verb a special meaning. They include **can, could, may, might, must, should, will** and **would**. A modal verb is followed by the **basic form** without to: “She can swim.” Modal verbs do not get an s with he, she and it. For questions and negatives you do not need do: “Can you help me?”

Mistakes often happen here. **Mustn't** expresses a **ban**: “You mustn't smoke here. It's forbidden.” **Don't have to**, on the other hand, means that something is **not necessary**: “Tomorrow is a holiday, so you don't have to come to work.” In German “du musst nicht” means exactly this. If you mean “du darfst nicht” (you are not allowed to), you need mustn't in English.

Modal verbs also express how sure you are. **Must** means: I am fairly sure. “He has been working for 12 hours. He must be exhausted.” **Can't** is the opposite: that is certainly not the case. “She can't be at home; I have just seen her at the station.” **Might** and **may** show that something is only possible.

With **should have** and the past participle you talk about the past. You say that something would have been right but did not happen. “You should have told me earlier! Now it's too late.” This sounds like **criticism**. About yourself, it expresses **regret**: “I should have studied more.”

Modal verbs do not have all tenses. For **can** in the past you use **could**: “When I was five, I could already read.” For the future you need the **substitute form** **will be able to**: “Next year I will be able to drive.” For must in the past you say had to. To ask politely for permission, you say **“May I open the window?”**

gewusst: Modal verbs have no -ing form and no to form. “To can” or “canning” in this sense do not exist.
Today shall is heard mainly in suggestions such as “Shall we go?”; otherwise it has become rather rare.

teile.einleitung: An **anglicism** is a word from English that is used in another language. German has a great many of them, for example Computer, Team or Ticket. Some words sound English, but are not used that way in England at all.
wichtigste: Anglicisms are words that have been borrowed from English.
Examples are Computer, Team, fair, Ticket and Weekend.
“Computer” comes from “to compute”, which means to calculate.
The sandwich is named after the Earl of Sandwich.
“Handy” is a false anglicism: in England people say “mobile phone”.
In Switzerland words such as “Weekend” are especially common.

abschnitte.text: English is a **world language**. It is used a lot in science, technology, music, sport and on the internet. That is why new words often reach German-speaking countries in English first. Words such as **Computer**, **E-Mail** or **Team** are now a perfectly normal part of German. A **team** is a group playing together, and if you play **fair**, you play justly.

Some words sound English but were invented in German or are used differently. They are called **false anglicisms**. The best-known example is the **Handy**, the German word for a mobile phone: in England people say “mobile phone” or “mobile”, in America “cell phone”. In English “handy” actually means “practical”. And what Germans call a **Beamer** is called a “projector” in English.

The **sandwich** got its name from John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich. He is said to have eaten filled slices of bread so that he did not have to interrupt his game. The **Pullover** (jumper) comes from “pull over”, because you pull it over your head. A **Ticket** is a travel ticket or an admission ticket.

In Switzerland people often say **Weekend** instead of the German “Wochenende”. “Week” means Woche and “end” means Ende. Words such as “Shop”, “Job” or “Bike” are also often heard in everyday life. Some people find anglicisms practical and modern; others would rather use German words. Both are common attitudes.

gewusst: English has also borrowed many German words, for example “kindergarten” or “rucksack”.
The German word “Smoking” for a dinner suit is a false anglicism. In English it is called a “tuxedo” or “dinner jacket”.

teile.einleitung: Clothes are part of the basic vocabulary of every foreign language, because you need the words when shopping, when packing for a holiday or to describe someone. For German speakers learning English, the German “Schuhe” are “shoes”, “Jacke” is “jacket” and “Handschuhe” are “gloves”. Some words are different in British and American English.
wichtigste: The German “Schuhe” are “shoes” in English, and “Socken” are “socks”.
“Hat” is the German “Hut”, and “jacket” is “Jacke”.
The German “Kleid” is a “dress”, and “Hose” is “trousers”.
“Gloves” are the German “Handschuhe”.
The T-shirt is called “T-shirt” in English too.
In the USA people say “pants” for trousers; in Britain they say “trousers”.
Some items of clothing only exist in the plural in English, such as “trousers”.

abschnitte.text: A T-shirt is called a **“T-shirt”** in English too, the German “Hemd” is a “shirt” and “Bluse” a “blouse”. The pullover is a “jumper” in Britain and a “sweater” in the USA. The German “Kleid” is a “dress” and “Rock” a “skirt”. In French the T-shirt is “le t-shirt” and the dress “la robe”.

In English the German “Hose” is **“trousers”**; in the USA people usually say “pants”. Careful: in Britain “pants” means underpants! Jeans are called “jeans” in English too, and short trousers “shorts”. In English trousers only exist in the plural, which is why you say “my trousers are new” or “a pair of trousers”.

When it is cold you wear a **“jacket”** or a thick “coat”. On your head you wear a “hat” or “beanie”, and round your neck a “scarf”. On your hands you wear **“gloves”** or “mittens”. By the way, the English word “hat” means any kind of head covering, with or without a brim.

The German “Schuhe” are **“shoes”**; trainers are “trainers” in Britain and “sneakers” in the USA. Boots are “boots” and sandals “sandals”. The German “Socken” are “socks”. In French shoes are “les chaussures” and socks “les chaussettes”.

In a clothes shop you ask **“Can I try it on?”** You ask about the size with “What size is it?” If something fits, you say “It fits.”; if it is too big, “It’s too big.” In French you ask “Je peux l’essayer ?”

In English “tragen”, for clothes, is **“to wear”**: “I’m wearing a red jacket.” “Anziehen” is “to put on”, and “ausziehen” is “to take off”. In many English schools the children wear a **school uniform**. In Switzerland this is not usual at state schools.

begriffe.erklaerung: The British word for the German “Hose”; in the USA people say pants.
The English word for gloves with separate fingers, the German “Handschuhe”.
Matching clothes that all the children at a school wear.
The English verb for having clothes on.

gewusst: If you tell people in London about your new “pants”, you are talking about underpants there, not trousers.
Jeans became known in the USA in the 19th century as tough work trousers.
The word “T-shirt” comes from the shape of the garment, which looks like the letter T.

teile.einleitung: A phrasal verb consists of a verb and a little word such as up, off or down. Together they often have a completely new meaning that you cannot guess from the separate words.
wichtigste: A phrasal verb is a verb with a particle such as up, down, off or into.
Give up means to stop trying, find out means to discover.
Look after means to take care of.
Turn down can mean to make quieter; put off means to postpone.
Run into somebody means to meet someone by chance.
With a pronoun, it goes between the verb and the particle: She picked it up.

abschnitte.text: A **phrasal verb** is made up of a verb and a **particle**. Particles are little words such as **up, down, off, out, after** or **into**. Together they often create a new meaning. **Give** means to hand something over, but **give up** means **to stop trying**. That is why it is best to learn phrasal verbs as vocabulary items of their own.

You need many phrasal verbs every day. “Can you **turn down** the music? It's too loud.” asks someone to make the music quieter. The opposite is **turn up**. **Look after** means **to take care of**: “I look after my little brother.” **Find out** means **to discover**: “I want to find out the truth.”

**Put off** means **to postpone**: “The meeting was put off until next week.” If you meet someone by chance, you say **run into**: “I ran into an old friend in Lucerne yesterday.” **Get along with somebody** means **to have a good relationship** with someone. So “I get along with my classmates” means that you like each other.

With many phrasal verbs the object can come before or after the particle: “She picked up the book” or “She picked the book up”. But if the object is a **pronoun** such as it, him or them, it must go in the **middle**. “**She picked it up**” is correct; “She picked up it” is wrong. With verbs such as look after or run into, the object always stays at the end.

Some phrasal verbs have several meanings. **Turn down** also means **to refuse**: “She turned down the offer.” **Take off** means to remove clothes, but also to leave the ground when a plane starts its flight. **Pick up** can mean to lift something from the floor or to collect someone. You can tell which meaning is intended from the context.

gewusst: German has something similar: separable verbs such as aufgeben (to give up) or anrufen (to phone), where part of the verb ends up at the end of the sentence.
Many phrasal verbs have a more formal equivalent, for example postpone for put off or discover for find out.

teile.einleitung: False friends, in French “faux amis”, are words that look similar in two languages but mean something different. They easily lead to funny misunderstandings. If you know them, you make fewer mistakes when speaking French.
wichtigste: “la librairie” is the bookshop; the library is called “la bibliothèque”.
“la cave” is the cellar, not a cave.
“la veste” is a jacket; the waistcoat is called “le gilet”.
“le poison” is poison; the fish is called “le poisson”.
“le magasin” is a shop; the magazine is called “le magazine”.
“l'hôtel de ville” is the town hall.
“le car” is a coach; the car is called “la voiture”.

abschnitte.text: In the “**librairie**” you buy books; it is the **bookshop**. If you want to borrow books, you go to the “**bibliothèque**”. “**Le magasin**” sounds like the German “Magazin” and the English “magazine”, but it is a **shop** or store. A magazine is called “le magazine”. And “l'**hôtel de ville**” is not a hotel, but a town's **town hall**.

abschnitte.titel: In the house and in the wardrobe
abschnitte.text: “**La cave**” is the **cellar**, where you keep wine, for example. A cave is called “la grotte” or “la caverne” in French. If you put on a “**veste**”, you are wearing a **jacket** or blazer. The sleeveless waistcoat, on the other hand, is called “**le gilet**”. By the way, in Switzerland people often say “Gilet” for a waistcoat in German too.

With some words a single letter is enough to cause a misunderstanding. “**Le poison**” with one s is **poison**. “**Le poisson**” with two s is **fish**. The pronunciation is different too: one s between two vowels sounds soft like a buzzing z, two s sound sharp. So if you want to order fish in a restaurant, you had better be careful.

abschnitte.titel: Out and about and at work
abschnitte.text: “**Le car**”, short for “autocar”, is a **coach**. The car is called “**la voiture**”. If someone in France does a “**stage**”, they are doing an **internship** or a course. It has nothing to do with a stage in a theatre, which is called “la scène”. Many false friends come from English or German and developed differently in the different languages.

gewusst: The expression “faux amis” was made known in 1928 by two language researchers in a book about French and English.
There are false friends between German and English too: the English word “become” means “werden” and not “bekommen” (to get).

teile.einleitung: Animals are a lovely topic for learning French. You know many animals from the farm, from the forest or from home.
wichtigste: The cat is called “le chat”, the dog “le chien”.
The cow is called “la vache”, the horse “le cheval”.
The goat is called “la chèvre”, the rabbit “le lapin”.
The bird is called “l'oiseau”, the fish “le poisson”.
The bear is called “l'ours”.
It is best to learn the article le or la together with every animal.

abschnitte.text: The best-known pet is **le chat**, the cat. The t at the end is not pronounced. The dog is called **le chien**, and in French it barks “ouaf ouaf”. **Le lapin**, the rabbit, also often lives with families. It has long ears and likes eating carrots. In the aquarium swims **le poisson**, the fish. Careful: “le poussin” is the chick.

In Switzerland you see lots of **vaches** on the alpine pastures in summer. The cow is called **la vache**. The horse is called **le cheval**, in the plural “les chevaux”. In the Jura there is a well-known Swiss breed of horse, the **Franches-Montagnes** (Freiberger in German). **La chèvre** is the goat. Goat's milk is also made into cheese.

**L'oiseau** is the bird. A bird has feathers and wings. **L'ours** is the bear. It is the heraldic animal of **Bern**, and there is even a bear park in the city. Before “oiseau” and “ours” the article becomes l', because both words begin with a **vowel**. That makes them easier to pronounce.

With animals the article often does not match German. “Die Katze” (the cat) is feminine in German, but “le chat” is **masculine**. “Der Fisch” (the fish) is masculine, and so is “le poisson”. That is why it is best to learn every animal **with its article**: le chat, le chien, la vache, la chèvre. The plural is usually formed with an s: les chats, les chiens.

gewusst: The plural of “l'oiseau” is “les oiseaux”, with an x at the end.
In French the cockerel says “cocorico” instead of “cock-a-doodle-doo”.

teile.einleitung: Some of the most important French verbs do not follow a fixed rule. They include aller, faire and prendre, which you need all the time in everyday life.
wichtigste: Irregular verbs have to be learnt by heart.
“Aller” means to go: je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont.
“Faire” means to do or make: je fais, il fait, nous faisons, vous faites, ils font.
The form “faisez” does not exist; the correct form is “vous faites”.
“Prendre” means to take: je prends, nous prenons, ils prennent.
“Ils prennent” has a double n, “nous prenons” only one.

abschnitte.text: **Aller** ends in -er, but it is conjugated completely irregularly. The forms are: je **vais**, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils **vont**. The stem of “je vais” looks completely different from the infinitive. You need aller very often: “Je vais à l'école” (I go to school), “Ils vont au cinéma” (they go to the cinema). Aller is also used to form the near future: “Je vais manger.” (I am going to eat.)

**Faire** means to do or to make. The forms are: je fais, tu fais, il fait, nous **faisons**, vous **faites**, ils font. In “nous faisons” the ai is pronounced like a weak, unstressed e. The form “faisez” does not exist. Faire appears in many expressions: “faire du sport” (to do sport), “faire la cuisine” (to cook), “faire ses devoirs” (to do your homework). Also for the weather: “Il fait beau.” (The weather is nice.)

**Prendre** means to take. The forms are: je prends, tu prends, il prend, nous **prenons**, vous prenez, ils **prennent**. In the singular the d stays; in the plural it disappears. Watch the n: “nous prenons” has only one n, “ils prennent” two. You say, for example, “Tu prends le bus” (you take the bus) or “Elles prennent le train” (they take the train).

Four very important verbs have a similar ils form ending in **-ont**: ils **vont** (aller), ils **font** (faire), ils **sont** (être) and ils **ont** (avoir). These forms rhyme and are easy to remember together. The vous form is also special in three verbs: vous **faites**, vous **êtes** and vous **dites**. Almost all other verbs end in -ez with vous.

gewusst: The verbs apprendre (to learn) and comprendre (to understand) are conjugated exactly like prendre.
“Aller” is made up of forms that go back to different Latin verbs.

teile.einleitung: The **Cambridge English Qualifications** are internationally recognised English exams from the University of Cambridge. They certify how well someone knows English. In Switzerland many young people take them at grammar school (Gymnasium) or vocational school.
wichtigste: The exams are based on the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR).
The Council of Europe's CEFR divides language skills into the levels A1 to C2.
B2 First used to be called FCE, C1 Advanced used to be called CAE.
C2 Proficiency is the highest Cambridge exam.
B2 First is passed with 160 points or more on the Cambridge English Scale.
Cambridge certificates have no expiry date.

abschnitte.text: The **Common European Framework of Reference for Languages**, **CEFR** for short, was published by the **Council of Europe** in 2001. It describes six levels: A1 and A2 for beginners, B1 and B2 for intermediate learners, C1 and C2 for very good knowledge. This makes it possible to compare language skills all over Europe. The Cambridge exams are matched exactly to these levels.

There are exams for every level, for example **A2 Key** and **B1 Preliminary**. Very widespread is **B2 First**, formerly the “First Certificate in English” or **FCE**. It is followed by **C1 Advanced**, formerly **CAE**, which is often required for university and work. The most demanding general exam is **C2 Proficiency**, formerly CPE. It shows near-native knowledge.

B2 First has four parts. In the **Reading and Use of English** part there are gap-fill texts, word-formation and rewriting tasks as well as reading tasks. These are followed by **Writing**, **Listening** and **Speaking**. The speaking test usually takes place **in pairs**: one examiner leads the conversation and a second one assesses it.

The results are given on the **Cambridge English Scale**. For B2 First, 160 to 172 points mean a pass with **Grade C**. With even more points there is Grade B or Grade A. With 180 points or more, the **C1** level is even certified. Anyone who scores just under 160 points can receive a certificate for level B1.

abschnitte.titel: How long is the certificate valid?
abschnitte.text: Cambridge certificates are in principle **valid for ever** and have no expiry date. However, individual universities or employers may require the proof not to be too old. In Switzerland the certificates are often included with applications for an apprenticeship or a university place.

gewusst: The first Cambridge English exams were held as early as 1913.
The exams are offered in a great many countries around the world, including many Swiss towns and cities.

teile.einleitung: Gefühle are called **feelings** in English. With simple words you can say whether you are happy, sad, tired or angry. This helps when you talk to others and want to feel understood.
wichtigste: “Happy” means glücklich, “sad” means traurig.
“Angry” means wütend and has nothing to do with the German word “Angst” (fear).
If you are müde, you are “tired”.
If you are “scared”, you are afraid.
“I am hungry” means Ich habe Hunger.
“Surprised” means überrascht, “bored” means gelangweilt.

abschnitte.text: **Happy** means glücklich or cheerful. That is why people say **Happy birthday**. If you are amazed by a surprise, you are **surprised**. If you are looking forward to something, you are **excited**. And if you are calm and content, you are **relaxed**.

Traurig is **sad**. **Angry** means wütend. Careful: it sounds a bit like the German word “Angst”, but it has nothing to do with it. If you are afraid, you are **scared** or **afraid**. All feelings are part of life, the difficult ones too. It often helps to talk about them.

Müde is **tired**: in the evening many children are tired. If you are hungry, you say **I am hungry**, “Ich habe Hunger”. If you are thirsty, you say **I am thirsty**. If nothing is happening, you are **bored**.

In English you usually express feelings with **I am** or, for short, **I'm**: **I'm happy**, **I'm tired**. In German people often say “Ich habe Hunger” (I have hunger), but in English it is “I am hungry”. You can ask **How do you feel?** or **Are you okay?** If you want to show sympathy, you say **I'm sorry**.

gewusst: “Bored” and “boring” have two different meanings: “I am bored” means you have nothing interesting to do, “It is boring” means the thing is dull.
Little pictures for feelings in messages are called emojis. The word comes from Japanese.

teile.einleitung: In this chapter you learn what the members of a family are called in French. With these words you can introduce your own family, for example to a child from French-speaking Switzerland.
wichtigste: “La mère” is the mother, “le père” is the father.
“Le fils” is the son, “la fille” is the daughter.
“Le frère” is the brother, “la sœur” is the sister.
“La grand-mère” and “le grand-père” are the grandparents.
“L'oncle” is the uncle, “la tante” is the aunt.
Children often say “maman”, “papa”, “mamie” and “papi”.

abschnitte.text: The mother is called **la mère**, the father **le père**. Together they are **les parents**, the parents. A son is **le fils**, a daughter is **la fille**. In “fils” you pronounce the “s” at the end, unlike in many other French words. In everyday life children usually just say “maman” and “papa”.

The brother is called **le frère**, the sister **la sœur**. In the word “sœur” the o and e stand close together as **œ**. You also find this letter in “l'œil” (the eye) or “le cœur” (the heart). Brothers and sisters together are called **les frères et sœurs**. So you ask: “Tu as des frères et sœurs ?”, meaning “Have you got any brothers or sisters?”.

The grandmother is **la grand-mère**, the grandfather **le grand-père**. Both together are **les grands-parents**. The words have a hyphen, like a compound word. Many children lovingly call their grandparents **mamie** and **papi**. The grandchildren are called **les petits-enfants**.

The brother of your mother or father is **l'oncle**, the uncle. The sister of your mother or father is **la tante**, the aunt. Their children are your cousins: **le cousin** and **la cousine**. Before a vowel, “le” or “la” simply becomes **l'**, which is why it is “l'oncle”. With “mon”, “ma” and “mes” you say “my”: “mon père”, “ma tante”, “mes cousins”.

gewusst: German borrowed the words “Onkel”, “Tante” and “Cousin” from French, and English “uncle”, “aunt” and “cousin” also come from French.
The word “fille” means both “daughter” and “girl”.

teile.einleitung: In the passive, the focus is not on who does something but on what happens to someone or something. In French the passive is formed with “être” and the participe passé. There are some important rules.
wichtigste: The passive is formed with “être” and the participe passé.
The participe passé agrees with the subject.
The person or thing doing the action is usually introduced with “par”.
With verbs of feeling such as “aimer”, “de” is traditionally used.
The tense is shown by “être”: “est construit”, “a été construit”, “sera construit”.
Only transitive verbs with a direct object have a personal passive.

abschnitte.text: In the active, the one doing the action comes first: “Le chat mange la souris.” (The cat eats the mouse.) In the **passive** the **object becomes the subject**: “La souris est mangée par le chat.” (The mouse is eaten by the cat.) The passive is formed with **être** and the **participe passé**. The participe passé agrees with the new subject. Because “la souris” is feminine, it is “mangée” with an extra e.

The one who carries out the action is called the **agent**. It is usually introduced with **par**: “La maison est construite par l'architecte.” (The house is built by the architect.) With verbs of **feeling** and state such as **aimer** or **respecter**, **de** is traditionally used. So you say “Il est aimé **de** tous”, “He is loved by everyone”. Often the agent is left out altogether.

The tense is always shown by **être**. In the present it is “Le pont **est** construit” (the bridge is built). In the passé composé “être” itself is in the passé composé: “Le pont **a été** construit en 1900” (the bridge was built in 1900). In the future it is “Le travail **sera** terminé demain” (the work will be finished tomorrow). The participe passé always agrees with the subject: “Les lettres ont été **écrites** hier” (the letters were written yesterday), because “les lettres” is feminine and plural.

A passive only works with **transitive verbs**, which have a direct object. A verb such as **dormir** (to sleep) is intransitive and therefore cannot be put into the passive. French also has the **pronominal passive** with a reflexive verb: “Ce vin **se boit** frais” means “This wine is drunk chilled”. In everyday life the passive is often replaced by **on**: “On a construit le pont” (they built the bridge) instead of “Le pont a été construit”.

gewusst: In German the passive is formed with “werden” (to become), in French with “être”, meaning “to be”, as in English.
The pronominal passive is often found in rules and instructions, for example “Ça ne se fait pas”, “That isn't done”.

teile.einleitung: With “have got” you say in English what someone has or owns. The form is especially popular in British English and is used very often in everyday life.
wichtigste: Have got means “haben” or “besitzen” (to have or to own).
With I, you, we and they it is have got; with he, she and it it is has got.
The short forms are I've got and he's got.
The negative is haven't got or hasn't got.
In questions have or has comes first: Have you got a pet?
Short answers are Yes, he has or No, he hasn't, without got.

abschnitte.text: With **have got** you say that you own something. “I have got a dog” means you own a dog. “I have got a bike” means you own a bike. It is also used for family and appearance: “I've got a sister” or “She has got blue eyes”. It works for illnesses too: “I've got a cold”.

Which form you use depends on the person. With **I, you, we** and **they** it is **have got**. With **he, she** and **it** it is **has got**. So: “I have got a dog”, but “She has got a cat”. This is like other verbs, which get an ending with s with he, she and it.

In conversation people almost always use **short forms**. I have got becomes **I've got**, he has got becomes **he's got**. In the same way: you've got, we've got, they've got, she's got and it's got. Careful: he's can also mean he is. But if got follows it, has is always meant.

For the **negative** you add not to have or has: “I **haven't** got a sister”. With he, she and it it is hasn't got. For a **question** you put have or has at the beginning: “Have you got a pet?” In **short answers** you leave out got: “Yes, he has” or “No, I haven't”.

Have got is typical of **British English**. In **American English** people usually just say have with do: “Do you have a pet?” and “I don't have a sister”. Both forms are correct and are understood everywhere. The only important thing is not to mix them. “Do you have got” is wrong.

gewusst: Have got is used almost only in the present. For the past you simply say had: “I had a dog.”
In casual American English you sometimes even hear just “I got a dog” without have.

teile.einleitung: With question words you can ask about people, places, times or reasons. There are only a few of them in French, and with them you can already get very far in a conversation.
wichtigste: “Qui” means “who”, “quoi” means “what”.
“Où” means “where”, “quand” means “when”.
“Comment” means “how”, “pourquoi” means “why”.
“Combien” means “how much” or “how many”.
To answer “pourquoi”, you say “parce que”, meaning “because”.
“Quelle heure est-il ?” means “What time is it?”.

abschnitte.text: You ask about a person with **qui**, which means “who”. “Qui est là ?” means “Who is there?”. You ask about a thing with **quoi** or **que**, which means “what”. Among friends people say “Tu fais quoi ?”, meaning “What are you doing?”. At the beginning of a sentence you usually need “qu'est-ce que”: “Qu'est-ce que tu manges ?” (What are you eating?).

You ask about a place with **où**, which means “where” or “where to”. “Où habites-tu ?” means “Where do you live?”. Careful: the word “ou” without an accent means “or”. You ask about time with **quand**, which means “when”. To ask the time you say “**Quelle heure est-il ?**”, because “l'heure” is the hour.

With **comment** you ask about the way something is done; it means “how”. A very well-known example is “Comment ça va ?”, meaning “How are you?”. With **pourquoi** you ask about the reason; it means “why”. The answer often begins with **parce que**, which means “because”. For example: “Pourquoi tu ris ? Parce que c'est drôle.” (Why are you laughing? Because it's funny.)

You ask about an amount with **combien**, which means “how much” or “how many”. In a shop you ask “C'est combien ?”, meaning “How much is it?”. The word **quel** means “which”. It adapts to the noun: “quel”, “quelle”, “quels” or “quelles”. All four forms sound the same.

gewusst: “Pourquoi” is made of “pour” (for) and “quoi” (what), so literally “for what”.
The words “où” and “ou” sound exactly the same; only the accent shows the difference.

teile.einleitung: Food is a lovely topic for learning French. You need many of the words every day, for example at breakfast or when shopping. As always, it is best to learn the words together with their article.
wichtigste: “le pain” is bread, “le beurre” butter.
“la pomme” is the apple, “la pomme de terre” the potato.
“l'eau” is water, “le lait” milk.
“l'œuf” is the egg.
“le gâteau” is the cake, “la fraise” the strawberry.

abschnitte.text: For breakfast there is often “**le pain**”, bread. In French-speaking Switzerland you buy it in the “boulangerie”. You spread “**le beurre**”, butter, on it. With it you drink “**le lait**”, milk, which comes from the cow. Perhaps there is also “**l'œuf**”, an egg that the hen has laid. In “l'œuf” the o and e are joined to form a special letter.

“**La pomme**” is the apple. An apple is a tasty mid-morning snack (in Swiss German “Znüni”) for break time. “**La pomme de terre**”, the potato, sounds very similar. Literally it means “apple of the earth”, just like the word “Erdapfel” in German. “**La fraise**” is the strawberry. Strawberries are red and ripen in early summer.

Water is called “**l'eau**”. You pronounce it almost like a long “o”. Because “eau” begins with a vowel, “la” is shortened to “l'”. It is the same with “l'œuf”. In “le lait”, milk, you do not hear the t at the end.

“**Le gâteau**” is the cake. On a birthday there is often a “gâteau” with candles. A strawberry cake is called “le gâteau aux fraises”. French-speaking Switzerland also has special treats, for example the “gâteau du Vully” from the area around Lake Murten, or the Fribourg “meringues” with double cream from the Gruyère region.

gewusst: The character “œ” in “l'œuf” joins o and e, and it also appears in “le cœur” (the heart).
In the plural, “les œufs” is pronounced differently from the singular: the f at the end is then silent.

teile.einleitung: English grammar is the set of rules for forming words and sentences in English. For German speakers a lot of it is simpler than German, because there is only one article, “the”, and hardly any cases. On the other hand, English has many tenses, fixed word order and some tricky special rules, which are mainly learnt in the higher years.
wichtigste: English has only one definite article, namely “the”.
Sentence structure usually follows the order subject, verb, object.
Questions and negatives are often formed with the auxiliary verb “do”.
In conditional sentences you say, for example, “If I had known, I would have come.”
The passive of the continuous form is, for example, “A new bridge is being built.”
In reported speech the tense is often moved back: “She said that she was tired.”
After “stop”, the -ing form means that you give something up, as in “He stopped smoking.”

abschnitte.text: English sentences almost always follow the fixed order **subject, verb, object**, as in “Tom plays football.” Unlike in German, the verb does not go at the end of the sentence, not even in subordinate clauses. For questions and negatives you usually need the auxiliary verb **“do”**: “Do you like pizza?” or “I don’t know.” After “Hardly” or “No sooner”, the word order is turned round, for example “Hardly had she arrived when the phone rang.”

English has many **tenses** and distinguishes precisely whether something is happening right now or regularly. “I play” means I play regularly, while “I am playing” means I am playing at the moment. The **present perfect**, as in “I have finished”, links the past with the present. Many common verbs are irregular, such as go, went, gone.

Sentences with “if” are called **conditional sentences**. For something unreal in the past you say “If I had known, I would have come.” In mixed sentences you link the past and the present: “If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.” In formal English there is also the subjunctive, as in “It is essential that he be on time.”

In the **passive**, the focus is on what happens to something: “They are building a new bridge.” becomes “A new bridge is being built.” In **reported speech** you pass on what someone has said. The tense usually moves back one step: “I am tired” becomes “She said that she was tired.” Pronouns change as well.

Some verbs are followed by the **-ing form**: “He stopped smoking.” means that he gave up smoking. “I am used to getting up early.” means that getting up early is normal for me. Question tags turn the statement round, which is why it is “Nobody called, did they?” The relative pronoun “that” must not introduce a non-essential relative clause set off by commas; there you use “which” or “who”.

In many cantons of German-speaking Switzerland, **English lessons** already begin at primary school. In some cantons on the language border, children learn French first and English later. Grammar is built up step by step, from simple present-tense sentences to conditional sentences and the passive at grammar school. At the end, many young people take an international **Cambridge certificate**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sentence with “if” that says what happens under a certain condition.
A sentence form in which what happens to something matters, not who does it.
A short question added at the end of a sentence, for example “isn’t it?”.
Reversed word order, in which the auxiliary verb moves in front of the subject.
The -ing form of a verb used like a noun, for example “smoking”.

gewusst: Over the centuries English has lost almost all the case endings that it used to have, like German.
The word “I” is the only pronoun in English that is always written with a capital letter.
Many English grammar books list more than 150 irregular verbs.

teile.einleitung: In French the little words “y” and “en” replace whole parts of a sentence. That way you do not have to keep repeating places, amounts and things.
wichtigste: “Y” replaces a place phrase with à, en, dans or chez: “J'y vais.”
“Y” also replaces a phrase with “à” referring to things: “J'y pense.”
“En” replaces an amount or a noun with des, du or de la.
“En” also replaces a phrase with “de”, for example a place someone comes from: “J'en reviens.”
Both pronouns come before the conjugated verb.
If they appear together, “y” comes first, then “en”: “il y en a”.

abschnitte.text: The pronoun **y** replaces a place phrase. To the question “Tu vas à Berne ?” (Are you going to Bern?) you answer “Oui, j'y vais.” (Yes, I'm going there.) “À Berne” simply becomes “y”. This also works with “en”, “dans” or “chez”: “Tu es chez toi ? Oui, j'y suis.” (Are you at home? Yes, I am.) In English “y” often corresponds to the word **there**.

Many verbs are followed by **à**, for example “penser à” (to think about) or “s'intéresser à” (to be interested in). If it is about a thing, you replace the phrase with y: “Tu penses à ton examen ? Oui, j'y pense.” (Are you thinking about your exam? Yes, I'm thinking about it.) Or: “Tu t'intéresses à la musique ? Oui, je m'y intéresse.” With **people** it is different. After “penser à”, school grammar says “Je pense à elle” (I am thinking of her).

The pronoun **en** replaces a noun with des, du or de la. “Tu as des frères ? Oui, j'en ai deux.” (Have you got any brothers? Yes, I have two.) The number stays at the end. You also need en with quantities such as “beaucoup” (a lot) or “un kilo”: “J'en veux beaucoup.” (I want a lot of it.) In English en is often translated as **of it** or **of them**, or left out.

En also replaces phrases with **de**. For where someone comes from: “Tu reviens de Lausanne ? Oui, j'en reviens.” (Are you back from Lausanne? Yes, I've just come back from there.) The same goes for verbs such as “s'occuper de” (to look after): “Tu t'occupes du jardin ? Oui, je m'en occupe.” With things, en is then the right choice. A very common expression is “il y en a”, which means “there is some” or “there are some”.

Normally y and en come **before the conjugated verb**: “J'y vais”, “Je n'en ai pas.” (I haven't got any.) If both appear, the order is **y before en**: “Il y a du pain ? Oui, il y en a.” (Is there any bread? Yes, there is some.) In the positive **imperative** they come after the verb with a hyphen. Verbs ending in -er then get an extra s so that it is easier to say: “Manges-en !” (Eat some!), “Vas-y !”

gewusst: The well-known exclamation “Vas-y !” literally means “Go there!”, but it is used in the sense of “Go on, do it!”.
“Il y a” (there is) also contains the pronoun y.

teile.einleitung: Albert Camus was a French writer and philosopher who grew up in Algeria. His novels “L'Étranger” and “La Peste” are among the best-known books of the 20th century. In 1957 he received the Nobel Prize in Literature.
wichtigste: Camus was born in 1913 in Algeria, which was French at the time.
In 1957, at the age of 44, he received the Nobel Prize in Literature.
“L'Étranger” (1942) begins with “Aujourd'hui, maman est morte.”
“La Peste” (1947) is set in the Algerian city of Oran.
At the centre of his thinking is the absurd.
His essay about Sisyphus ends with “Il faut imaginer Sisyphe heureux.”
After “L'Homme révolté” (1951) his friendship with Jean-Paul Sartre broke down.

abschnitte.text: **Albert Camus** was born in 1913 in Mondovi, today Dréan, in **Algeria**, which was French at the time. He grew up in poor circumstances in **Algiers**. A teacher recognised his talent and supported him. The sun, the sea and the poverty of his childhood shape many of his works. During the Second World War he worked in Paris for the resistance newspaper “Combat”.

His novel **“L'Étranger”** (in English “The Outsider” or “The Stranger”) appeared in 1942. It begins with the famous plain sentence: “**Aujourd'hui, maman est morte.**” (Mother died today.) The main character **Meursault** seems indifferent and distant. After he has shot a man on a beach near Algiers, he is put on trial and convicted, partly because he did not cry at his mother's funeral. The book asks how society deals with someone who does not share its rules.

The novel **“La Peste”** (The Plague) from 1947 is set in the Algerian city of **Oran**. Plague breaks out there, and the city is sealed off. The doctor **Bernard Rieux** fights the epidemic together with others. The novel is often also read as a parable of the German occupation of France. It tells of solidarity and of doing the right thing, even when it seems hopeless.

At the centre of Camus' thinking is **the absurd**. It arises when people ask about the meaning of life, but the world gives no answer. Camus responds not with despair but with **revolt**. His essay “Le Mythe de Sisyphe” is about the mythical figure **Sisyphus**, who rolls a stone up a mountain for ever. The essay ends with the sentence: “**Il faut imaginer Sisyphe heureux.**” (One must imagine Sisyphus happy.)

abschnitte.titel: Nobel Prize and quarrel with Sartre
abschnitte.text: In 1951 the essay **“L'Homme révolté”** (The Rebel) appeared. In it Camus criticises revolutionary violence and totalitarian ideologies. The magazine “Les Temps modernes” of **Jean-Paul Sartre** reacted sharply, and the friendship between the two broke down. In 1957, at 44, Camus received the **Nobel Prize in Literature**, as one of its youngest winners. He died in 1960 in a car accident in France.

gewusst: In his youth in Algiers, Camus played football as a goalkeeper and later said he had learnt a lot about morality from it.
Jean-Paul Sartre turned down the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1964; Camus had accepted it seven years earlier.

teile.einleitung: Laïcité means that the state and religion are separate. In France this principle is especially important and is even written into the constitution. In Switzerland, too, there are cantons that have separated church and state.
wichtigste: With the law of 1905 France separated church and state.
Since then the Republic has not recognised, paid or supported any religion.
Article 1 of the 1958 constitution calls France a secular republic.
In Alsace and the Moselle département a special law still applies today.
Since 2004 pupils have been forbidden to wear conspicuous religious symbols at state schools.
In Switzerland the cantons regulate the relationship between church and state.

abschnitte.text: The word **laïcité** is translated into English as **secularism**. It means that the state and religious communities are **separate**. The state is neutral and does not favour any religion. At the same time it guarantees **freedom of conscience** and the free practice of religion. Article 1 of the French constitution of 1958 says that France is a “République indivisible, laïque, démocratique et sociale” (an indivisible, secular, democratic and social Republic).

As early as the 1880s, the minister **Jules Ferry** changed schools. The laws of 1881 and 1882 made state primary school **free, compulsory and secular**. Religious education was taken out of the curriculum. In 2004 another law was added. It forbids pupils at state schools from wearing **conspicuous religious symbols**; discreet symbols are still allowed. This law was much debated in France.

On **9 December 1905** the law on the separation of the churches and the state came into force, the “Loi de séparation des Églises et de l'État”. It ended the **Concordat of 1801**, an agreement with the Pope. Article 2 says that the Republic does not recognise, pay or support any religion. This ended the state's payment of the clergy. One of the fathers of the law is considered to be **Aristide Briand**, who later received the Nobel Peace Prize.

In 1905 **Alsace** and the **Moselle** département belonged to the German Empire. That is why the separation law did not apply there, and after 1918 the old law remained in force. To this day the state pays certain clergy there. In Switzerland the relationship between church and state is **a matter for the cantons**, so it is arranged slightly differently everywhere. The canton of **Geneva** abolished the state church budget in 1907. Its constitution of 2012 states: “L'État est laïque.” (The state is secular.)

gewusst: The word “laïque” comes from the Greek word for “people” and used to mean people who are not clergy.
In many other Swiss cantons the Reformed and Catholic churches are officially recognised under public law as national churches.

teile.einleitung: We wear clothes every day, light ones in summer and warm ones in winter. Here you learn the most important items of clothing in French. That way you can say what you are wearing.
wichtigste: Clothes are called “les vêtements” in French.
“Le pantalon” is trousers, and in French it is singular.
“La robe” is the dress, “la jupe” the skirt.
“Le pull” is the jumper, “la veste” the jacket.
“La chaussure” is the shoe, “les chaussettes” are the socks.
“Le chapeau” is the hat, “le bonnet” the woolly hat.

abschnitte.text: Clothes are called **les vêtements** in French. A jumper is called **le pull** for short; it keeps you warm in winter. Over it you put on **la veste**, the jacket. A T-shirt is also called **le t-shirt** in French. A long, warm coat is **le manteau**.

Trousers are called **le pantalon**. Unlike in English or German, where people often use the plural, in French it is **singular**. **La jupe** is the skirt, which goes from the waist downwards. **La robe** is the dress, which is all one piece, top and bottom. Shorts are called **le short**.

The shoe is called **la chaussure**, two shoes are **les chaussures**. Inside your shoes you wear **les chaussettes**, the socks. Both words begin in a similar way, which helps you remember them. Trainers are called **les baskets**. In winter people often wear warm boots, **les bottes**.

The hat is called **le chapeau**, the warm woolly hat **le bonnet**. Round your neck you wrap **l'écharpe**, the scarf. On your hands you put **les gants**, the gloves. To say what you are wearing, you need the verb **porter**, “to wear”: “Je porte un pull rouge.” (I am wearing a red jumper.)

gewusst: The German word “Robe” for a formal dress, and the English word “robe”, come from the French “la robe”.
“Mettre” means “to put on”: “Je mets mon manteau” means “I am putting on my coat”.

teile.einleitung: The futur antérieur is a compound future tense. You use it to say that something will already be finished in the future before something else happens. It corresponds to the English future perfect and the German Futur II.
wichtigste: The futur antérieur consists of “avoir” or “être” in the futur simple and the participe passé.
Example: “j'aurai fini”, “I will have finished”.
It expresses something completed earlier in the future, often after “quand” or “dès que”.
It can also express a guess about something in the past.
Verbs with “être” make the participe passé agree with the subject.
It corresponds to the German Futur II.

abschnitte.text: The futur antérieur has two parts: the **auxiliary verb in the futur simple** and the **participe passé**. With “avoir” the forms are “j'aurai, tu auras, il aura, nous aurons, vous aurez, ils auront”. This gives, for example, **j'aurai fini** (I will have finished) or **nous aurons fait** (we will have done). With “être” they are “je serai, tu seras, il sera, nous serons, vous serez, ils seront”. Which auxiliary you need is the same as in the passé composé.

Verbs of movement such as **aller**, **arriver** or **partir** form the futur antérieur with **être**. Then the participe passé agrees with the subject. A boy says “je serai allé”, a girl writes “je serai allée”. With “elle” it is **sera arrivée**, with an extra e. With “ils” it is **seront partis**, with an s for the plural.

abschnitte.titel: Something completed earlier in the future
abschnitte.text: Most often the futur antérieur shows that something in the future will be finished **before something else**. “Quand tu **auras fini** tes devoirs, tu pourras sortir.” (When you have finished your homework, you can go out.) First the homework is done, then you may go out. Typical words are **quand**, **dès que**, **lorsque** or **après que**. The part that happens later is in the futur simple.

The futur antérieur can also express a **guess about something in the past**. “Paul n'est pas venu, il **aura oublié** le rendez-vous” means: Paul probably forgot the appointment. German says something similar: “Er wird es vergessen haben” (he will have forgotten it). This German tense is called **Futur II**, for example “Ich werde gegessen haben” (I will have eaten). But German uses the Futur II less often than French speakers use their futur antérieur.

gewusst: “Antérieur” means “before” or “earlier”, which fits the idea of something happening first.
In German the perfect tense often follows “wenn” where French requires the futur antérieur: “Wenn du fertig bist” (when you have finished) is “Quand tu auras fini”.

teile.einleitung: Every language has holidays, and people often wish each other something nice for them. Here you learn what the most important festivals and greetings are called in French, just as people use them in French-speaking Switzerland.
wichtigste: “La fête” is the festival or party; “Bonne fête !” means “Have a lovely celebration!”.
On 1 January people say “Bonne année !”.
“Joyeux anniversaire” is sung on birthdays.
“La Pentecôte” is Whitsun (Pentecost), “l'Ascension” is Ascension Day.
“Le Vendredi saint” is Good Friday.
In French-speaking Switzerland, Santa Claus's Swiss cousin Samichlaus is called “Saint Nicolas”.

abschnitte.text: The word for festival or party is **la fête**. If someone is celebrating, you wish them **“Bonne fête !”**. On 1 January you say **“Bonne année !”**, meaning “Happy New Year!”. “L'année” is the year. At Christmas you wish **“Joyeux Noël !”**. A public holiday, when you have the day off, is called **un jour férié**.

The birthday is called **l'anniversaire**. The birthday song begins with **“Joyeux anniversaire”**. Mother's Day is **la fête des mères**, because “la mère” is the mother. It is celebrated in May, and people give their mothers presents. There is also a Father's Day: **la fête des pères**.

Easter is called **Pâques**. The Friday before it is **le Vendredi saint**, Good Friday, because “vendredi” means Friday and “saint” means holy. Forty days after Easter comes **l'Ascension**, Ascension Day. It is always on a Thursday. Seven weeks after Easter people celebrate **la Pentecôte**, Whitsun or Pentecost.

On 6 December **Saint Nicolas** comes, called Samichlaus in Swiss German. In the town of Fribourg he walks through the old town with a donkey every year. Christmas is called **Noël** and is celebrated on 25 December. The Christmas tree is called **le sapin de Noël**. On the national holiday, people in French-speaking Switzerland simply say **“le 1er août”** (the 1st of August).

gewusst: The word “Pentecôte” comes from Greek and means “the fiftieth day”.
In France Father Christmas is called “le Père Noël”, literally “Father Christmas”.

teile.einleitung: English is spoken and written differently in Great Britain and in the USA. Many everyday words are different, and some words even mean something else. Even so, British and American people understand each other without any trouble.
wichtigste: A home on one floor of a building is a “flat” in British English and an “apartment” in American English.
The lift is called a “lift” in British English and an “elevator” in American English.
British “chips” are what Americans call French fries; potato chips are called “crisps” in Britain.
Americans write “color”, the British “colour”.
Autumn is “autumn” in British English and often “fall” in American English.
Holidays are a “holiday” in British English and a “vacation” in American English.

abschnitte.text: In London people live in a **flat**, in New York in an **apartment**. To go up, the British take the **lift**, Americans the **elevator**. A moving staircase is called an **escalator** in both countries. The underground railway is the **underground** in Britain and the **subway** in America. In Great Britain, on the other hand, a “subway” is a pedestrian tunnel under a road.

A sweet biscuit (in Swiss German “Guetzli”) is called a **biscuit** in Britain and a **cookie** in America. In the USA a “biscuit” is more like a soft bread roll. If you order **chips** in Great Britain, you get French fries, for example with “fish and chips”. Potato crisps are called **crisps** in Britain, but “chips” in America. Chips are called **French fries** in the USA.

Long trousers are called **trousers** in Britain and **pants** in America. Careful: in Great Britain “pants” are underpants. A jumper is often called a **jumper** in Britain and a **sweater** in America. Sports shoes are called **trainers** in Britain and **sneakers** in America.

In American English the u is dropped in words like **colour**: **color**, **favorite**, **neighbor**. “-re” often becomes “-er”: **centre** becomes **center**, **theatre** becomes **theater**. Many of these spellings go back to the American **Noah Webster**. He published an influential dictionary in 1828 and wanted to simplify spelling.

Autumn is called **autumn** in Britain and very often **fall** in America, because that is when the leaves fall. Holidays away from school or work are a **holiday** in Britain and a **vacation** in America. In the USA “holiday” rather means a public holiday. Dates are also written differently: Americans give the month first, the British the day first.

gewusst: At school in Switzerland pupils mostly learn British English, but both varieties are considered correct.
The British pronounce the letter Z “zed”, Americans “zee”.

teile.einleitung: The definite article stands in front of a noun, like “the” in English or “der”, “die” and “das” in German. In French there are only “le”, “la”, “l'” and “les”. Because French words often have a different gender from German ones, it is best to learn the article together with the word.
wichtigste: “le” comes before masculine words in the singular: le chat.
“la” comes before feminine words in the singular: la maison.
Before a vowel, “le” and “la” become “l'”: l'école.
In the plural there is only “les”: les chats, les fleurs.
The gender is often different from German: le soleil, la lune.
In the plural the noun usually gets an s: les livres.

abschnitte.text: French has only two genders: **masculine** and **feminine**. There is no neuter gender like the German “das”. Before masculine words you use “**le**”, for example “le chat” (the cat). Before feminine words you use “**la**”, for example “la fleur” (the flower). That is why it is best to learn every new word together with its article.

A French word often has a different gender from the German one. “**La maison**” (the house) is feminine, although in German it is “das Haus”. “**Le soleil**” (the sun) is masculine, but in German it is “die Sonne”. The other way round, “**la lune**” (the moon) is feminine, while in German it is “der Mond”. Sometimes, though, it is the same: “la fleur” is feminine like “die Blume”.

If a word begins with a **vowel** (a, e, i, o, u), “le” and “la” are shortened to “**l'**”. So you do not write “la école”, but “**l'école**” (the school). In the same way it is “l'ami” (the friend) and “l'eau” (the water). This makes the word easier to say. It also happens before many words with a silent h, for example “l'hôtel”.

In the plural it is very simple: there is only one article, “**les**”. It is used for masculine and feminine words. “Le livre” becomes “**les livres**” (the books), “la fleur” becomes “les fleurs”. The noun usually gets an **s**, but you cannot hear it. Before a vowel you link “les” to the word when speaking: “les‿amis” sounds like “lesamis”.

gewusst: In French-speaking Switzerland people say “le natel” for a mobile phone, a word that is not used in this way in France.
Some words change their meaning with the article: “le tour” is the round or lap, “la tour” the tower.

teile.einleitung: Ordering in English at a restaurant is not at all difficult. With a few words and polite sentences you will get through the evening easily in London, New York or Sydney.
wichtigste: The Speisekarte is called the “menu”.
The first course is the “starter”, then comes the “main course”, and at the end the “dessert”.
A woman who serves you is a “waitress”, a man a “waiter”.
You order politely with “I'd like ..., please”.
The bill is called “bill” in Britain and “check” in America.
The Trinkgeld is called a “tip”.

abschnitte.text: Often you wait at the entrance until you are given a table. The staff ask, for example, “How many people?”. Then you are given the **menu**. If you have booked, you say “I have a reservation”. A Tisch is called a “table” in English.
A meal often has several courses. First comes the **starter**, for example a soup. Then follows the **main course**. At the end there is the **dessert**. Drinks are called “drinks”.

The waitress asks: “Are you ready to order?” She wants to know whether you would like to order, because **to order** means bestellen. You answer politely with **I'd like**, the short form of “I would like”. For example: “I'd like a glass of water, please.” The word “please” makes every request friendlier, and “thank you” always belongs too.

With a steak people often ask how well cooked it should be. **Rare** means still red inside. **Medium** is in between. **Well done** means cooked right through. That way you get your meat exactly the way you like it.

At the end you ask: “Could I have the bill, please?” In Great Britain it is called the **bill**, in the USA the **check**. The extra money for the staff is called a **tip**. In the USA about 15 to 20 per cent is usual, because the staff earn a large part of their wages this way. In Switzerland service is usually already included in the price, and a tip is voluntary.

gewusst: In the USA many restaurants give you a glass of water with ice without being asked.
The word “restaurant” comes from French and is spelt the same way in English.

teile.einleitung: Relative pronouns join two sentences into one. In French there are several of them, and which one you choose depends on its job in the relative clause.
wichtigste: “Qui” stands for the subject in the relative clause, for people and things.
“Que” stands for the direct object.
“Dont” replaces a phrase with “de”, for example with “parler de” or “avoir besoin de”.
“Où” stands for places and also for time expressions such as “le jour où”.
After a preposition, a form of “lequel” is used for things.
With “ce” in front you get “ce qui”, “ce que” and “ce dont”.

abschnitte.text: If the relative clause is missing its **subject**, you use **qui**: “La femme qui parle est ma prof.” (The woman who is speaking is my teacher.) Here “qui” is the subject of “parle”. If, on the other hand, the **direct object** is missing, you use **que**: “L'homme que tu vois est mon oncle.” (The man you see is my uncle.) The subject is “tu”, and “l'homme” is what you see. A trick: if a subject such as tu or je follows straight after, que is usually right.

The pronoun **dont** replaces a phrase with **de**. Many verbs require de, for example “parler de” (to talk about) or “avoir besoin de” (to need). That is why you say: “Le livre dont je parle est passionnant.” In English this is “the book I am talking about”. Dont is short and practical, because it already contains “de”.

As a relative pronoun, **où** stands for a **place**: “La ville où je suis né s'appelle Genève.” In English that is “the town where I was born is called Geneva”. Unlike in German, où is also used after **time expressions**: “Le jour où il est arrivé, il neigeait.” (On the day when he arrived, it was snowing.) After “le moment” or “l'année” you also say où.

After a preposition such as avec, pour or sur, a form of **lequel** is used for things. It agrees with the word it refers to: lequel, laquelle, lesquels, lesquelles. “Le stylo avec lequel j'écris est bleu.” (The pen I am writing with is blue.) With “à” the forms merge: auquel, auxquels, auxquelles. That is why you say “Les amies auxquelles je pense sont en vacances.” (The friends I am thinking of are on holiday.) With people “à qui” is also possible.

abschnitte.titel: Ce qui, ce que, ce dont
abschnitte.text: If there is no noun to refer to, you put **ce** in front. Here ce means “what” or “the thing that”. “Ce qui me plaît, c'est la musique” (what I like is music): here the subject of “plaît” is missing. “Ce que je veux, c'est dormir” (what I want is to sleep): here the object is missing. “Ce dont j'ai besoin, c'est du repos” (what I need is rest): here “avoir besoin de” requires the word dont.

gewusst: In German you say “der Tag, an dem” (the day on which); in French simply “le jour où”.
The word “dont” comes from Latin and originally meant “from where”.

teile.einleitung: Kleidung is called clothes in English. You need the words for it when shopping, when packing for the holidays and when describing what someone is wearing.
wichtigste: Shoes means Schuhe, socks means Socken.
Jacket means Jacke, dress means Kleid.
In British English the German “Hose” is called trousers.
Scarf means Schal, hat means Hut, gloves means Handschuhe.
Kleidung is called clothes and is always plural.
With wear you say what someone has on: She is wearing a dress.

abschnitte.text: The word for Kleidung is **clothes**. It exists only in the **plural**, so you say “My clothes are wet”. The most important items include a **T-shirt**, a **pullover** or **jumper** and a **jacket**. A **dress** is a Kleid, a **skirt** a Rock.

In **British English** a Hose is called **trousers**. In **American English** it is called **pants**. In Great Britain, however, pants means underpants, so you have to be careful. Jeans and shorts are also kinds of trousers. All these words are always plural, even when it is only one item.

Some items of clothing come in pairs: **shoes**, **socks** and **gloves**. If you want to count them, you say **a pair of**: a pair of socks, two pairs of shoes. With trousers, too, you say **a pair of trousers**, although it is only one item. The two trouser legs are the reason for this.

In a Swiss winter you need warm things. A **scarf** is a Schal, a **hat** a Hut. A warm knitted hat is often called a **woolly hat** or **beanie**. Then there are **gloves** and a warm **coat**. For rain there is the **raincoat** and **boots**.

With **wear** you say what someone has on: “He is wearing a blue jacket.” For getting dressed you say **put on**, for getting undressed **take off**. “Put on your shoes!” is something parents often say. In a shop you ask: “Can I **try** it **on**?” If something is too big, you say “It's too big”.

gewusst: Clothes and cloth are different words: cloth means fabric or a piece of material.
The word pullover was borrowed into German, but in Great Britain many people call it a jumper.
